title: Step 0: Task Design and BIDS/fMRIPrep Ingestion
section: Practical Considerations, Pre-Flight QC Checklist, and Handoff to Step 1
text:
Practical Considerations, Pre-Flight QC Checklist, and Handoff to Step 1
Before passing sub_obj into estimate_crossrun_hrf() (Step 1):

Screen high-motion runs via $confounds$summary: Runs with pct_censored > 25–30% or very short contiguous unmasked segments (< 15–20 TRs) carry limited effective degrees of freedom; consider excluding severely corrupted individual runs before cross-fitting (retaining the participant if \(\ge 2\) clean runs remain, or falling back to single-run sub-block cross-fitting if 1 clean run remains).
Verify event onset units and bounds: Check range(sub_obj$events$onset) per run. Event times must be in seconds (never TR indices or milliseconds) and fall within \([0, (T_r - 1)\cdot\text{TR} + \text{time\_offset}]\). Events occurring within the final 4–6 seconds of a run before scanner shutoff have truncated causal HRF support and will be gated automatically by Step 3’s min_bold_coverage rule.
Verify condition tables across runs: Confirm via table(sub_obj$events$run, sub_obj$events$condition) that your target_condition appears with consistent spelling in every task run and that missed/timeout occurrences are labeled distinctly rather than dropped.
Scope handoff: Step 0 assembles validated, clock-aligned run matrices, spatial metadata, censoring masks, and complete event schedules without fitting any statistical parameters; out-of-sample HRF identification and \(\text{AR}(p)\) noise estimation begin in Step 1. For side-by-side visual examples of dummy-volume clock shifts and TR-index onset errors, see the Visual QC and Troubleshooting Gallery.



Mathematical & Simulation Details


Non-aggressive ICA-AROMA oblique projector (apply_aroma()): Let \(M \in \mathbb{R}^{T_r \times C}\) denote a run’s MELODIC mixing matrix partitioned into accepted components \(M_{\text{acc}}\) and rejected noise components \(M_{\text{rej}}\) (classification == "rejected"), and let \(\tilde{M} = M - \mathbf{1}\bar{m}_I^\top\) center each component on the fitting frame index set \(I\) (all frames when fit_valid = FALSE, or valid_rows when fit_valid = TRUE). apply_aroma(..., mode = "nonaggressive") solves the SVD-stabilized joint least-squares system \([\mathbf{1}, \tilde{M}][\hat{\mu}^\top; \hat{B}^\top]^\top = Y\) on \(I\) and subtracts only the centered rejected block across all \(T_r\) rows (preserving each voxel’s baseline mean \(\hat{\mu}\) while avoiding intercept shifts when component sample means are nonzero): \[
Y_{\text{nonagg}} = Y - \tilde{M}_{\text{rej}}\hat{B}_{\text{rej}} = P_{\text{aroma}} Y + (I - P_{\text{aroma}})\mathbf{1}\hat{\mu}^\top, \qquad P_{\text{aroma}} = I - \tilde{M}_{\text{rej}}\bigl[(\tilde{M}^\top \tilde{M})^+ \tilde{M}^\top\bigr]_{\text{rej}}.
\] When aroma_clean_nuisance = TRUE, read_fmriprep_confounds() applies the identical partial-regression operator \(P_{\text{aroma}}\) (followed by column re-centering and rank pruning) to the selected nuisance matrix \(Z_r\) so subsequent joint nuisance projection in Steps 1–2 operates strictly within the AROMA-cleaned subspace (Lindquist et al., 2019). By contrast, mode = "aggressive" applies the orthogonal projector \(I - \tilde{M}_{\text{rej}}(\tilde{M}_{\text{rej}}^\top \tilde{M}_{\text{rej}})^+ \tilde{M}_{\text{rej}}^\top\), which strips neural signal proportional to \(\tilde{M}_{\text{rej}}^\top x_{\text{task}} \neq 0\).
Part 1 (Design & Jitter Benchmarks): 20 Monte Carlo replications per condition (TR = 1.0 s, generating HRF peak 3.13 s, AR(1) \(\rho = 0.45\), 6 voxels in Target_Parcel with cue response \(1.2 + 0.45 c_i\) and feedback response \(0.9 + 0.60\,\text{RPE}_i\), 6 voxels in CueOnly_Parcel with cue response \(1.4 + 0.55 c_i\) and zero feedback response, \(\operatorname{Cor}(c_i, \text{RPE}_i) = 0.50\)). Run-structure comparisons hold total trials fixed at 60 (1×60, 2×30, 3×20, 4×15) with elevated noise on Run 1 (2.1× baseline SD) to reflect realistic inter-run scan quality variation.
Part 2 (On-Disk BIDS + fMRIPrep Ingestion): Builds a complete temporary BIDS + fMRIPrep subject directory (3 runs \(\times\) 240 4D NIfTI volumes, 3D masks, 2-parcel atlas.nii.gz, *_bold.json, *_desc-confounds_timeseries.tsv with 4 non_steady_state_outlier columns and FD spikes, and *_events.tsv with 18 trials/run including 3 "missed_feedback" timeouts and "n/a" tokens) and ingests it live via read_fmriprep_subject().
Part 3 (On-Disk fMRIPost-AROMA Benchmark): Builds a 3-run BIDS + fMRIPrep (space-MNI152NLin6Asym_res-2) + sibling derivatives/fmripost-aroma/ (*_res-2_desc-melodic_mixing.tsv + *_desc-aroma_metrics.tsv, 2 accepted neural ICs + 6 rejected motion ICs including IC_3 correlated \(r = 0.62\) with convolved feedback RPE, shared physiological csf/white_matter noise contaminated by motion ICs, and AR(1) \(\sigma_{\text{obs}} = 0.030\), \(\rho = 0.45\)) subject and runs all four AROMA/confound regimes end to end through Steps 0–3.

title: Step 1: Cross-Run HRF and Noise Estimation
text:
Overview
In task fMRI, neural events are observed through a regional hemodynamic response function (HRF) that delays and smooths activity over 15–30 seconds, superimposed on serially correlated scanner and physiological noise. Both properties vary across brain territories and scans: sensory and subcortical regions often peak 1–2 seconds earlier than association cortex, while CSF-adjacent cortex exhibits stronger temporal autocorrelation than deep gray matter.
Step 1 (hrf_library() + estimate_crossrun_hrf()) estimates both components before deconvolution begins. To keep vascular shape estimation independent of the noise in the run being deconvolved, Step 1 uses leave-one-run-out cross-fitting: for each target run \(r\), it evaluates a physiological library of candidate HRFs using only the participant’s other runs (\(s \neq r\)), pools shape evidence across parcels or local cortical neighborhoods, and forms a regularized composite HRF that shrinks smoothly back toward a canonical reference where task signal is weak. Holding that cross-fitted HRF fixed, Step 1 then estimates run \(r\)’s own stationary \(\text{AR}(p)\) noise parameters on task-adjusted residuals.
library(medusa)

candidates <- hrf_library(tr = tr, preset = "medusa")
hrf_fit <- estimate_crossrun_hrf(
  bold            = bold,
  events          = events,
  tr              = tr,
  kernel_grid     = candidates,
  spatial_groups  = parcel_ids,
  pooling         = "parcel",
  amplitude_model = "auto",
  selection_mode  = "soft_average",
  noise_pcs       = "auto"
)
The walkthrough below develops Step 1 across five substeps—from defining a physiological HRF basis manifold (1.1), to cross-run candidate scoring across condition, modulator, and Empirical-Bayes fractional-ridge trial models (1.2), SNR-adaptive spatial evidence pooling (1.3), post-selection \(\text{AR}(p)\) noise estimation (1.4), and cross-validated background noise-pool PC extraction (1.5)—highlighting the modeling choice at each stage.

title: Step 1: Cross-Run HRF and Noise Estimation
section: Goals, Inputs, and Outputs
text:
Goals, Inputs, and Outputs

Goals of Step 1

Estimate regional HRF timing, dispersion, and undershoot out of sample: Learn each target run’s vascular filter from training runs (\(s \neq r\)) so filter selection does not adapt to target-run noise.
Stabilize shape selection in low-SNR regions: Borrow evidence across parcels or geodesic gray-matter neighborhoods and shrink uncertain regions smoothly toward a canonical reference waveform.
Separate hemodynamic shape from serial noise autocorrelation: Fit run-specific \(\text{AR}(p)\) cascade parameters (\(\rho, \psi_1, \dots, \psi_4\)) after projecting out task responses and nuisance drift under the learned HRF.
Bundle forward timing and noise metadata for downstream steps: Record run clocks, observation masks, composite HRFs, and noise parameters in a single "crossrun_hrf" object carried forward into Steps 2–4.



Inputs: What Step 1 Receives and Why



Input
Structure
Why It Is Set Up That Way




bold
Named list of numeric matrices (time × voxel), one per run, or a "medusa_nifti_ts" object from read_nifti_ts() / read_fmriprep_subject()
Keeping runs as separate list elements defines the leave-one-run-out folds (\(s \neq r\)), supports unequal run lengths, and prevents AR filters or HRF convolution tails from crossing run boundaries.


events
Named list of data.frames (onset, optional duration, condition) matching names(bold) (or a combined BIDS event table)
Event timestamps anchor neurovascular delay without needing behavioral or computational trial predictors, keeping downstream hypothesis variables unseen during HRF estimation.


tr & time_offset
Positive scalar TR (s); scalar or per-run acquisition start time (s)
Maps continuous event times in seconds onto discrete acquisition bins with sub-TR fractional interpolation.


kernel_grid
Numeric matrix (L_hrf × K) from hrf_library(), with column 1 as canonical reference
Pre-discretizes normalized candidate HRF waveforms onto the acquisition tr grid for batched evaluation and provides column 1 as a well-defined canonical baseline (fallback_kernel = 1L).


valid_rows, nuisance, & highpass
Optional per-run logical masks (length == nrow(bold[[r]])), numeric nuisance matrices (or "medusa_confounds"), and slow drift cutoff (128 s default)
Marking censored frames with valid_rows = FALSE keeps every retained volume at its true physical timestamp while excluding high-motion frames from regression and likelihood scoring; nuisance and clock-aligned < 1/128 Hz DCT cosine bases remove motion and scanner drift consistently across Steps 1–2.


amplitude_model, hrf_modulators, & fracridge
amplitude_model = c("condition", "trial", "trial_ridge", "auto"); optional event-level modulator names/matrices; fractional-ridge target (0.25)
Governs how training-run event amplitudes are parameterized during HRF scoring—combining crisp condition-mean scoring with optional explicit centered modulators (hrf_modulators) or automatic Empirical-Bayes fractional-ridge trial rescue ("auto") when regions encode zero-mean fluctuations (\(\beta_0 \approx 0\)).


noise_pcs, max_noise_pcs, & noise_pool
"auto" (or integer 0..K), integer cap (10L), and optional background voxel mask/indices/IDs
Extracts GLMdenoise-style cross-validated temporal PCs from task-unrelated background cortex (noise_pcs = "auto") to suppress narrowband aliased physiological and global vascular waves prior to HRF selection and Step 2 deconvolution.


pooling, spatial_groups, & spatial_graph
pooling = c("voxel", "parcel", "graph"); optional parcel vector or "medusa_spatial_graph" from build_spatial_graph()
Specifies how out-of-sample HRF scores and REML noise parameters borrow strength across space—either within nominal parcels ("parcel"), across local 26-connected geodesic neighborhoods ("graph"), or at single voxels ("voxel").

estimate_crossrun_hrf() returns an S3 object of class "crossrun_hrf" whose elements map directly to their roles in Steps 2–4:

The realized HRFs used in Step 2. Storing a waveform matrix per run and voxel accommodates leave-one-run-out folds and represents continuous soft_average blends directly.

Records the candidate weights combining columns of kernel_grid into selected_kernels, making composite HRFs transparent and reproducible.

crumbs: 5  Step 1: Cross-Run HRF and Noise Estimation

title: Step 1: Cross-Run HRF and Noise Estimation
section: Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points
text:
Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points

1.1 Construct a physiological HRF candidate library
Consider a single brief neural impulse at \(t = 0\). In a vascular territory with impulse response \(h\), that event evokes a delayed, smooth BOLD deflection (Figure 5.2). Rather than estimating unconstrained free FIR parameters on noisy runs, hrf_library() spans plausible neurovascular shapes using a low-dimensional family of two-gamma waveforms varied across peak delay, width (dispersion), and post-stimulus undershoot depth (Figure 5.1), placing the standard canonical shape \((6\text{ s}, 1.0, 6)\) in column 1.






Figure 5.1: Three physiological dimensions spanned by hrf_library(..., preset = "medusa") under positive-lobe normalization: peak delay (left), width/dispersion (middle), and post-stimulus undershoot depth including zero-undershoot subcortical shapes (right).









Figure 5.2: Simulated neural event amplitudes (top) and resulting noisy BOLD signals in a fast-HRF versus slow-HRF parcel (bottom) from the Step 1 demonstration (TR = 0.65 s).



Because deconvolution recovers latent amplitudes relative to the scale of \(h\), candidate waveforms require a shared normalization rule. Under preset = "medusa", each candidate is normalized by its positive-lobe sum (\(\sum_{t: h_t > 0} h_t = 1\)). Compared with signed-sum normalization (\(\sum_t h_t = 1\)), positive-lobe normalization keeps the positive BOLD peak comparable between cortical waveforms with a venous undershoot and subcortical waveforms without one (undershoot_ratio = Inf), so regional undershoot differences do not rescale recovered neural amplitudes.
Choice point — Candidate library (preset): Use hrf_library(tr, preset = "medusa") (~44 evenly spaced 3D candidates spanning \(2.5\text{--}8.0\text{ s}\) delays) as the standard choice across cortical and subcortical studies. Switch to preset = "canonical_27" when restricting strictly to cortical delays (\(4.0\text{--}8.0\text{ s}\)) with a fixed undershoot ratio, or pass a 1-column library (candidates[, 1, drop = FALSE]) when benchmarking against a fixed canonical HRF under matched downstream settings.



1.2 Score candidate HRFs out of sample across runs
Suppose a participant completes \(R = 3\) task runs. If we selected the best-fitting HRF on Run 1 and immediately deconvolved Run 1 with that selected filter, random noise peaks in Run 1 would pull the filter toward themselves and inflate apparent trial effects. Instead, for each target run \(r\), estimate_crossrun_hrf() scores the \(K\) library candidates exclusively on training runs \(s \neq r\) (Figure 5.3). Consequently, even strong synthetic perturbations added to bold$run1 leave Run 1’s learned HRF weights unchanged to machine precision (0; Figure 5.4).






Figure 5.3: Cross-fitting separation in a three-run dataset: candidate HRF evidence for target run \(r\) comes strictly from runs \(s \neq r\), while serial noise parameters are refit on run \(r\) itself.









Figure 5.4: Invariance verification: adding strong synthetic oscillations to target Run 1 leaves its cross-fitted HRF candidate weights completely unchanged.



On each training run \(s \neq r\), MEDuSA whitens usable observations under a first-pass noise filter, projects out nuisance drift, and convolves the event schedule with candidate \(h_m\) to compute degree-of-freedom-adjusted partial \(R^2\) and an effective-DF \(F\)-test (selected_task_p; Figure 5.5). When a dataset contains only a single scan (\(R = 1\)), hrf_single_run_subblocks() replaces cross-run folds with guard-buffered leave-one-subblock-out cross-validation, separating interior sub-blocks by a \(\ge 16\text{ s}\) hemodynamic and \(\text{AR}(p)\) guard zone (isolating any pre-block guard-zone event tails into nuisance carryover columns) and evaluating each held-out sub-block strictly from condition amplitudes and encompassing departures estimated on the remaining sub-blocks.






Figure 5.5: Out-of-sample adjusted partial \(R^2\) surfaces for target Run 1 across the 27-candidate cortical slice (Fast truth: \(4.5\text{ s}, 0.9\); Slow truth: \(7.5\text{ s}, 1.1\); Null: pure \(\text{AR}(3)\) noise). Crosses mark generating parameters.



To build that training regression design, MEDuSA supports four amplitude parameterizations (amplitude_model) alongside optional explicit event modulators (hrf_modulators):

amplitude_model = "condition" (with optional hrf_modulators): Collapses each condition to one mean column per run (plus centered parametric modulator columns when hrf_modulators names event-table columns or per-run matrices, e.g., hrf_modulators = "rpe"). When events evoke a consistent nonzero deflection (\(\beta_0 \neq 0\)) or when key modulators are supplied explicitly, this low-rank design provides maximal degrees of freedom and fastest runtime—while remaining blind to unmodeled zero-mean fluctuations (\(\beta_0 = 0\)) if hrf_modulators is omitted.
amplitude_model = "trial" (unregularized OLS): Assigns a free amplitude to each event (one condition freed at a time). On well-spaced schedules (\(\text{ITI} \gtrsim 4\text{ s}\)) it captures unsigned zero-mean trial variance (Figure 5.6), but under rapid event-related jitter (\(\text{ITI} \lesssim 2.5\text{ s}\)) adjacent trial columns become collinear and span temporal derivatives that can overfit noise.
amplitude_model = "trial_ridge" (Empirical-Bayes REML fractional ridge, fracridge = 0.25): Retains the unpenalized condition-mean (and any hrf_modulators) subspace while modeling orthogonal trial-to-trial deviations via an Empirical-Bayes Gaussian marginal (REML) fractional-ridge profile score (hrf_score_run_fracridge()). Because slower HRFs act as stronger low-pass filters whose top singular subspaces are contained inside faster HRFs, hrf_score_run_fracridge() pairs per-voxel method-of-moments variance-ratio estimation (\(\hat{\gamma}_v\)) with a shared-spectrum Satterthwaite task \(F\)-test and an exact scale-free two-chisquare pairwise likelihood-ratio \(F\)-test projected onto the low-rank Gram subspace \(\operatorname{span}(U_{k_0}, U_j)\) (\(O(r^3)\) rather than \(O(T^3)\))—recovering fast (4.2 s) and slow (7.4 s) HRFs symmetrically under rapid ITIs without collinearity blowup.
amplitude_model = "auto" (recommended general-purpose setting): Scores training runs under "condition" first and automatically adopts "trial_ridge" exclusively on parcels or voxels that lack condition-mean task support on the training runs yet pass candidate-corrected trial_ridge task evidence. Regions with \(\beta_0 \neq 0\) retain crisp condition-mean scoring, while pure zero-mean signed modulator regions (\(\beta_0 = 0\)) are rescued automatically—preventing spurious multi-second vascular latency artifacts downstream and keeping modulated regions out of the background noise pool (Substep 1.5).







Figure 5.6: Zero-mean alternating trial amplitudes (amplitude_model = "condition" vs. "trial" / "auto"): freeing or ridge-scoring trial amplitudes recovers the true \(7.5\text{ s}\) HRF where an unmodulated condition-mean regressor averages out to zero.



Choice point — Training amplitude model (amplitude_model & hrf_modulators): Use amplitude_model = "auto" as the standard general-purpose choice across event-related tasks. When known centered trial modulators are already present in events (and Step-1 modulator conditioning aligns with your analysis plan), passing hrf_modulators = c("rpe", ...) with "condition" or "auto" achieves near-oracle 2-column degrees of freedom; use pure "condition" only when all regions of interest carry nonzero condition-mean responses.



1.3 Pool spatial evidence and form a composite HRF
At the single-voxel level, BOLD noise makes discrete candidate selection jittery across neighboring voxels (Figure 5.7). However, averaging raw BOLD time series across a parcel before scoring HRFs can cancel signals if sub-regions carry opposite task signs. Step 1 resolves this by pooling squared candidate evidence (precision-weighted adjusted partial \(R^2\) profiles) rather than raw time series: voxels with positive and negative task effects both produce positive \(R^2\) peaks at the same vascular delay and reinforce one another cleanly.






Figure 5.7: Voxelwise hard selection vs. parcel-pooled selection across heterogeneous voxel noise levels (0.012 to 0.055). Parcel pooling eliminates noisy single-voxel jumps.



Once pooled candidate scores are combined across training runs, Step 1 converts them into a target-run HRF waveform using three calibrated safeguards:

Training-only spatial noise correlation & finite-parcel Student-\(t\) calibration: Within each parcel, spatial correlation among voxels (group_spatial_cor) is estimated strictly from training-run task-free whitened innovations—taking the minimum of raw innovation correlation and second-difference (\(\Delta^2 z_t\)) correlation so unmodeled smooth trial modulations are attenuated \(>30\times\) rather than mistaken for shared noise—while finite-parcel score-difference ratios (df = V - 1) are mapped to exact Gaussian \(Z\)-equivalents via qnorm(pt(t_diff, df = V - 1)) so compact 3-voxel parcels never suffer heavy-tail \(t_2\) inflation.
SNR- and breadth-adaptive Empirical-Bayes de-shrinking: Regions without calibrated task support across training runs (Null in Figure 5.5 and v17 in Table 5.1) remain at the canonical reference (fallback_prespecified). Conversely, when both parcel spatial breadth and pooled shape-departure \(Z\)-statistics are strong (hrf_adaptive_canonical_strength()), the canonical distance prior decays smoothly as \(O(1 / z_{\text{deshrink}}^2)\) and departure weight \(\omega \to 1\), preventing canonical over-shrinkage on fast (4.3 s) or slow (7.0–7.5 s) territories in multi-region latency cascades.
Soft composite averaging over local sub-grid cones (selection_mode = "soft_average"): Instead of snapping discontinuously to a single grid column ("hard"), compatible candidates and immediate sub-grid bracket neighbors (kernel_cos >= 0.90, \(R^2 \ge 0.90\,R^2_{\max}\)) receive smooth Boltzmann softmax weights—interpolating sub-grid vascular delays cleanly even when pairwise encompassing tests reject individual grid endpoints alone (Figure 5.8).







Figure 5.8: Generating HRFs, hard-selected library nodes, and soft_average composite HRFs for the Fast and Slow parcels in Run 1.

Choice point — Spatial pooling (pooling) and composite rule (selection_mode): Pair selection_mode = "soft_average" with the spatial pooling mode matched to your representation:

pooling = "parcel" (with spatial_groups = parcel_ids) pools uniformly within predefined ROIs or homogeneous parcels. By default (min_parcel_voxels = 5L), parcels with fewer than 5 voxels retain the canonical fallback waveform to avoid noisy small-parcel switches; lower min_parcel_voxels explicitly (e.g., 2L or 3L) when targeting tiny subcortical nuclei at standard \(2\text{--}3\text{ mm}\) resolution.
pooling = "graph" (with parcel_boundary = "soft") on volumetric "medusa_nifti_ts" inputs builds a 26-connected in-mask geodesic lattice graph (build_spatial_graph()), pooling candidate profiles bilaterally across concordant gray-matter neighbors while stopping at sulcal CSF gaps and functional borders (see Spatial Graph Pooling).
pooling = "voxel" keeps single-voxel HRF fits for task-supported voxels (using parcel fallback on low-SNR voxels when an atlas is attached).




1.4 Refit run-specific \(\text{AR}(p)\) noise covariance on task-adjusted residuals
With each target run’s out-of-sample HRF \(\hat{h}^{(-r)}\) fixed, the final substep estimates run \(r\)’s own serial noise structure. Why wait until after HRF selection to estimate noise? Evoked BOLD waves evolve slowly over time; if residuals were formed under a misspecified canonical HRF (for example, applying a \(6.0\text{ s}\) kernel to a \(4.5\text{ s}\) Fast region), unmodeled task-timing mismatch would leak into the residuals and bias estimated autocorrelation upward.
Using \(\hat{h}^{(-r)}\), estimate_crossrun_hrf() projects out run intercept/trend, user nuisance columns, slow \(<1/128\text{ Hz}\) cosine drift terms (discrete cosine transform, DCT), free-trial responses, and HRF Taylor derivatives, then performs a two-pass pooled REML fit within contiguous unmasked segments of valid_rows[[r]]. Under noise_model = "ar1", this fits a stationary \(\text{AR}(1) \times \text{AR}(q)\) cascade \((1 - \rho B)(1 - \sum_{j=1}^q \psi_j B^j)\varepsilon_t = u_t\) (\(q \le 4\) selected adaptively for multiband sampling rates). As shown in Table 5.2 and Figure 5.9, refitting under the cross-fitted HRF recovers the true \(\text{AR}(3)\) cascade (\(\rho = 0.65, \psi_1 = 0.20, \psi_2 = -0.30\)) accurately across Fast, Slow, and Null parcels and whitens residual autocorrelation across all lags.

Choice point — Serial noise model (noise_model): Keep noise_model = "ar1" with evidence = "calibrated"; at fast TRs it automatically accommodates higher-order oscillatory physiological autocorrelation through \(\psi_1\)–\(\psi_4\) while collapsing cleanly to first-order \(\text{AR}(1)\) at slower TRs.



1.5 Suppress narrowband physiological and global vascular noise via cross-validated background PCs (noise_pcs = "auto")
In multiband and whole-cortex acquisitions without external pulse-oximeter or respiratory-belt recordings (RETROICOR), aliased cardiac (~0.25–0.35 Hz) and respiratory (~0.15–0.25 Hz) oscillations plus slow systemic vascular waves span dozens of parcels simultaneously. Because Step 2 deconvolution applies an inverse hemodynamic gain \(|H(\omega)|^{-1}\) that rises \(6\text{--}9\times\) across 0.15–0.30 Hz, removing spatially pervasive physiological fluctuations in BOLD time-series space before deconvolution is far more powerful than relying solely on post-deconvolution parcel covariance modeling.
Adapting the GLMdenoise principle (Kay et al., 2013) to MEDuSA’s cross-run operator framework, noise_pcs = "auto" (hrf_identify_noise_pool() + hrf_extract_cv_noise_pcs()) constructs run-specific nuisance principal components under four strict anti-leakage and anti-overfitting guards:

Active-parcel and edge-PSF exclusion (hrf_identify_noise_pool()): When noise_pool = NULL, the noise pool is restricted to task-uninformative cortex (status == "fallback_prespecified"), excluding any parcel containing a supported voxel (including parcels rescued by amplitude_model = "auto"), excluding immediate spatial-graph neighbors of active voxels to block point-spread-function bleed, and requiring at least 24 background voxels across 8 parcels in "auto" mode so compact ROI cohorts never incur small-pool Global Signal Regression (GSR) negative correlations (Murphy et al., 2009). Users may also pass an explicit noise_pool (logical mask, integer indices, or voxel IDs, e.g., eroded WM/CSF or non-task cortex).
Broadband AR(1) prewhitening without resonant notch suppression: Background series are prewhitened by scalar AR(1) (rho clamped to [-0.80, 0.80]) rather than higher-order AR(4) filters, ensuring narrowband cardiac and respiratory harmonics remain prominent in the singular spectrum rather than being notched out prior to SVD.
Four-stage selection of \(K^* \in \{0, \dots, \text{max\_noise\_pcs}\}\): Candidate temporal PCs must pass (i) the Gavish–Donoho (2014) aspect-ratio optimal singular-value threshold, (ii) Owen–Perry (2009) 2-fold spatial bi-cross-validation reducing out-of-sample residual MSE on held-out background parcels, (iii) an exact Beta-distribution task-orthogonality guard (\(R^2_{\text{task}} \le q_{\text{Beta}}(0.99)\) against convolved task designs), and (iv) orthogonal division-of-labor gates requiring temporal delocalization (top3_share <= 0.22, leaving transient framewise motion spikes to Step 2’s rwls = "auto") and spectral/temporal coherence (max_acf >= 0.28 or periodogram crest factor >= 11.0, leaving temporally white spatial covariance to Step 4/6’s poet_covreg). On pure spatially independent AR(1) noise, \(K^* = 0\) is selected cleanly with zero degrees-of-freedom loss.
Within-run spatial cross-fitting & target-run isolation: During Step 1 HRF scoring, single-run noise PCs are extracted strictly within each run \(r\) (bold[r] only, preserving exact bitwise target-run exclusion) and scored via 2-fold spatial cross-fitting across disjoint halves of pool_voxels so no background voxel is ever evaluated against an in-sample PC containing its own noise; in Step 2 (deconvolve_crossrun_hrf()), cross-run hrf_fit$selections refines the noise pool before pre-projecting the selected PCs alongside < 1/128 Hz DCT drift.

title: Step 1: Cross-Run HRF and Noise Estimation
section: Recommended Settings
text:
Recommended Settings
Putting all four substeps together on preprocessed NIfTI/fMRIPrep inputs:

library(medusa)

# 0. Stream preprocessed 4D NIfTI runs + fMRIPrep confounds & BIDS events
#    (or call read_fmriprep_subject() to bundle BOLD, masks, confounds, and events in one call)
ts <- read_nifti_ts(
  niftis = c(run1 = "sub01_run1.nii.gz", run2 = "sub01_run2.nii.gz", run3 = "sub01_run3.nii.gz"),
  mask   = "sub01_mask.nii.gz",
  atlas  = "schaefer200.nii.gz",
  tr     = tr
)
conf <- read_fmriprep_confounds(
  c("sub01_run1_desc-confounds_timeseries.tsv",
    "sub01_run2_desc-confounds_timeseries.tsv",
    "sub01_run3_desc-confounds_timeseries.tsv"),
  bold                 = ts,
  strategy             = "24p",
  fd_threshold         = 0.3,
  motion_bandstop_bpm  = c(12, 20),   # optional respiratory notch for fast TRs (TR <= 1.0 s)
  motion_filter_target = "fd_only"
)

# 1. Build the 3D physiological HRF manifold (~44 candidates, positive-lobe normalized)
candidates <- hrf_library(tr = ts$tr, preset = "medusa")

# 2. Cross-fit HRF shapes across runs, extract CV noise-pool PCs, and refit own-run AR(p) noise
hrf_fit <- estimate_crossrun_hrf(
  bold            = ts,
  events          = events,
  kernel_grid     = candidates,
  nuisance        = conf,
  pooling         = "graph",          # or "parcel" for uniform ROI pooling
  parcel_boundary = "soft",
  amplitude_model = "auto",           # condition scoring + automatic REML fracridge rescue
  fracridge       = 0.25,
  noise_model     = "ar1",
  noise_pcs       = "auto",           # cross-validated background noise-pool PCs (0..10)
  evidence        = "calibrated",
  selection_mode  = "soft_average",
  return_scores   = TRUE
)

title: Step 1: Cross-Run HRF and Noise Estimation
section: Practical Considerations, Special Regimes, and Diagnostics
text:
Practical Considerations, Special Regimes, and Diagnostics

Single-run sessions and resting/baseline runs
When a participant has only a single task run (length(bold) == 1L), estimate_crossrun_hrf() automatically partitions usable observations into temporal sub-blocks separated by a \(\ge 16\text{ s}\) hemodynamic/AR guard buffer (hrf_single_run_subblocks(), 3 blocks when \(n_{\text{valid}} \ge 150\), 2 halves otherwise, isolating pre-block guard-zone event tails into carryover nuisance columns), scores candidate shapes strictly out-of-sample via Leave-One-Subblock-Out (LOBO) cross-validation with Bartlett-calibrated sub-block compatibility checks, and returns a single continuous HRF for the intact run. Runs with zero task events (such as resting-state scans) are also accepted and receive the canonical reference HRF alongside pure-nuisance \(\text{AR}(p)\) noise estimates.


Respiratory motion filtering for fast-TR censoring
In fast-TR multiband acquisitions (\(\text{TR} = 0.60\text{--}1.0\text{ s}\)), volume realignment resolves normal breathing (\(12\text{--}20\text{ breaths/min} \approx 0.20\text{--}0.33\text{ Hz}\)): chest-wall motion perturbs the \(B_0\) field along the phase-encoding axis and produces rhythmic \(0.25\text{--}0.45\text{ mm}\) fluctuations in raw Power (2012) framewise displacement (FD) even when the head is still (Fair et al., 2020; Gratton et al., 2020). Censoring raw fast-TR FD at \(0.30\text{ mm}\) can fragment valid_rows into short islands and reduce downstream trial retention, whereas simply raising fd_threshold to \(0.60\text{ mm}\) misses genuine sub-millimeter head jerks.
read_fmriprep_confounds() (and read_fmriprep_subject()) addresses this cleanly by applying zero-phase forward-backward frequency filtering (which removes oscillatory respiratory frequencies without shifting movement timing) to the 6 rigid-body realignment parameters before computing FD:

Choice of filter: motion_bandstop_bpm = c(12, 20) applies a narrowband band-stop (notch) filter that removes the breathing frequency band while preserving sharp step displacements on their original millimeter FD scale (pair with standard fd_threshold = 0.30). Alternatively, motion_lowpass_hz = 0.20 applies a smooth low-pass filter (Butterworth; pair with a proportionally lower fd_threshold = 0.15–0.20, following Gratton et al., 2020).
Keeping nuisance regressors unfiltered (motion_filter_target = "fd_only"): Because standard fMRIPrep BOLD volumes retain real respiratory \(B_0\) signal fluctuations, "fd_only" filters motion only for FD censoring while keeping unfiltered 24p/36p regressors in $nuisance so Steps 1–2 project respiratory \(B_0\) variance out of BOLD. (At slower TRs near the Nyquist boundary or on BrainGnomes files that already carry framewise_displacement_filtered, read_fmriprep_confounds() adapts or reuses filtered FD automatically.)
Combining with non-aggressive ICA-AROMA: When fMRIPost-AROMA or legacy ICA-AROMA mixing matrices are available, read_fmriprep_subject(..., aroma = "nonaggressive", strategy = "csf_wm", motion_bandstop_bpm = c(12, 20), fd_threshold = 0.3) computes respiratory-filtered FD on the physical 6-parameter motion estimates before AROMA partial regression so abrupt spin-history jerks are still masked via valid_rows, while avoiding 24/36-parameter collinearity with AROMA components; see Step 0 §0.5.

Diagnostic checklist and scope handoff to Step 2
Before passing hrf_fit to deconvolve_crossrun_hrf() (Step 2):

Check cross-fitting provenance: Confirm hrf_fit$training_runs lists non-target runs \(s \neq r\) and review hrf_fit$signal_status.
Plot realized waveforms (hrf_fit$selected_kernels): Under soft_average, selections$kernel_index identifies only the top-weight library column, whereas selected_kernels shows the actual composite HRF used in Step 2.
Check hrf_fit$noise for stationarity boundary hits: Widespread \(\hat{\rho} = 0.90\) estimates typically point to unmodeled scanner drift, uncensored motion spikes, or omitted task events (see Pair 1 in the Visual QC Gallery).
Scope boundary: Step 1 estimates the forward neurovascular filter and serial noise structure without modifying bold or evaluating behavioral trial hypotheses; continuous latent signal reconstruction begins in Step 2.



Mathematical Details & Reproduction


Cross-fitted evidence pooling & Empirical-Bayes REML fractional-ridge scoring: For candidate \(m\) on training run \(s \neq r\), whitened nuisance-orthogonalized BOLD \(y_{s,\perp}\) is regressed onto whitened candidate design \(X_{s,m,\perp}\) (rank \(d_{s,m}\) over \(m_s\) valid frames), yielding adjusted partial \(R^2_{s,m} = 1 - (1 - R^2_{s,m})\frac{m_s - p_Z}{m_s - p_Z - d_{s,m}}\). Under amplitude_model = "trial_ridge" (and "auto" rescue), orthogonal trial deviations \(\tilde{X}_{d,m} = U_{d,m}\operatorname{diag}(s_{d,m})V_{d,m}^\top\) with column-standardized eigenvalues \(\tilde{s}_{m,j}^2\) are scored via the Gaussian marginal REML log-likelihood gain \(\ell_{\text{gain},m}(v) = -\frac{1}{2}\bigl[\nu\log(q_{m,v}/\|y_{\perp,v}\|_2^2) + r_c + \sum_j \log(1 + \hat{\gamma}_v \tilde{s}_{m,j}^2)\bigr]\) (\(R^2_{\text{REML},m} = 1 - \exp(-2\ell_{\text{gain},m}/\nu)\)), while pairwise candidate tests (fallback_p, incompatible_p) evaluate exact scale-free Satterthwaite two-chisquare \(F\)-ratios on the low-rank Gram subspace \(\operatorname{span}(U_{k_0}, U_j)\) under \(H_{k_0}: Y \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 \Sigma_{k_0}(\gamma_{\text{pair}}))\).
SNR-adaptive soft-average de-shrinking: Compatible candidates and sub-grid bracket neighbors (kernel_cos >= 0.90) receive Boltzmann weights \(w_m \propto \exp\bigl((R^2_m - c_{\text{eff}} d_{m,1}) / (T_{\text{eff}}\Delta R^2)\bigr)\) blended with column 1 ((1 - \omega) e_1 + \omega w), where \(c_{\text{eff}} = c_0 / \bigl(1 + 0.35\max(0, z_{\text{deshrink}} - 2.5)^2\bigr)\) decays canonical pull smoothly as parcel breadth and shape-departure evidence \(z_{\text{deshrink}}\) grow.
Exact gapped covariance: When valid_rows[[r]] masks interior frames, AR estimation restricts lag products strictly within contiguous unmasked runs of frames, while Step 2’s whitener \(W_r\) inverts the exact stationary Toeplitz submatrix \(\Sigma_{\text{AR}}[I_r, I_r]\) on retained timestamps \(I_r\) so multi-TR scrub gaps decay correlation by \(\gamma(|t_a - t_b|)\).
Zero-phase respiratory IIR filtering: For sampling rate \(f_s = 1/\text{TR}\) and stopband \([f_1, f_2] = \text{BPM}/60\) (\(f_0 = (f_1 + f_2)/2\), \(\Delta f = f_2 - f_1\), \(Q = f_0/\Delta f\), \(\omega_0 = 2\pi f_0/f_s\), \(\alpha = \sin\omega_0/(2Q)\)), read_fmriprep_confounds() designs the RBJ biquad notch transfer function \(H(z) = \frac{1 - 2\cos\omega_0 z^{-1} + z^{-2}}{(1 + \alpha) - 2\cos\omega_0 z^{-1} + (1 - \alpha)z^{-2}}\) (or bilinear-warped Butterworth poles for motion_lowpass_hz) and applies forward-backward Direct Form II Transposed filtering (filtfilt) with steady-state initial conditions and reflection padding to all 6 realignment parameters before computing Power (2012) FD.

title: Step 2: Event-Informed Continuous Deconvolution
text:
Overview
Given each run’s cross-fitted HRF and serial noise model from Step 1, Step 2 (deconvolve_crossrun_hrf()) reconstructs a continuous latent neural activity time series \(\widehat{a}_r(t)\) on the original acquisition grid for every run and voxel. Because hemodynamic convolution smooths rapid neural fluctuations over 15–30 seconds, Step 2 solves a smoothness-penalized, \(\text{AR}(p)\)-whitened generalized least squares (GLS) inverse problem that recovers continuous neural dynamics while controlling high-frequency noise amplification.
The defining feature of MEDuSA’s Step 2 is its event-informed continuous architecture: the latent time series \(\widehat{a}_r(t)\) itself is estimated continuously and unconstrained across the entire run, while an auxiliary event-informed GLS regression model calibrates the three quantities that govern inversion quality—(1) task-free observation-noise scaling (scaling = "noise_sd"), (2) neural-safe downweighting of transient scanner glitches (rwls = "auto"), and (3) SNR-stratified cross-run smoothing (lambda_mode = "auto").
library(medusa)

decon <- deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(
  bold          = bold,
  hrf_fit       = hrf_fit,
  scaling       = "noise_sd",
  penalty       = "sobolev",
  lambda_mode   = "auto",
  rwls          = "auto",
  nuisance_mode = "preproject",
  noise_pcs     = "auto"
)
The five substeps below develop this estimator from the basic continuous GLS inverse (2.1), through observation-noise standardization (2.2), adaptive glitch weighting (2.3), and SNR-stratified smoothing (2.4), culminating in a direct comparison between event-informed continuous GLS and blind deconvolution (2.5).

title: Step 2: Event-Informed Continuous Deconvolution
section: Goals, Inputs, and Outputs
text:
Goals, Inputs, and Outputs

Goals of Step 2

Recover continuous, unconstrained latent neural time courses: Estimate a time × voxel activity matrix \(\widehat{a}_r\) on the intact acquisition grid via prewhitened penalized GLS.
Standardize voxels and runs by pure observation noise: Estimate marginal observation-noise SD (\(\hat{\sigma}_{\text{marg}}\)) from task-projected GLS residuals (scaling = "noise_sd") so strong task activation does not compress recovered amplitudes.
Downweight transient non-task glitches safely: Attenuate isolated sub-scrubbing motion or RF spikes (rwls = "auto") while leaving genuine high-amplitude neural bursts unclipped.
Adapt regularization (lambda) to regional task SNR: Tune smoothness automatically across runs while grouping voxels from quiet background cortex up to strong task foci so noisier regions receive stronger smoothing (lambda_mode = "auto").
Carry exact linear operator metadata into Steps 3–6: Package activity together with scaling, task-free noise_innovations, frame_weights, and (HRF, AR, lambda) stratum keys so downstream steps de-mix overlapping epochs and propagate analytical standard errors.



Inputs: What Step 2 Receives and Why



Input
Structure
Why It Is Set Up That Way




bold
Named list of time × voxel numeric matrices (or "medusa_nifti_ts" object) matching hrf_fit
Aligns each run’s observations 1-to-1 with its cross-fitted HRFs, valid_rows masks, and \(\text{AR}(p)\) noise parameters from Step 1.


hrf_fit
"crossrun_hrf" S3 object from estimate_crossrun_hrf()
Supplies out-of-sample selected_kernels, own-run noise cascades, out-of-sample task-SNR summaries (selections), events, nuisance, and valid_rows.


scaling
"noise_sd" (recommended), "zscore", "demean", "psc", or "none"
Standardizes each run and voxel before applying the roughness penalty so a shared \(\lambda\) carries a consistent bias–variance meaning across units of differing gain.


penalty
"sobolev" (recommended), "diff2", "diff1", "matern1", or "ridge"
Defines the symmetric positive semi-definite roughness matrix \(P\) governing how rapid fluctuations and baseline drift are penalized.


lambda, lambda_mode, & lambda_grid
NULL (auto-tuned), scalar, or length-\(V\) vector; lambda_mode = c("auto", "global", "stratified")
Controls smoothing strength, tuned automatically across runs over lambda_grid = 10^seq(-2, 1, length.out = 16) either globally or across monotone task-SNR tiers.


rwls, nuisance_mode, highpass, & noise_pcs
rwls = "auto"; nuisance_mode = c("preproject", "ignore", "joint"); highpass = 128; noise_pcs = "auto"
Govern transient glitch weighting (rwls), clock-aligned pre-orthogonalization of < 1/128 Hz DCT drift, nuisance confounds, and cross-validated background noise-pool PCs (noise_pcs = "auto") prior to \(|H(\omega)|^{-1}\) inversion, and exclusion of valid_rows == FALSE frames (observation_mask = "fit").





Outputs: What Step 2 Produces and Why It Is Set Up That Way
deconvolve_crossrun_hrf() returns an S3 "crossrun_decon" object designed to be passed intact into Step 3 (decon_epoch_regression()):



Output Component
Structure
Why It Is Set Up That Way




activity
Named list of n_time × n_voxels matrices (with tr, time_offset, and observation_mask attributes)
Retains the full acquisition grid—even across interior censored frames—so event timestamps and continuous diagnostics stay aligned to run seconds.


scaling
Named list of per-run data.frames (voxel, center, scale, noise_sd, lambda, status)
Records the pre-deconvolution divisor (scale), marginal observation-noise SD (noise_sd), and per-voxel penalty (lambda), enabling Step 3 to restore physical BOLD units (restore_scale = TRUE) and propagate exact SEs.


noise_innovations, bold_obs, & whitened_sketch
Named lists of task-free whitened residuals and uncensored BOLD (\(\le 16{,}384\) voxels) or compact \(m_r \times 64\) subspace sketches (\(> 16{,}384\) voxels)
Captures spatial and dynamic error structure without retaining full 4D BOLD arrays in memory, enabling bold-free Adaptive-POET + covariance-regression shared-error estimation in Steps 3–6.


frame_weights
Named list of length-n_valid_rows vectors in \((0, 1]\)
Preserves any adaptive rwls glitch weights so Step 3 reconstructs the exact weighted inverse operator and error covariance.


hrf_fit, settings, voxel_map, & geometry
Embedded crossrun_hrf + tuning tables (lambda_strata, lambda_tuning) + NIfTI metadata
Allows Steps 3–4 to rebuild stratum operators \(D_r\) on the fly without storing gigabytes of dense \(T_r \times m_r\) matrices in memory, and supports direct NIfTI export via write_nifti_ts().

title: Step 2: Event-Informed Continuous Deconvolution
section: Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points
text:
Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points

2.1 Formulate the continuous prewhitened GLS deconvolution objective
Start with a single run \(r\) and voxel whose centered, standardized usable BOLD observations \(\tilde{y}_{r,o}\) follow the forward convolution model \(\tilde{y}_{r,o} = M_{r,o} H_r a_r + \varepsilon_{r,o}\), where \(H_r\) convolves latent neural activity \(a_r \in \mathbb{R}^{T_r}\) with Step 1’s HRF, \(M_{r,o}\) selects the \(m_r\) unmasked frames (valid_rows[[r]] == TRUE), and \(W_r\) whitens the \(\text{AR}(p)\) error covariance.
Because \(H_r\) acts as a low-pass filter, high-frequency oscillations in \(a_r\) leave convolved BOLD almost unchanged (Figure 6.1). Inverting \(H_r\) with virtually no penalty (lambda = 0.0001) therefore amplifies high-frequency noise dramatically, whereas an overly large penalty (lambda = 3) smooths away phasic peaks (Figure 6.2).






Figure 6.1: High-frequency forward ambiguity: adding rapid alternating neural fluctuations produces virtually identical convolved BOLD.









Figure 6.2: Effect of varying lambda (0.0001, 0.03, 3) on the same noisy BOLD series under the sobolev penalty.



Step 2 estimates \(\widehat{a}_r\) by minimizing the penalized prewhitened GLS objective across the full \(T_r\)-sample run grid: \[
\widehat{a}_r = \arg\min_{a \in \mathbb{R}^{T_r}} \left\| W_r \bigl(\tilde{y}_{r,o} - M_{r,o} H_r a\bigr) \right\|_2^2 + \lambda a^\top P a.
\] Notice that no event timestamps appear inside \(P\) or restrict \(a\): spontaneous inter-trial fluctuations, sustained deliberation plateaus, and brief phasic bursts can occur anywhere on the acquisition clock, and the solution is a linear map \(\widehat{a}_r = D_r \tilde{y}_{r,o}\).






Figure 6.3: Comparison of all five penalty families (ridge, diff1, diff2, matern1, sobolev) on the same run.

Choice point — Roughness penalty (penalty) and nuisance projection (nuisance_mode):

Penalty geometry: penalty = "sobolev" combines a gentle first-difference slope penalty with a strong second-difference curvature penalty (\(0.10 D_1^\top D_1 + 0.90 D_2^\top D_2\), a discrete Sobolev norm) and is recommended as the standard choice. Pure second-difference curvature smoothing ("diff2") leaves global linear ramps unpenalized, whereas pure "ridge" shrinks each time point toward zero without sharing smoothness across neighboring TRs; "sobolev" (and "matern1") gently anchors baseline drift while keeping phasic transitions crisp (Figure 6.3, Table 6.1).
Clock-aligned drift, confound, and noise-pool pre-projection (nuisance_mode = "preproject" & noise_pcs = "auto"): Because the Sobolev penalty vanishes on constant/ultra-slow modes while \(H(0) = 1\), leaving < 1/128 Hz scanner drift or motion confounds unprojected (nuisance_mode = "ignore" on raw BOLD) lets slow drift pass directly into \(\widehat{a}_r(t)\) even though Step 1’s noise_sd excluded drift variance—inflating trial variance without matching se_demixed. Conversely, projecting nuisance columns jointly inside \((A_r^\top A_r + P_\lambda)^{-1}\) (nuisance_mode = "joint") can amplify collinear slow neural modes. nuisance_mode = "preproject" (automatic default whenever nuisance, highpass = 128, or noise_pcs are active) orthogonalizes [1, linear_trend, DCT(< 1/128 Hz), nuisance, noise_pcs] on valid_rows before continuous deconvolution and carries that exact projection into Step 3 (decon_epoch_regression()), diagnose_crossrun_recovery(), and Stage-3 poet_covreg. Simultaneously, noise_pcs = "auto" projects out cross-validated background physiological PCs (Step 1 §1.5) before \(|H(\omega)|^{-1}\) amplifies 0.15–0.30 Hz respiratory and aliased cardiac harmonics. Use "ignore" only when BOLD and events were already matched-projected upstream.







Figure 6.4: Joint vs. ignored nuisance handling when drift remains in bold (top) and bridging a masked valid_rows = FALSE artifact window 70–80 s under observation_mask = "fit" (bottom).






2.2 Standardize runs using event-informed marginal noise scaling
Before solving the penalized GLS objective across thousands of voxels, each run and voxel is centered and divided by a reference scale so \(\lambda\) acts comparably everywhere. A common convention in blind deconvolution is whole-run z-scoring (scaling = "zscore"), which divides by total temporal \(\text{SD}(y)\). However, in a strongly task-responsive voxel, \(\text{SD}(y)\) combines background noise and task-evoked BOLD variance—inflating the denominator and compressing recovered neural slopes relative to quieter voxels.
To separate observation noise from task signal without constraining \(\widehat{a}_r\), scaling = "noise_sd" fits an auxiliary event-informed GLS regression containing run drift, user nuisance columns, free per-trial convolved event regressors under Step 1’s HRF, and 1st/2nd HRF Taylor derivatives (absorbing trial-to-trial latency jitter). From the outlier-trimmed, leverage-adjusted residuals of this projection (Winsorized GLS residuals), MEDuSA extracts two quantities:

Uncontaminated marginal observation-noise SD (\(\hat{\sigma}_{\text{marg}}\)): Tracks true background noise uniformly across high-gain, moderate-gain, and null voxels (Figure 6.5 and Table 6.2).
Task-free whitened noise_innovations: Orthonormalized residual series carried forward to measure pure spatial noise correlations in Steps 4 and 6.







Figure 6.5: Comparison of whole-run BOLD SD (zscore), event-informed GLS noise_sd, and true generating observation-noise SD across 8 voxels of varying task gain.

2.3 Guard against transient scanner glitches without clipping neural bursts
Even after binary motion censoring (valid_rows), fMRI runs occasionally contain sub-threshold micro-movements or RF spikes (\(\text{FD} \approx 0.2\text{--}0.3\text{ mm}\)) that would cause oscillatory ringing in an unweighted linear inverse. At the same time, naive outlier downweighting risks mistaking an unusually large, genuine neural response (such as a surprise prediction-error burst) for an artifact.
Under rwls = "auto", Step 2 screens the most task-informative voxels across whole-brain maps (ranking selected_adjusted_partial_r2 up to 4,096 voxels with numerical QR/SVD fallbacks via hrf_safe_svd()), measures cross-voxel residual energy orthogonal to the modeled [trial HRF, dHRF/dt] task subspace, and widens frame tolerance in proportion to the convolved task envelope:

On clean Gaussian runs, a whole-brain tail-energy test calibrated for spatially correlated voxels (via the Liu–Tang–Zhang, 2009 moment approximation) keeps all weights at \(w_t = 1\) so standard unweighted GLS is preserved exactly.
When genuine non-task glitches occur, isolated 1–2 TR spikes are absorbed by adding transient observation-noise variance at only those flagged volumes (\(\Sigma_{\text{AR}} + \operatorname{diag}(\delta^2)\), solved via low-rank Woodbury Sparse Bayesian Learning updates so high-\(\rho\) AR filters do not smear a single-volume spike into neighboring frames), while multi-TR physiological bursts receive smooth innovation-space downweighting—all while keeping \(w_t = 1\) across heavy task-evoked neural bursts.

Choice point — Glitch downweighting (rwls): Leave rwls = "auto" enabled for empirical data; set rwls = "none" only when testing exact unweighted operator identities in synthetic benchmarks.



2.4 Tune smoothing strength (lambda) across task-SNR strata
Choosing \(\lambda\) by ordinary observation-space out-of-sample prediction error—approximated via generalized cross-validation (GCV)—targets BOLD curve fitting rather than downstream trial estimation, and averaging GCV across thousands of task-silent voxels pulls a single global penalty toward oversmoothing.
When lambda = NULL, Step 2 pools prewhitened GCV across usable runs alongside Stage-3 gain-restored trial level/contrast variance and modulation transfer weighted by Step 1’s out-of-sample task SNR (Figure 6.6). Furthermore, on volumetric maps where focal task regions coexist with quiet background cortex, lambda_mode = "auto" stratifies voxels by out-of-sample task SNR and enforces that smoothing never increases as task signal strengthens:

Cross-run false-discovery gate: Combines Step 1 per-run task \(p\)-values across runs (Fisher combination + Benjamini–Hochberg FDR); if no voxels pass \(q \le 0.10\) (e.g., pure-null maps), "auto" collapses safely to one global penalty.
Monotone task-SNR tiers: When focal signal is present, voxels are grouped into a quiet background tier (\(q > 0.20\), graph-stabilized \(R^2 < 0.025\)) and ascending active task-\(R^2\) quantiles (max_lambda_strata = 4L), enforcing \(\lambda_{\text{quiet}} \ge \lambda_{\text{low-SNR}} \ge \dots \ge \lambda_{\text{high-SNR}}\) via a monotone ordering constraint (weighted pool-adjacent-violators, PAVA; see Spatial Graph Pooling).







Figure 6.6: Comparison of raw prewhitened GCV versus MEDuSA’s adaptive task-weighted criterion (top) and the underlying gain-restored level and contrast variance proxies (bottom).



Choice point — Smoothing mode (lambda & lambda_mode): Keep lambda = NULL and lambda_mode = "auto" as the standard choice. Use lambda_mode = "global" (or a fixed scalar lambda) only when holding an identical roughness penalty constant across every voxel in a comparison.



2.5 Why event-informed calibration improves over blind deconvolution
Stepping back across Substeps 2.1–2.4 clarifies how MEDuSA relates to both blind deconvolution (deconvolve_nlreg() / Bush & Cisler, 2013; deconvolve_reglin()) and standard task GLMs:



Method Family
HRF & Noise Model
Scaling Reference
Glitch vs. Burst Handling
Latent Output & Downstream SEs




Blind Nonlinear (deconvolve_nlreg / Bush & Cisler, 2013)
Fixed canonical HRF; unwhitened OLS
Whole-run zscore (mixes task variance into divisor)
Logistic sigmoid squashes all excursions into \((0,1)\)
Bounded nonlinear encoding; no linear operator or analytical trial SEs


Blind Linear (deconvolve_reglin)
Fixed HRF; optional scalar AR(1)
Whole-run zscore or raw \(\Delta^2\)
Unweighted (glitches ring) or GCV oversmoothed by null voxels
Continuous linear series without cross-run HRF, task-free innovations, or epoch de-mixing


Standard Parametric GLM / LSS
Assumed HRF/basis; fixed event boxcars
Residual error
Fixed trial basis; zero neural activity assumed outside events
Scalar trial betas only; no continuous lag-flexible trajectory


MEDuSA Event-Informed Continuous GLS (deconvolve_crossrun_hrf)
Cross-fitted 3D HRF + 2-pass REML \(\text{AR}(p)\)
Event-projected GLS marginal noise_sd
rwls = "auto" downweights non-task glitches while protecting neural bursts
Unconstrained continuous \(\widehat{a}_r(t)\) plus exact operator \(D_r\), noise_innovations, and propagated trial covariance



Figure 6.7 and Table 6.3 demonstrate all of these differences on identical simulated BOLD containing a genuine heavy neural burst at \(65\text{ s}\) (3.8 units) and an isolated non-task scanner glitch at \(124\text{ s}\) (+0.55 BOLD units): event-informed continuous GLS preserves burst height (0.746 vs. 0.676 blind linear) and waveform correlation (0.835 vs. 0.699 Bush nonlinear) while keeping frame weight \(w_t = 1.00\) on the \(65\text{ s}\) burst and cutting \(124\text{ s}\) glitch ringing in half (0.200 vs. 0.391 unweighted).

section: Recommended Settings

Recommended Settings

decon <- deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(
  bold             = bold,
  hrf_fit          = hrf_fit,
  lambda           = NULL,
  lambda_mode      = "auto",
  scaling          = "noise_sd",
  penalty          = "sobolev",
  rwls             = "auto",
  nuisance_mode    = "preproject", # pre-projects < 1/128 Hz DCT drift, nuisance, & noise_pcs
  noise_pcs        = "auto",       # cross-validated background physiological PCs (0..10)
  observation_mask = "fit",
  tail_padding     = 0L
)

# Inspect conditional gain and event cross-talk under your study's schedule:
recovery <- diagnose_crossrun_recovery(decon, lags = 0)

# Optional: stream 4D deconvolved activity or 3D log10(lambda) maps to NIfTI

title: Step 2: Event-Informed Continuous Deconvolution
section: Practical Considerations: Operator Resolution, Boundaries, and Handoff to Step 3
text:
Practical Considerations: Operator Resolution, Boundaries, and Handoff to Step 3

Why continuous activity has finite resolution—and why Step 3 handles de-mixing: Under any positive \(\lambda > 0\), the continuous resolution matrix \(R_r = D_r M_{r,o} H_r\) attenuates isolated impulse height (\(R_{tt} < 1\)) and spreads energy smoothly across neighboring TRs and closely spaced events (Figure 6.8, Figure 6.9). Simply dividing \(\widehat{a}_r\) pointwise by \(R_{tt}\) would amplify side-lobe noise everywhere (Figure 6.8, bottom). Instead, diagnose_crossrun_recovery(decon) audits self-gain and neighbor cross-talk on your event schedule, and passing the full decon object to Step 3 (decon_epoch_regression()) performs matrix de-mixing and gain restoration specifically at the trial epochs of interest.
Bridging censored gaps (observation_mask = "fit"): Across masked frames (70–80 s in Figure 6.4, bottom), the smoothness penalty interpolates cleanly from surrounding unmasked BOLD without letting artifacts corrupt adjacent trials; Step 3 will automatically check causal BOLD support (obs_frac_tau >= 0.20) so deeply masked events are flagged as NA rather than treated as observed data.
Run-end boundaries (tail_padding = 0L) and HRF timing (Figure 6.10): Appending synthetic zero BOLD frames after the end of a run (tail_padding > 0) pulls genuine late-run activity downward, while a 2-second HRF delay misspecification shifts recovered peaks in the opposite direction—confirming the value of tail_padding = 0L and Step 1’s cross-run HRF estimation. For side-by-side visual diagnostics of over-smoothing gain collapse and uncensored motion-spike ringing, see the Visual QC and Troubleshooting Gallery.







Figure 6.8: Impulse resolution curves \(R_{:,91}\) at weak, moderate, and strong \(\lambda\): raw recovery (top) versus scalar division by diagonal gain (bottom).









Figure 6.9: Event-by-event normalized excess cross-talk matrix from diagnose_crossrun_recovery() across 15 Run 1 events.









Figure 6.10: Sensitivity to run-end zero padding (tail_padding = 33L vs. 0L, top) and a 2-second HRF delay misspecification (bottom).





Mathematical Reference & Reproduction

Let \(I_r \subset \{1, \dots, T_r\}\) index the \(m_r\) valid frames (valid_rows[[r]] == TRUE), \(M_{r,o}\) select rows \(I_r\), \(H_r \in \mathbb{R}^{T_r \times T_r}\) be the causal Toeplitz HRF convolution matrix for stratum kernel \(h\), and \(Z_{r,o}\) be the active nuisance basis ([1, trend, nuisance] under nuisance_mode = "joint", empty under "ignore").

Exact gapped whitening & Woodbury SBL: \(W_r = L_r^{-1}\) is the inverse Cholesky factor of the stationary \(\text{AR}(p)\) correlation submatrix \(\Sigma_{\text{AR}}[I_r, I_r]\). Under rwls_space = "woodbury" with transient variances \(\delta_t^2 = (1 - w_t)/w_t\) on flagged frames \(S\), MEDuSA whitens against \(\Sigma_{\text{AR}}[I_r, I_r] + \operatorname{diag}(\delta^2)\) via a rank-\(|S|\) Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury update in \(O(m_r |S|)\) operations. Orthogonalizing \(Q_Z = \operatorname{orth}(W_r Z_{r,o})\) projects out nuisance terms jointly via \(\tilde{W}_r = (I - Q_Z Q_Z^\top) W_r\).
Linear inverse operator: With \(A_r = \tilde{W}_r M_{r,o} H_r\) and penalty \(P_{\lambda} = \lambda P + \epsilon_{\text{ridge}} I_{T_r}\), the frozen inverse operator is \[
D_r = \bigl(A_r^\top A_r + P_{\lambda}\bigr)^{-1} A_r^\top \tilde{W}_r \in \mathbb{R}^{T_r \times m_r},
\] evaluated across voxel batches via Cholesky solves in C++ (backend = "cpp", agreeing with backend = "r" to 2.71e-14), with restore_scale reproducing demean units to 3.11e-15. Internal R helpers implementing Substeps 2.2–2.4 in R/crossrun_hrf.R are hrf_estimate_gls_noise_sd(), hrf_estimate_rwls_weights(), hrf_tune_decon_lambda(), hrf_tune_decon_lambda_stratified(), and hrf_pava_nonincreasing().

title: Step 3: Epoch Alignment, De-Mixing, and Uncertainty Propagation
text:
Overview
Step 2 produces a continuous deconvolved time series \(\widehat{a}_r(t)\) on the acquisition grid, whereas cognitive hypotheses typically concern event-locked trial responses—for example, neural activity across lags \(-2\text{ s}\) to \(+4\text{ s}\) around feedback onset, or sustained deliberation activity across variable reaction times. Because regularized deconvolution smooths slightly across time, simply slicing \(\widehat{a}_r(t)\) at event timestamps yields readouts that combine the target trial’s signal with regularization attenuation and spillover from nearby cues or adjacent trials.
Step 3 (decon_epoch_regression()) converts continuous deconvolved activity into conditionally unbiased, additive-error trial readouts accompanied by exact propagated measurement uncertainties. Passing the forward event schedule through Step 2’s frozen linear operator \(D_r\), it samples requested peri-event lags via smooth local time-averaging (symmetric kernel quadrature), subtracts spillover from non-target events, inverts target-to-target mixing to restore amplitude gain, and propagates \(\text{AR}(p)\) observation noise through the composite operator to deliver per-trial standard errors (se_demixed), Empirical-Bayes precision weights, and optional within-run decorrelated (*_whitened) variables.
library(medusa)

epochs <- decon_epoch_regression(
  deconvolution       = decon,
  covariates          = covariates,
  events              = events,
  target_condition    = "feedback",
  lags                = seq(-2, 4, by = 1),
  restore_scale       = TRUE,
  whiten_panel        = TRUE,
  return_panel        = TRUE
)
Following the same measurement-model progression used in two-step multilevel inference (Vig & Hallquist, 2026), the four substeps below move from defining the event source and readout kernel (3.1), to writing the epoch measurement model and removing non-target bleed (3.2), inverting target mixing onto an additive-error scale (3.3), and propagating trial error covariances and precision weights (3.4).

title: Step 3: Epoch Alignment, De-Mixing, and Uncertainty Propagation
section: Goals, Inputs, and Outputs
text:
Goals, Inputs, and Outputs

Goals of Step 3

Sample peri-event lag trajectories with explicit duration semantics: Read out continuous activity around each target event across requested lags, supporting brief impulses, fixed windows, and RT-matched sustained intervals ("rate" vs. "integral").
Remove non-target spillover and target-to-target mixing: Use the Step 2 operator \(D_r H_r\) to subtract interfering event bleed (demix_other_events) and invert target cross-talk (demix_target_trials) while matching centered predictors through the post-demixing operator \(M_{\text{post}}\).
Propagate observation-noise covariance analytically to every trial: Compute per-trial measurement standard errors (se_demixed) and lag-1 trial error correlations (error_ac1) directly from the composite linear operator without resampling.
Construct stabilized trial precision weights and optional decorrelated panels: Combine propagated measurement error with Empirical-Bayes biological trial variance (\(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2\), stabilized across functionally concordant cortical neighbors on NIfTI maps via "graph_eb") to form cohort-ready weights and decorrelated trial columns.



Inputs: What Step 3 Receives and Why



Input
Structure
Why It Is Set Up That Way




deconvolution
"crossrun_decon" S3 object from deconvolve_crossrun_hrf()
Carries activity together with hrf_fit, scaling, noise_innovations, and frame_weights so Step 3 reconstructs the exact stratum inverse operator \(D_r\) and noise covariance \(\Sigma_r\).


events & target_condition
Run-named list of event data.frames (inherited from hrf_fit by default); character scalar naming target events
Retaining all task events in events while naming target_condition identifies both the target trials to read out and the non-target events (cues, motor responses) whose spillover into target windows should be subtracted.


covariates
NULL (covariate-agnostic panel mode), or numeric matrix/data.frame/formula/column names matching target events
Passing covariates = NULL produces a general-purpose de-mixed panel reusable across many downstream Step 5–6 models; supplying covariates adds within-participant regression tables (coefficients) and paired *_whitened predictor columns.


lags & readout_kernel
Numeric vector of lag offsets in seconds (e.g., seq(-2, 4, by = 1)); "triangle", "linear", "boxcar", or "gaussian"
Evaluates event-locked readouts at arbitrary offsets without resampling BOLD, shifting both the readout window and modeled target source to \(t_i + \tau\).


source_model, trial_durations, & duration_scale
"impulse", "window", or "duration"; optional target durations (s); "rate" or "integral"
Specifies the latent neural waveform represented by each trial amplitude so variable reaction times can be modeled either as firing height ("rate") or time-integrated activity ("integral").


demix_other_events, other_event_model, demix_target_trials, & demix_within_trial
Logical flags + other_event_model = c("auto", "trial", "condition"), demix_ridge (0.05), & within_trial_ridge (0.06)
Separately control collateral non-target subtraction ("auto" switches cleanly to GCV-stabilized joint (T, O) trial-level subtraction whenever non-target events overlap within the HRF horizon), trial-to-trial target de-mixing, and optional single-subject cross-lag sharpening.


tau2_shrinkage & spatial_graph
tau2_shrinkage = c("auto", "graph_eb", "eb", "none"); optional "medusa_spatial_graph"
Stabilizes biological trial variance \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2\) and sandwich residual scales without smoothing trial slopes ("auto" selects bilateral "graph_eb" automatically on voxelwise NIfTI maps).


shared_error_method & variance_confounds
"poet_covreg" (default), "legacy", or "none"; optional "medusa_confounds" / "medusa_nifti_ts" / run-list envelopes
Fits subspace-debiased Adaptive-POET + multi-lag Toeplitz and LTZ-gated dynamic covariance regression (switching automatically above 512 units to voxel-safe lowrank_voxel factor mode) for Step 6 connectivity and post-hoc aggregate_decon_panel().





Outputs: What Step 3 Produces and Why It Is Set Up That Way



Output Component
Structure
Why It Is Set Up That Way




panel
Tidy data.table keyed by run, trial, event_index, onset, evt_time, and voxel/parcel
Primary trial table for Steps 5–6. Stores both trial (1..\(m\) target counter) and event_index (row in events[[r]]) alongside decon_raw, decon_demixed, se_demixed, precision_weight, precision_weight_cohort, error_ac1, tau2_bio, decon_eb, Block-PAF list-columns (shared_noise_vec, lag_noise_vec, trial_cor_vec), and optional *_whitened columns.


coefficients & summary
Per-unit × lag × term data.frame (beta_raw, beta_corrected, beta_unweighted, beta_weighted, beta_gls, SEs, moderated df, \(t\), \(p\)); lag summary
Places uncorrected (beta_raw) and de-mixed/GLS slopes side by side under the same Step 2 inverse so the impact of operator de-mixing and precision weighting is transparent.


lag_resolution & lag_error_cor
Per-unit \(L \times L\) cross-lag resolution and trial error correlation matrices
Carried forward so medusa_multilag_infer() (Step 5) can apply group-level spectral deblurring, P-spline smoothing, and simultaneous bands across lags.


shared_error_model, unit_error_cor, & parcel_weights
POET + covariance-regression shared-error model (v3), unit-by-unit error correlation matrix, and voxel weights
Supplies stationary and dynamic cross-region error covariances (shared_noise_vec / shared_noise_loading in panel) for Step 6 connectivity disattenuation and post-hoc aggregate_decon_panel().

title: Step 3: Epoch Alignment, De-Mixing, and Uncertainty Propagation
section: Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points
text:
Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points

3.1 Define the event-locked neural source and kernel readout
Consider reading out continuous deconvolved activity \(\widehat{a}_r\) around target event \(i\) at timestamp \(t_i + \tau\). Because \(t_i + \tau\) rarely lands on an exact integer TR, Step 3 forms a row-normalized weight vector \(S_\tau[i, :]\) over nearby acquisition samples (Figure 7.1). While "linear" uses 2-point bracket interpolation, "triangle" (width \(1.5 \times \text{TR}\)) averages 9 symmetrically weighted sub-interval points across adjacent samples (symmetric kernel quadrature)—respecting sub-TR jitter while attenuating high-frequency inverse noise.






Figure 7.1: Acquisition-grid readout weights around an off-grid target timestamp (20.35 s, TR = 1 s) for "linear", "boxcar", "triangle", and "gaussian" kernels.



Alongside the readout window, Step 3 asks a substantive question about source duration: what neural time course does trial \(i\)’s amplitude \(\theta_i\) multiply? Suppose deliberation neural activity stays at a constant firing rate (1.8 units/s) across trials whose reaction times vary from 0.4 to 2.8 s. Because longer deliberation produces larger integrated BOLD deflections, different source models estimate distinct quantities (Figure 7.2):

source_model = "impulse" treats every trial as a brief unit impulse, attributing longer-duration BOLD accumulation to higher amplitude and producing a positive slope against RT (beta = 1.392).
source_model = "duration", duration_scale = "rate" matches both the forward boxcar and midpoint readout window to each trial’s duration [onset + lag, onset + lag + RT], recovering a flat firing-rate slope invariant to RT (beta = 0.015, near true 0.00).
source_model = "duration", duration_scale = "integral" normalizes each forward boxcar to unit area, explicitly estimating time-integrated neural activity (1.8 × duration, recovering slope 1.806 vs. true 1.800).







Figure 7.2: Same simulated constant-rate variable-duration BOLD series analyzed under three source specifications: impulse height (left), duration-matched rate (middle), and duration-integrated neural mass (right).



Choice point — Source model (source_model & duration_scale) and readout_kernel: Pair readout_kernel = "triangle" (readout_width = 1.5 * tr) with source_model = "impulse" for brief phasic events (e.g., feedback delivery). For variable-duration epochs (e.g., choice deliberation), pass source_model = "duration" with trial_durations = rt and choose duration_scale = "rate" to test neural intensity per unit time or "integral" to test cumulative activity.



3.2 Write the epoch measurement model and subtract non-target spillover
Now consider a cue–feedback paradigm where each Cue precedes Feedback by 1–3 seconds. Let \(\theta_T\) denote true target (Feedback) trial amplitudes with forward BOLD design \(G_\tau\), and \(\theta_O\) denote non-target (Cue) amplitudes with forward design \(G_O\). Applying readout \(S_\tau\) to deconvolved activity \(\widehat{a}_r = D_r y_r\) yields a raw trial readout whose conditional expectation contains two distinct terms:
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\hat{z}_{\text{raw},\tau} \mid \theta_T, \theta_O\bigr]
= \underbrace{(S_\tau D_r G_\tau)\,\theta_T}_{\text{attenuated & mixed targets}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{(S_\tau D_r G_O)\,\theta_O}_{\text{non-target spillover}}.
\]
In simulate_step3.R, a Cue_only voxel responds to cues but has zero true feedback slope (\(\beta = 0\)), while reaction time links cue–feedback spacing to covariate x. Because of the second term above, raw feedback readouts in Cue_only pick up spurious cue spillover (beta_raw = -0.115; Table 7.1).
Enabling demix_other_events = TRUE estimates and subtracts the operator-predicted non-target contribution \((S_\tau D_r G_O) L_{\text{other}} y_r\), forming cleaned readout rows \(S_{\text{clean},\tau}\) before target amplitudes are evaluated (Figure 7.3).






Figure 7.3: Estimated feedback slopes in the null-feedback Cue_only voxel under constant cue amplitude (left) versus trial-varying cue amplitude correlated with x (right), comparing default condition-mean de-mixing (0.05) against joint trial-level de-mixing (0.02).



Choice point — Non-target subtraction (demix_other_events, other_event_model, & demix_ridge): Keep demix_other_events = TRUE and other_event_model = "auto" (default). Earlier prototypes gated trial-varying collateral subtraction on a numeric demix_ridge < 0.03 threshold, which left demix_ridge = 0.05 vulnerable to trial-by-trial cue bleed when upstream cues covaried with target predictors (e.g., expected value covarying with feedback RPE). other_event_model = "auto" decouples model structure from demix_ridge: whenever non-target events overlap target windows within the hemodynamic horizon, "auto" fits a GCV/block-ridge-stabilized joint (T, O) trial operator that removes both mean and trial-varying collateral spillover automatically (Figure 7.3, right), while collapsing to low-variance "condition" subtraction when phases are well separated. Furthermore, for variable-duration epochs (source_model = "duration"), post-subtraction target rows \(S_{\text{clean},\tau}\) are passed directly into solve_duration_demix_operator() (K_unc = S_clean_tau %*% D_r %*% G_tau_unc) so adjacent encode/probe subtraction never under-restores sustained delay gain.



3.3 Invert target-to-target mixing to recover an additive-error readout
After removing non-target spillover, the cleaned readout still reflects Step 2’s regularization blur across target trials, \(K_{\text{clean},\tau} = S_{\text{clean},\tau} D_r G_\tau\). Writing this in the exact measurement-model form of Vig & Hallquist (2026) by adding and subtracting \(\theta_T\):
\[
S_{\text{clean},\tau}\widehat{a}_r
= \theta_T - (I - K_{\text{clean},\tau})\theta_T + S_{\text{clean},\tau} D_r \varepsilon_r.
\]
Without inverting \(K_{\text{clean},\tau}\), diagonal shrinkage (\([K_{\text{clean},\tau}]_{ii} < 1\)) and neighbor overlap attenuate the true 0.70 feedback slope in Target down to beta_raw = 0.088 (Table 7.1). Enabling demix_target_trials = TRUE applies a ridge-stabilized inverse \(W_\tau\) on run-centered trials (Tikhonov regularization) with diagonal gain restoration \(\tilde{G}_\tau\) (decon_demixed), sharpening the 20×20 target resolution matrix toward the identity (Figure 7.5) and recovering the true 0.70 slope cleanly (Target = 0.705, Noisy_target = 0.673; Figure 7.4, Table 7.1). To ensure any small ridge stabilization in \(W_\tau\) at rapid ISIs never biases trial regressions, centered covariates are multiplied by the matched post-demixing resolution matrix \(M_{\text{post}}\) so predictor and response share identical coordinates.






Figure 7.4: Run-centered trial readouts vs. true injected feedback amplitudes in Target across raw readout, target-only de-mixing, and full cue + target de-mixing.









Figure 7.5: Target-by-target resolution matrix \(K_\tau\) before (Raw target response) and after (Corrected target response) Step 3 regularized de-mixing.
