When multiple peri-event lags are requested, adjacent lags within the same trial also share deconvolution smoothness. Setting demix_within_trial = TRUE applies an additional ridge-stabilized cross-lag inverse within each participant, narrowing single-subject lag curves at the cost of larger per-lag SEs (Figure 7.6).






Figure 7.6: Effect of demix_within_trial = TRUE on estimated lag slopes (top) and conditional per-trial measurement SE (bottom).



Choice point — Target and cross-lag de-mixing (demix_target_trials, demix_ridge, & demix_within_trial): Keep demix_target_trials = TRUE in all operator analyses. For single-trial readout fidelity or rapid-ITI designs with strong biological trial fluctuations (e.g., estimating individual working-memory capacity plateaus \(K_s\)), set demix_ridge = "auto" (tune_demix_ridge_sure()), which selects \(\lambda_{\text{demix}} \in [0.006, 0.10]\) per run and stratum by minimizing analytical post-gain-restoration trial MSE using propagated Stage-2 readout noise covariance (without peeking at covariates), opening to lighter ridge (~0.006–0.016) at high trial SNR while retaining conservative stabilization (0.05–0.10) on noisy units. Leave demix_within_trial = FALSE when passing outputs to medusa_multilag_infer() in Step 5 (which sharpens cross-lag blurring at the group level via spectral deblurring, where SNR is \(\sqrt{N}\) higher), and enable demix_within_trial = TRUE when inspecting descriptive single-subject curves or fitting single-lag models where sharper lag localization is desired.



3.4 Propagate observation-noise covariance and construct trial precision weights
Because every operation from centered BOLD to decon_demixed is captured in the composite linear map \(B_{r,\tau} = \tilde{G}_\tau W_\tau S_{\text{clean},\tau} D_r\), the conditional sampling covariance of the de-mixed trial vector is known analytically: \[
\Omega_{r,\tau} = \operatorname{Cov}(e_{r,\tau} \mid B_{r,\tau}) \propto Q_m B_{r,\tau} \Sigma_{\text{obs},r} B_{r,\tau}^\top Q_m.
\] MEDuSA evaluates \(\Omega_{r,\tau}\) in fast factored form without forming dense \(T \times T\) covariance matrices, matching dense matrix multiplication to 6.07e-18 and reproducing 2,500-draw Monte Carlo noise SDs trial by trial (se_demixed; Figure 7.7).






Figure 7.7: Ratio of 2,500-draw Monte Carlo trial SD to analytical se_demixed across all 20 target trials in Run 1.



Trials near run boundaries, scrub gaps, or rapid event clusters naturally have larger measurement error \(s_{ri}^2 = \texttt{se\_demixed}_{ri}^2\). However, trials also vary due to genuine biological trial-to-trial variability \(\tau_{\text{bio}}^2\). Just as composite weights in multilevel moment estimation combine structural disturbance variance with measurement-error variance (Vig & Hallquist, 2026), Step 3 estimates \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2\) and forms Empirical-Bayes composite precision weights \(w_{ri} \propto (\hat{\tau}_{\text{eff}}^2 + s_{ri}^2)^{-1}\) (precision_weight normalized to mean 1 within unit; precision_weight_cohort left unnormalized for multi-subject models), downweighting high-SE trials smoothly without letting a single low-SE trial dominate (Figure 7.8). When requested (whiten_panel = TRUE), Step 3 also applies a run-mean-preserving symmetric decorrelation transform that removes off-diagonal within-run trial error correlations while keeping each trial aligned as closely as possible to its original ordering (regularized zero-phase component analysis, or ZCA whitening; Figure 7.9).






Figure 7.8: Pure measurement-only inverse-variance weights (precision_weight_op) versus biological-variance-stabilized Empirical-Bayes weights (precision_weight).









Figure 7.9: Within-run total trial correlation matrix \(\Sigma_{\text{tot}}\) before and after symmetric trial decorrelation (whiten_panel = TRUE, regularized ZCA).



Choice point — Variance shrinkage (tau2_shrinkage), physical units (restore_scale), and trial decorrelation (whiten_panel):

Variance stabilization (tau2_shrinkage = "auto"): In single-voxel NIfTI analyses (aggregate_by_parcel = FALSE), raw per-voxel \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{raw}}^2 = \hat{\sigma}_{\text{tot}}^2 - s_{\text{obs}}^2\) has wide sampling variance over 40–80 trials and frequently truncates to zero. "auto" automatically activates edge-preserving neighborhood variance pooling ("graph_eb"), which stabilizes the dimensionless ratio \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{raw}}^2 / s_{\text{obs}}^2\) across functionally concordant cortical neighbors before zero-truncation. To keep neighborhood pooling calibrated, it discounts shared scanner noise between neighbors (via Isserlis’ squared-correlation identity), caps how far isolated focal hotspots can be pulled toward quiet surround voxels (at \(2.5\) standard errors via Efron–Morris limited translation), and borrows residual scale precision across concordant neighbors (Empirical-Bayes variance moderation; Smyth, 2004)—without ever smoothing trial slopes \(\hat{\beta}\) (see Spatial Graph Pooling). In parcel mode (aggregate_by_parcel = TRUE), "auto" defaults to "none", while setting "graph_eb" explicitly builds a 3D parcel-centroid graph for fine parcellations (e.g., Schaefer-400/1000).
Scale restoration & trial decorrelation: Set restore_scale = TRUE whenever pooling runs or participants so decon_demixed and se_demixed return to physical BOLD units, and set whiten_panel = TRUE alongside return_panel = TRUE to export paired *_whitened columns (via regularized ZCA) for rapid-ISI designs.

title: Step 3: Epoch Alignment, De-Mixing, and Uncertainty Propagation
section: Practical Considerations: Descriptive Alignment, Censoring Support, and Scope
text:
Practical Considerations: Descriptive Alignment, Censoring Support, and Scope

When to use descriptive align_medusa_ts() vs. inferential decon_epoch_regression(): When you want descriptive peri-event waveform interpolation without a forward de-mixing model—for example, plotting raw peri-event BOLD averages, inspecting blind deconvolve_nlreg() / deconvolve_reglin() trajectories, or auditing explicit collision rules (overlap_policy = "allow" | "truncate" | "exclude")—use align_medusa_ts() (or evt_align_decon_files() for disk-backed .csv.gz archives). For primary inferential modeling on deconvolve_crossrun_hrf() outputs, use decon_epoch_regression(), which removes neighbor mixing and propagates analytical se_demixed. (Because epochs$panel is already event-aligned, it goes directly to Steps 5–6 without calling align_medusa_ts().)
Causal BOLD observability gating (obs_frac_tau >= 0.20): If at least 80% of the forward HRF energy evoked by a target event at \(t_i + \tau\) falls inside censored frames (valid_rows == FALSE) or past the end of the run, Step 3 records that trial-lag as NA rather than extrapolating from the smoothness penalty (while partial scrubbing inside the HRF window elevates se_demixed; see the Visual QC Gallery). Always inspect retained trial counts across runs and conditions before group modeling.
Scope handoff: Step 3 operates within a single participant. Aggregating voxels into anatomical parcels with spatial noise propagation is covered next in Step 4 (executed inside the same decon_epoch_regression(..., parcel_groups = ...) call), followed by population modeling in Step 5 and connectivity disattenuation in Step 6.



Mathematical Reference & Reproduction

For run \(r\), lag \(\tau\), valid observation frames \(I_r\) (\(m_r\) of \(T_r\) volumes), and frozen Step 2 inverse \(D_r \in \mathbb{R}^{T_r \times m_r}\):

Non-target subtraction (other_event_model = "auto"): Let \(S_{r,0}\) (build_epoch_readout_matrix()) read out all events at lag 0 and \(G_{r,0}\) be their column-centered forward HRF design. build_other_demix_operator() forms \(L_{\text{other}}\) via GCV/block-ridge-stabilized joint (T, O) trial inversion whenever non-target events overlap within the HRF horizon under other_event_model = "auto" (or "trial"), collapsing to condition-mean least squares under "condition", yielding cleaned target readout rows \(S_{\text{clean},\tau} = S_\tau - (S_\tau D_r G_{r,0,\text{other}}) L_{\text{other}}\). On multi-lag sweeps (length(lags) > 1), target demixing applies a uniform lag-wise operator across all requested lags (n_lags == 1L guard on single-lag L_target_0 shortcuts) so lag = 0 never incurs a discontinuous gain notch prior to Step 5 spectral deblurring (medusa_build_deblur_operator(..., alpha1 = 0.05, alpha0_sq = 0.020)).
Target cross-talk & post-subtraction duration gain calibration: Given uncentered and column-centered target forward designs \((G_{\tau,\text{unc}}, G_\tau)\), solve_duration_demix_operator() evaluates post-subtraction target matrices \(S_{\text{clean},\tau} D_r G_{\tau,\text{unc}}\) and \(S_{\text{clean},\tau} D_r G_\tau\), row-normalizes \(R_{\text{unc}} = \operatorname{diag}(g_{\text{safe}})^{-1} S_{\text{clean},\tau} D_r G_{\tau,\text{unc}}\), solves \((R_{\text{unc}}^\top R_{\text{unc}} + \lambda_{\text{demix}} Q_m + 10^{-8} I) W_{\text{unc}} = R_{\text{unc}}^\top \operatorname{diag}(g_{\text{safe}})^{-1}\) (penalizing centered fluctuations \(Q_m = I_m - \frac{1}{m}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top\)), applies a Sherman–Morrison rank-1 centering update to obtain \(W_\tau\), and restores exact post-subtraction centered diagonal gain \(\tilde{G}_\tau\).
Exact noise propagation & \(M_{\text{post}}\) alignment: The composite linear map from centered run BOLD to de-mixed target trials is \(B_{r,\tau} = \tilde{G}_\tau W_\tau S_{\text{clean},\tau} D_r\), with centered trial error covariance \(\Omega_{r,\tau} = \frac{\sigma_{\text{eff}}^2}{1 - 1/m} Q_m B_{r,\tau} C_{\text{obs}} \Sigma_{\text{AR}}[I_r, I_r] C_{\text{obs}}^\top B_{r,\tau}^\top Q_m\) evaluated via compute_ar1_operator_factor(). Centered covariates \(X_{r,c}\) are multiplied by \(M_{\text{post}} = Q_m (\tilde{G}_\tau W_\tau S_{\text{clean},\tau} D_r G_\tau) Q_m\) prior to regression and ZCA whitening.
Bilateral Graph-EB variance & scale moderation (tau2_shrinkage = "graph_eb"): Defining untruncated \(\hat{\theta}_u = \hat{\tau}_{\text{raw}, u}^2 / s_{\text{obs}, u}^2\) with sampling variance \(v_u \approx \frac{2}{\nu_u}(1 + \max(0, \tilde{\theta}_u))^2\), bilateral weights \(\alpha_{uv}\) combine geodesic distance, Cauchy pilot-jump stopping, and orthogonalized residual sign concordance. Discounting neighbor squared-error correlation \(\rho_{ab}^2\) yields local prior \((\mu_{\text{loc}, u}, \tau_{\text{prior}, u}^2)\), shrinkage \(B_u = v_u / (v_u + \tau_{\text{prior}, u}^2)\), limited-translation posterior \(\theta_u^{\text{EM}} = \hat{\theta}_u + \operatorname{clip}(B_u(\mu_{\text{loc}, u} - \hat{\theta}_u), -2.5\sqrt{v_u}, +2.5\sqrt{v_u})\), and \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}, u}^2 = s_{\text{obs}, u}^2 \max(0, \theta_u^{\text{EM}})\), paired with bilateral Smyth (2004) moderation of sandwich residual scales.

title: Step 4: Parcel Aggregation and Analysis Panels
text:
Overview
Many task-fMRI hypotheses are formulated at the level of anatomical regions or functional parcels rather than single voxels. Combining voxels within a parcel boosts trial-level signal-to-noise ratio substantially, provided aggregation happens at the right point in the pipeline: after each voxel’s run has been deconvolved under its own HRF and \(\text{AR}(p)\) whitener, and before trial-level event de-mixing and precision weighting.
Step 4—executed inside decon_epoch_regression(..., parcel_groups = parcel_ids) (or post-hoc on an existing voxelwise panel via aggregate_decon_panel())—pools continuous deconvolved time series within each parcel using cross-run precision and task-support weights, accumulates exact multi-stratum linear operators when intra-parcel voxels differ in HRF or noise stratum, estimates stationary and dynamic spatial error covariances via the Adaptive-POET + covariance-regression engine (shared_error_method = "poet_covreg"), and outputs a tidy participant panel ready to stack across a cohort for Steps 5 and 6.
library(medusa)

ep <- decon_epoch_regression(
  deconvolution    = decon,
  covariates       = covariates,
  events           = events,
  target_condition = "feedback",
  lags             = seq(-2, 4, by = 1),
  parcel_groups    = parcel_ids,
  restore_scale    = TRUE,
  whiten_panel     = TRUE,
  return_panel     = TRUE
)
ep$panel[, id := subject_id]
The walkthrough below develops Step 4 in four substeps: computing SNR-informed voxel weights (4.1), combining mixed intra-parcel operator strata (4.2), propagating spatial noise correlations without task contamination (4.3), and constructing cohort-ready weights and panel columns (4.4).

title: Step 4: Parcel Aggregation and Analysis Panels
section: Goals, Inputs, and Outputs
text:
Goals, Inputs, and Outputs

Goals of Step 4

Aggregate voxels using cross-run SNR-optimal weights (parcel_weights): Weight constituent voxels inversely by their cross-run observation-noise variance and upweight voxels with stronger cross-fitted Step 1 task \(R^2\).
Preserve intra-parcel (HRF, AR, lambda) heterogeneity: Combine per-stratum forward and inverse operators (\(\sum_s w_s D_s F_s\)) directly rather than approximating a parcel with a single averaged HRF.
Propagate within- and between-parcel spatial noise correlation accurately: Estimate parcel measurement noise and cross-parcel error correlations from Step 2’s task-free whitened noise_innovations.
Produce a self-contained participant trial panel for cohort inference: Export aligned de-mixed readouts, conditional standard errors, cohort-comparable precision weights, paired within-run decorrelated (*_whitened) variables, and cross-parcel shared-noise loadings.



Inputs: What Step 4 Receives and Why
In addition to the Step 3 arguments (deconvolution, events, target_condition, lags, covariates), Step 4 uses four spatial and panel parameters:



Input
Structure
Why It Is Set Up That Way




parcel_groups
Named character/factor vector mapping voxel_ids to parcel labels (or ts$parcel_ids from read_nifti_ts())
Naming elements by voxel_ids guarantees exact column alignment and automatically enables aggregate_by_parcel = TRUE.


deconvolution$bold_obs / whitened_sketch & noise_innovations
Cached automatically inside deconvolution (bold_obs up to \(16{,}384\) voxels; compact \(m_r \times 64\) whitened_sketch above \(16{,}384\) voxels)
Supplies bold-free whitened residuals so Stage 4 separates task-evoked BOLD variance from stationary and dynamic scanner/physiological noise without retaining full 4D BOLD arrays.


shared_error_method & variance_confounds
"poet_covreg" (default), "legacy", or "none"; optional "medusa_confounds" / "medusa_nifti_ts" / per-run envelopes
Fits subspace-debiased Adaptive-POET + multi-lag Toeplitz and LTZ-gated dynamic covariance regression across task, covariate, rWLS, and motion/physiological envelopes (FD, DVARS, RVT).


tau2_mode & tau2_shrinkage
tau2_mode = c("auto", "marginal", "residual"); tau2_shrinkage = c("auto", "graph_eb", "eb", "none")
Govern how parcel biological trial-to-trial variance \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2\) is estimated ("auto" defaults to "none" on standard coarse parcels; setting "graph_eb" builds a 3D parcel-centroid Euclidean graph for fine 400–1000-parcel atlases).


restore_scale & whiten_panel
Logical flags (TRUE recommended for scalar/trajectory panels; use_whitened = FALSE in Step 6)
Place runs onto physical BOLD units before pooling and export paired within-run symmetrically decorrelated (*_whitened, regularized ZCA) outcome and predictor columns on the parcel covariance.





Outputs: What Step 4 Produces and Why It Is Set Up That Way



Panel Column / Object Field
Meaning & Units
Downstream Role




run, trial, event_index, onset, evt_time, parcel
Composite observation keys (attach id before stacking subjects)
event_index indexes exact rows of events[[run]] for behavioral merges; (id, run, event_index, evt_time, parcel) uniquely keys every cohort row.


decon_raw & decon_demixed
Uncorrected readout vs. de-mixed, gain-restored parcel readout
decon_demixed serves as the primary neural outcome in Step 5 and neural predictor/target in Step 6; decon_raw provides a comparison baseline.

Propagated per-trial parcel SE; lag-1 trial error correlation
Quantify conditional sampling uncertainty for Step 5 weights and Step 6 predictor measurement-error subtraction.

Within-unit mean-1 weight vs. unnormalized \((\hat{\tau}_{\text{eff}}^2 + s_{ri}^2)^{-1}\)
precision_weight weights trials within one person; precision_weight_cohort preserves between-participant reliability differences in Step 5 mixed_by().

Empirical-Bayes shrunk readout \(\bar{y}_r + \text{rel}_{ri}(y_{ri} - \bar{y}_r)\)
Stabilizes single-trial plots and descriptive visualizations using within-run trial reliability.

Remove residual serial trial error correlation when analyzed as matched pairs in Step 5.

title: Step 4: Parcel Aggregation and Analysis Panels
section: Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points
text:
Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points

4.1 Weight voxels within each parcel by cross-run precision and task support
Consider a parcel containing four voxels whose observation-noise SDs range from 0.013 (interior gray matter) to 0.032 (noisy pial edge). An unweighted average gives the noisy edge voxel the same influence as the quietest voxel. Instead, Step 4 forms fixed cross-run voxel weights \(u_v\) normalized to \(\sum_{v \in g} u_v = 1\):
\[
u_v \propto \frac{1 + \overline{R}^2_{\text{cv},v} / \bigl(0.05 + \operatorname{med}(\overline{R}^2_{\text{cv}})\bigr)}{\max\!\bigl(\overline{\sigma}_v^2,\; 0.10\,\operatorname{med}(\overline{\sigma}^2)\bigr)}.
\]
Quieter voxels with stronger cross-fitted Step 1 task \(R^2\) receive higher weight, and if a single voxel becomes invalid in one scan (for instance, partial field-of-view dropout in Run 2), the remaining valid voxels in that run renormalize smoothly to sum to 1 (Figure 8.1).






Figure 8.1: Nominal four-voxel parcel weights in Run 1 (sd = 0.013, 0.018, 0.022, 0.032) and automatic renormalization in Run 2 when Voxel 1 is marked invalid.



Choice point — Parcel panels (parcel_groups) vs. voxelwise Graph-EB mapping: Parcel aggregation is ideal when hypotheses target network ROIs, multi-lag group trajectories (medusa_multilag_infer()), or region-to-region connectivity (decon_connectivity_repair()). When effects may occupy small sub-parcel nuclei (\(< 15\%\) of a parcel) or cross shifted individual functional boundaries, omit parcel_groups to run voxelwise Graph-EB mapping (see Spatial Graph Pooling for a direct benchmark).



4.2 Accumulate exact multi-stratum parcel operators
Suppose voxels inside the same parcel belong to different (HRF, AR, lambda) strata—for example, when Step 1 used pooling = "graph" (separating pial-vein autocorrelation from interior gray matter) and Step 2 used lambda_mode = "auto". Because matrix inversion is nonlinear, deconvolving under a single parcel-averaged HRF \(\bar{h} = \frac{1}{2}(h_4 + h_8)\) differs systematically from averaging voxelwise deconvolved series (16.6% waveform discrepancy in Figure 8.2: \(\frac{1}{2}(D_1 F_1 + D_2 F_2) \neq D(\bar{h})F(\bar{h})\)).
Step 4 preserves exact operator correspondence by first forming the weighted parcel continuous series \(\widehat{a}_{r,g} = \sum_{v \in g} u_v \widehat{a}_{r,v}\) and simultaneously accumulating the exact stratum-weighted forward/inverse operator \(\sum_s w_s D_s F_s\) used in Step 3 de-mixing (Figure 8.2).






Figure 8.2: Exact multi-stratum parcel reconstruction (MEDuSA multi-stratum parcel operator) vs. a single averaged-HRF approximation when a two-voxel parcel mixes 4 s and 8 s HRFs.






4.3 Estimate spatial noise covariance from task-free innovations
To compute valid parcel standard errors (se_demixed), we need the effective observation-noise variance of the weighted parcel combination \(\sum_{v \in g} u_v e_v\). For voxel noise SDs \(\sigma_v\) and spatial noise correlations \(R_{\text{spatial}, uv}\), that variance is
\[
\sigma_{\text{parcel}}^2 = \sum_{u \in g} \sum_{v \in g} u_u u_v \sigma_u \sigma_v R_{\text{spatial}, uv}.
\]
In our 4-voxel example (simulate_step4.R), \(\sigma_{\text{parcel}}\) equals 0.0091 if voxel errors are independent (\(R_{\text{spatial}} = I\)), but rises nearly twofold to 0.0171 if all four voxels share common noise (\(R_{\text{spatial}} = \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top\)). Estimating spatial correlation from second differences of deconvolved activity (\(\Delta^2 \hat{a}\)) conflates shared task-evoked neural responses with shared noise—pegging estimated noise near the 0.0171 ceiling even when true noise is independent (0.00) or negatively correlated (-0.20).
By instead projecting \(u \odot \sigma\) onto Step 2’s task-free whitened residuals (\(\hat{\sigma}_{\text{parcel}} = \|Z_r (u \odot \sigma)\|_2\)), MEDuSA recovers the true spatial noise SD across all four correlation regimes (Figure 8.3, Table 8.1) and matches analytical se_demixed to 9.71e-17. Under shared_error_method = "poet_covreg" (default), Step 4 further applies subspace-debiased Adaptive-POET (Fan, Liao & Mincheva, 2013) with Tukey-Hanning tapered multi-lag Toeplitz cross-spectra and LTZ-gated covariance regression (Hoff & Niu, 2012) across task, covariate, Step-2 rwls, and external variance_confounds envelopes—producing shared_error_model, unit_error_cor, and per-trial Block-PAF list-columns (shared_noise_vec, lag_noise_vec, trial_cor_vec) for Step 6. Above 512 analysis units (e.g., whole-brain voxelwise panels), the engine switches automatically to a dual-space factor mode (mode = "lowrank_voxel") that never allocates \(V \times V\) matrices, and aggregate_decon_panel() can collapse any voxelwise fit or saved table to parcels post-hoc while propagating exact parcel se_demixed and inter-parcel error vectors.






Figure 8.3: Effective parcel BOLD noise SD across four spatial correlation regimes (-0.20, 0.00, 0.65, 0.95): true oracle spatial SD vs. MEDuSA’s task-free innovation estimator vs. a naive \(\Delta^2\) activity proxy.

4.4 Compute biological trial variance, cohort weights, and panel columns
On the aggregated parcel series, Step 4 estimates biological trial-to-trial variance \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2\) and builds three complementary sets of panel columns:

Within-person vs. cohort precision weights (Figure 8.4): Both use composite inverse variance \((\hat{\tau}_{\text{eff}}^2 + s_{ri}^2)^{-1}\). precision_weight normalizes to mean 1 within each participant/parcel, whereas precision_weight_cohort retains unnormalized inverse variance so Step 5 mixed_by() appropriately downweights high-noise scans and participants across the cohort.
Empirical-Bayes shrunk readouts (decon_eb, Figure 8.5): Shrinks noisy individual trials toward the run mean using trial reliability \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{eff}}^2 / (\hat{\tau}_{\text{eff}}^2 + s_{ri}^2)\) for clean single-trial visualization.
Paired within-run decorrelated columns (whiten_panel = TRUE, Figure 8.6): Applies a run-mean-preserving symmetric decorrelation map (regularized zero-phase component analysis, or ZCA whitening) equally to decon_demixed and supplied covariates on the parcel covariance \(\Sigma_{\text{tot}}\), removing serial trial error correlations while keeping each trial aligned to its original ordering.







Figure 8.4: Relative precision_weight vs. se_demixed under "marginal" and "residual" working trial-variance modes.









Figure 8.5: Empirical-Bayes shrunk trial readouts (decon_eb) vs. decon_demixed colored by reliability_trial (Nearly common parcel, Run 1).









Figure 8.6: Within-run parcel correlation matrix \(\Sigma_{\text{tot}}\) before and after paired regularized ZCA (Nearly common parcel, Run 1).



Choice point — Working trial variance (tau2_mode & tau2_shrinkage) and whiten_panel: Use tau2_mode = "auto" when covariates are supplied at Step 4, or "marginal" when building a covariate-agnostic panel (covariates = NULL) to reuse across multiple behavioral models. Keep tau2_shrinkage = "auto" on standard parcellations (100–200 parcels), or set tau2_shrinkage = "graph_eb" on dense 400–1000-parcel atlases to borrow variance precision across 3D parcel centroids.

ep <- decon_epoch_regression(

title: Step 4: Parcel Aggregation and Analysis Panels
section: Practical Considerations: Voxel Dropout, Role-Specific Columns, and Handoffs
text:
Practical Considerations: Voxel Dropout, Role-Specific Columns, and Handoffs

Checking run-to-run voxel coverage: When partial FoV clipping drops voxels from a small parcel in one run, renormalization shifts the parcel’s spatial center slightly; inspect decon$scaling[[r]]$status whenever dropout is non-trivial.
Pre-aggregation (parcel_groups) vs. post-hoc aggregate_decon_panel(): Supplying parcel_groups directly inside decon_epoch_regression() is fastest when your target atlas is fixed. When you also want voxelwise maps—or plan to evaluate several atlases without repeating Step 3—fit decon_epoch_regression(..., aggregate_by_parcel = FALSE) once (automatically using memory-safe lowrank_voxel mode above 512 voxels) and call aggregate_decon_panel(ep_vox, parcel_groups = atlas_vec) per parcellation.
Matching panel columns to their statistical role: Mirrors the distinction between unshrunk likelihood-only readouts and shrunken EB predictions (Skrondal & Laake, 2001; Vig & Hallquist, 2026):

Use decon_demixed (with weights = "precision_weight_cohort") for Step 5 outcomes and Step 6 M-MOMS connectivity; reserve decon_eb for plotting stabilized trial values rather than entering it into regressions without accounting for shrinkage (see the Visual QC Gallery for a visual demonstration of decon_eb slope attenuation).
When using ZCA-whitened variables, pair decon_demixed_whitened exclusively with matched <var>_whitened predictors from the same (parcel, evt_time) split.

Cohort storage handoff: Attach id (and session if longitudinal) before combining participants. Saving subject_epochs as .rds, writing partitioned Parquet (arrow::write_dataset()), or exporting pipe-delimited CSV/.csv.gz via medusa_write_table() (read back via medusa_read_table() or directly by decon_connectivity_repair()) preserves shared_noise_vec, lag_noise_vec, and trial_cor_vec for Step 6 alongside scalable disk streaming for Step 5 mixed_by().



Mathematical Reference & Reproduction


Within-parcel effective noise variance: Let \(Z_r \in \mathbb{R}^{m_r \times V}\) denote Step 2’s column-unit-norm task-projected whitened innovations (colSums(Z_r^2) == 1). For parcel \(g\) with valid voxels \(V_g\), normalized weights \(u_g\), and voxel observation-noise SDs \(\sigma_{r,V_g}\), define \(\zeta_{r,g} = Z_{r,V_g} (u_g \odot \sigma_{r,V_g})\). Because \(\mathbb{E}[Z_{r,i}^\top Z_{r,j}] = R_{\text{spatial},ij}\), \(\|\zeta_{r,g}\|_2^2 = \sum_{i,j \in V_g} u_i u_j \sigma_i \sigma_j \hat{R}_{\text{spatial},ij}\) estimates parcel observation-noise variance without task contamination, bounded into \([0.05\,\sigma_{\text{ind}}^2, \sigma_{\text{ceil}}^2]\).
Subspace-debiased Adaptive-POET & LTZ-gated covariance regression (poet_covreg): On uncensored whitened residuals projected orthogonal to each stratum’s convolved [trial, duration, dHRF/dt] subspace \(M_{s_g}\) (with exact \(\operatorname{tr}((I - M_{s_g})(I - M_{s_h}))\) degrees-of-freedom debiasing), medusa_fit_shared_error_covreg() separates pervasive global physiological/scanner factors above the Marchenko–Pastur + Tracy–Widom bulk edge from firm-thresholded idiosyncratic residual correlations (poet_regularize_cor()), estimates Tukey-Hanning tapered multi-lag error cross-spectra, and fits Liu–Tang–Zhang (2009) spatial-\(\chi^2\)-gated heteroskedastic variance slopes over task drive, covariates, Step-2 rwls bursts, and variance_confounds (restoring the baseline intercept via exact Schur complement whenever null confound columns are gated to zero). Block-PAF factorization embeds the resulting trial-by-parcel error covariance onto panel$shared_noise_vec, panel$lag_noise_vec, and panel$trial_cor_vec.

title: Step 5: Group and Trajectory Inference
text:
Overview
Once participant trial panels are assembled in Step 4, Step 5 tests how behavioral or experimental variables relate to deconvolved neural activity across the participant population—and characterizes how those effects unfold over peri-event time. Because neural activity decon_demixed sits on the left-hand side as the outcome (Neural ~ Behavior) on an additive-error scale, conditionally mean-zero measurement noise enters the residual without attenuating fixed-effect slopes, while composite precision weights account for varying reliability across trials, runs, and participants (Skrondal & Laake, 2001; Vig & Hallquist, 2026).
Step 5 provides two complementary modeling pathways plus direct volumetric brain-map export:
library(medusa)

# Pathway A: Split-wise multilevel model across parcels and lags
group_models <- mixed_by(
  group_panel,
  outcomes           = "decon_demixed",
  rhs_model_formulae = ~ value_within + value_mean + (1 + value_within || id) + (1 | id:run),
  split_on           = c("parcel", "evt_time"),
  weights            = "precision_weight_cohort"
)
The four substeps below walk from centering predictors (5.1), through split-wise mixed modeling (5.2), joint multi-lag trajectory inference (5.3), and window contrasts, latency estimation, and brain-map export (5.4).

title: Step 5: Group and Trajectory Inference
text:
Split-wise linear mixed-effects models (mixed_by()): Fits a multilevel formula independently at each (parcel, evt_time) split—in memory or streamed from disk-backed Parquet/.rds datasets—accommodating participant random slopes, nested run intercepts, and rich cross-level interactions.
Joint multi-lag trajectory inference (medusa_multilag_infer()): Models the full lag vector of a (parcel, term) profile jointly using cross-lag resolution and covariance matrices to sharpen blurred lag profiles (spectral deblurring), fit smooth penalized-spline (P-spline) trajectories, and compute simultaneous Max-|T| confidence bands, cluster-enhanced (1D TFCE) tests, planned window contrasts, and peak/latency summaries.
Volumetric NIfTI backprojection (backproject_medusa()): Maps parcel-level group statistics directly onto 3D/4D NIfTI brain volumes for visualization in ggbrain.

title: Step 5: Group and Trajectory Inference
section: Goals, Inputs, and Outputs
text:
Goals, Inputs, and Outputs

Goals of Step 5

Separate within-person trial fluctuations from between-person trait differences: Decompose predictors into person/run-centered deviations and person means so cross-sectional differences do not confound phasic trial slopes.
Anchor population inference to participants via random slopes: Model inter-individual slope heterogeneity across independent participants rather than treating repeated trials as independent population draws.
Incorporate heterogeneous trial and scan precision: Weight observations by composite inverse total variance (precision_weight_cohort) across trials, runs, and participants.
Leverage cross-lag covariance for trajectory inference and contrasts: Combine Step 3/4 lag operators with empirical cross-lag slope covariance to compute simultaneous confidence bands, 1D TFCE, window contrasts, and latency intervals.

title: Step 5: Group and Trajectory Inference
section: Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points
text:
Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points

5.1 Decompose behavioral predictors into within-person and between-person components
A raw trial predictor \(x_{sri}\) (participant \(s\), run \(r\), trial \(i\)) combines phasic trial-to-trial variation around a participant’s mean with stable differences across participants: \[
x_{sri} = \underbrace{(x_{sri} - \bar{x}_s)}_{\text{within-person state } x^W_{sri}} + \underbrace{\bar{x}_s}_{\text{between-person mean}}.
\] Testing whether high-value trials evoke stronger activity than low-value trials within the same person is distinct from comparing participants who experience higher average value overall. In Figure 9.1, the true within-person slope is \(+0.55\) while the between-person slope is \(-0.72\); entering uncentered \(x_{sri}\) estimates a confounded pooled slope of -0.432, whereas decomposing x_within and x_mean recovers 0.521 and -0.731 cleanly.






Figure 9.1: Simulated participant means slope down across people even though the within-participant lines slope up (six representative participants shown).



Compute centered predictors on the behavioral table before merging on (id, run, event_index) so censored fMRI frames in one parcel never alter a participant’s behavioral mean in another:


Show behavioral centering and keyed trial merge
key <- c("id", "run", "event_index")
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(trial_behavior[, ..key]))

trial_behavior[, `:=`(
  value_mean     = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
  value_within   = value - mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
  entropy_within = entropy - mean(entropy, na.rm = TRUE)
), by = id]

group_panel <- merge(
  activity_panel,
  trial_behavior[, .(id, run, event_index, value_mean, value_within, entropy_within)],
  by = key, all.x = TRUE
)


Choice point — Centering grain (by = id vs. by = .(id, run)): Center within participant (by = id) when predictor distributions are stationary across runs, or center within each participant-run (by = .(id, run)) when contingencies or block drifts shift across runs and pure within-run trial contrasts are desired.



5.2 Fit participant random-slope mixed models with cohort precision weights
At a single (parcel, evt_time) split, the standard multilevel model expresses de-mixed trial readout \(\widehat{z}_{sri}\) (decon_demixed) as
\[
\widehat{z}_{sri} = \beta_0 + \beta_W x^W_{sri} + \beta_B \bar{x}_s + b_{0s} + b_{Ws} x^W_{sri} + a_{sr} + \varepsilon_{sri},
\]
with participant random intercept and slope \((b_{0s}, b_{Ws})\) ((1 + x_within || id)) and participant-nested run intercept \(a_{sr}\) ((1 | id:run)). In a balanced design with \(S\) participants, \(m\) trials per participant, slope variance \(\sigma_b^2\), and trial residual variance \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2\), the sampling variance of the population slope is
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_W) = \frac{\sigma_b^2}{S} + \frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{Sm}.
\]
Adding more trials \(m\) sharpens each participant’s slope (\(\sigma_\varepsilon^2 / Sm \to 0\)) while leaving between-participant heterogeneity \(\sigma_b^2 / S\) unchanged. Including the random slope \(b_{Ws}\) reflects that structure: in Figure 9.2 (12 participants, \(\beta_W = 0\), \(\sigma_b > 0\)), random-slope/participant-slope inference holds nominal Type I error at 5.2% at 192 trials per person, whereas trial-row OLS without random slopes reaches 79.8%.






Figure 9.2: Two tests of the same zero population slope across 3,000 replications per trial count (12 participants, nonzero slope heterogeneity). Participant-slope inference stays near 5%, whereas trial-row OLS inflates with trial count.



Simultaneously, conditional residual variance varies across trials and scans because \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_{sri}) = \tau_{\text{latent}}^2 + s_{sri}^2\). Passing weights = "precision_weight_cohort" supplies \((\hat{\tau}_{\text{eff}}^2 + s_{sri}^2)^{-1}\) normalized across the full cohort split, allowing noisier runs and participants to carry appropriately wider conditional residual spread (0.191 and 0.396 vs. true 0.194 and 0.403 in Figure 9.3, compared with 0.313 unweighted). Moreover, when upstream Step 3 panels were exported covariate-agnostically (covariates = NULL), panel tau2_bio reflects marginal trial variance (\(\beta_s^2 \operatorname{Var}(x) + \tau_{\text{resid},s}^2\)), which would otherwise downweight participants with the largest true neural slopes \(|\beta_s|\); under reweight_conditional_tau2 = "auto" (default), mixed_by() automatically re-estimates each participant’s conditional residual biological variance \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{resid},s}^2\) (shrunk across participants via Empirical Bayes) after projecting out the within-participant fixed-effect predictors in model_formula before forming cohort weights.






Figure 9.3: Conditional residual spread recovered by weighted vs. unweighted lmer() across a quiet run (SD = 0.194) and a noisy run (SD = 0.403).



Across 3 simulated parcels (Phasic, Sustained, Null) × 8 lags × 2 focal predictors (\(48\) planned tests; Figure 9.4, Figure 9.5), Benjamini–Yekutieli ("BY") adjustment isolates 7 true discoveries around the phasic value_within peak (\(+1\text{ s}\)) and sustained entropy_within plateau (\(+1\) to \(+4\text{ s}\)) while filtering out isolated pointwise fluctuations (9 unadjusted hits).






Figure 9.4: Simulated population slope profiles across three parcels with pointwise 95% Satterthwaite intervals (dashed lines mark generating truth).









Figure 9.5: Multiplicity map across the 48 parcel × lag × term tests: teal cells survive Benjamini–Yekutieli FDR control across the family; orange cells pass unadjusted p <= .05 only.



Choice point — Split-wise mixed_by() vs. joint medusa_multilag_infer(), and disk streaming: Choose mixed_by() when testing specific planned lags, complex random-effects structures, or trial-by-trait interactions; for large whole-cortex cohorts, pass a Hive-partitioned Parquet directory directly to mixed_by(data = ..., split_filter = ...) so Arrow streams one split at a time with minimal RAM. Choose medusa_multilag_infer() (Substep 5.3) when your primary question concerns the full peri-event waveform, simultaneous epoch bands, or window contrasts.



5.3 Model multi-lag trajectories jointly with medusa_multilag_infer()
Because neighboring lags share both deconvolution smoothness (\(R_{\text{lag}}\)) and correlated observation noise (\(C_{\text{lag}}\)), modeling the lag vector \(\widehat{b} = (\widehat{b}_1, \dots, \widehat{b}_L)^\top\) jointly is substantially more informative than treating lags as unrelated splits:

Joint within-run regression and available-case lag pooling: medusa_multilag_infer() fits all supplied time-varying covariates together within each run (routing any participant-constant trait covariates to between-participant weighted least squares with leverage-adjusted HC2 standard errors) and pools participant slopes across lags using available cases—retaining participants at interior lags even if boundary censoring removed an edge lag.
Cross-lag sharpening and uncertainty-aware spline smoothing: Under trajectory_mode = "auto" (with upstream demix_within_trial = FALSE), medusa_multilag_infer() first gently inverts the known cross-lag blurring matrix \(R_{\text{lag}}\) (regularized spectral deblurring; "deblur", Figure 9.6) and then fits a smooth penalized spline ("deblur_pspline"), folding uncertainty from the smoothing penalty itself into \(\Sigma_{\text{multilag}}\) (Marra–Wood posterior covariance; Marra & Wood, 2012) rather than treating the smooth curve as bias-free.
Finite-sample cross-lag calibration (n_perm draws): Because the \(L \times L\) cross-lag covariance is estimated from a finite cohort of participants, medusa_multilag_infer() simulates null covariance draws that propagate that finite-sample covariance uncertainty (studentized Wishart draws). From those joint draws it computes simultaneous Max-|T| bands (p_maxT, conf.low.sim, conf.high.sim), threshold-free cluster enhancement (p_tfce, accumulating contiguous same-sign deflections without an arbitrary cutoff), and a multivariate departure test across the whole epoch (omnibus_p, Mahalanobis test; Figure 9.7, Figure 9.8).







Figure 9.6: Spectral cross-lag deblurring on a deterministic coefficient curve spread by C_blur: the deblurred trajectory recovers the underlying phasic width.









Figure 9.7: Raw lag estimates, pointwise 95% intervals, simultaneous 95% Max-|T| band, and smoothed P-spline trajectory on the simulated Phasic parcel.









Figure 9.8: Epoch-level significance summaries (min_p_maxT, min_p_tfce, omnibus_p) across Phasic value, Sustained entropy, and Null entropy trajectories (4,000 Wishart draws).



In Figure 9.8, both generated effects hit the 4,000-draw floor (min_p_maxT = 0.0002, omnibus_p = 0.0005), while the null trajectory stays well above .05 (omnibus_p = 0.269). Custom first-stage participant slope tables can also enter directly via the coefficient-table interface:


Show optional custom participant slope-table call
partial_trajectory <- medusa_multilag_infer(
  subject_slopes,
  lag_resolution  = resolution_by_parcel,
  lag_error_cor   = error_cor_by_parcel,
  trajectory_mode = "deblur",
  n_perm          = 4000L,
  seed            = 6205L
)


Choice point — Trajectory mode (trajectory_mode) and multiplicity: Use trajectory_mode = "auto" as the standard setting (or "none" when inspecting raw unsmoothed lag averages). Within one (parcel, term) curve, p_maxT and p_tfce already control familywise error across lags; when testing multiple parcels or covariates, adjust latency$omnibus_p across the planned parcel–term family using Holm or BY.



5.4 Evaluate planned window contrasts, continuous latency, and volumetric NIfTI maps
To compare early vs. late epoch activity (contrasts = list(late_minus_early = list(early = c(0, 1), late = c(3, 4)))), medusa_multilag_infer() evaluates \(c^\top \widehat{b}_*\) with cross-lag SE \(\sqrt{c^\top \Sigma_* c}\):



contrast_source
Curve evaluated
Recommended use




"unsmoothed" (default)
Spectrally deblurred curve prior to P-spline smoothing
Standard inferential choice: retains resolution recovery without spline curvature shrinkage between windows.


"raw"
Raw group lag estimates
Direct test of raw lag window averages without cross-lag deblurring.


"multilag"
Deblurred + P-spline smoothed curve
Descriptive contrast matching the plotted smooth curve (worked comparison).



On our simulated panel, late_minus_early distinguishes the decaying phasic value response (estimate = -0.177, \(t_{23} = -7.49\), \(p = 1.3e-07\)) from the sustained entropy response (estimate = 0.082, \(t_{23} = 4.26\), \(p = 0.0003\)), while $latency summarizes natural-spline peak_lag (1.02 s, 95% CI [0.92, 1.11] s for Phasic) and center-of-mass / FWHM (com_lag = 2.45 s, fwhm = 3.94 s for Sustained) on trajectories that pass omnibus gating.
Finally, parcel-level group tables from either mixed_by() or medusa_multilag_infer() map directly onto 3D or 4D NIfTI volumes via backproject_medusa(..., brain_mask = decon, fill = NA_real_) (see recipe below and Spatial Graph Pooling).

section: Recommended Settings
text:
Recommended Settings

Pathway A: Split-wise mixed models (mixed_by()) & NIfTI backprojection

library(medusa)

group_formula <- decon_demixed ~ value_within + value_mean + entropy_within +
  (1 + value_within + entropy_within || id) + (1 | id:run)

group_models <- mixed_by(
  group_panel,
  model_formulae = list(trial_effects = group_formula),
  split_on       = c("parcel", "evt_time"),
  weights        = "precision_weight_cohort",
  calculate      = "parameter_estimates_reml",
  padjust_by     = NULL,
  tidy_args      = list(effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE),
  return_models  = TRUE
)

focal_tests <- subset(
  group_models$coef_df_reml,
  term %in% c("value_within", "entropy_within")
)
focal_tests$p_by <- p.adjust(focal_tests$p.value, method = "BY")

Matched coordinates when using ZCA-whitened panels (use_whitened = TRUE): In rapid-ISI designs where conditional residuals retain serial correlation, set whiten_panel = TRUE in Step 4 and pair decon_demixed_whitened with *_whitened predictors from the same (parcel, evt_time) split (forming any within-run interaction columns before Step 4 whitening, since \(T(x \odot z) \neq (Tx) \odot (Tz)\)).
Interpreting between-person effects: Because Step 2 centers BOLD within each run, tonic run-constant baselines are removed; person-mean predictors (x_mean) test differences in average event-locked phasic deflections across people (or cross-level x_within * trait moderation), scaled in physical BOLD units under Step 1’s HRF normalization (normalize = "positive_lobe").
Scope transition to Step 6: Step 5 treats neural activity as the dependent outcome predicted by error-free task or behavioral covariates (for visual diagnostics of uncentered predictors and omitted random slopes, see the Visual QC Gallery). Whenever a deconvolved neural readout moves to the right-hand side to predict another brain region (Target ~ Seed * Task) or behavior (Behavior ~ Seed), proceed to Step 6 (decon_connectivity_repair()) to correct predictor measurement error and shared regional noise.

title: Step 6: Trial-Level Connectivity and PPI
text:
Overview
Whereas Step 5 places deconvolved neural activity on the left-hand side as an outcome (Neural ~ Behavior), Step 6 moves a deconvolved parcel readout onto the right-hand side (Target ~ Seed + Task + Seed:Task or Behavior ~ Seed) to test trial-to-trial functional connectivity and psychophysiological interaction (PPI).
When an estimated quantity with trial-level sampling error is used as a regression predictor, two measurement properties directly affect structural slopes (Fuller, 1987; Vig & Hallquist, 2026): predictor measurement error inflates the observed design variance \(X^\top X\) (attenuating both main connectivity and PPI interaction slopes toward zero), and any shared scanner or physiological noise between seed and target shifts the cross-product \(X^\top Y\). Step 6 (decon_connectivity_repair(), backed by medusa_fit_mmom()) subtracts Step 4’s analytical per-trial error variances (se_demixed^2) alongside stationary and dynamic cross-parcel error covariances from the Adaptive-POET + covariance-regression engine (shared_error_model / shared_noise_vec) while guarding against unstable small denominators in noisy scans (Modified Method of Moments with Step-up Regularization, M-MOMS), computes cross-trial sandwich standard errors and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom (crosstrial_se = TRUE, supporting calibrated single-subject \(N = 1\) inference), and aggregates participant slopes across cohorts using Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman (HKSJ) random-effects \(t\)-intervals.
library(medusa)

ppi <- decon_connectivity_repair(
  panel_dt             = subject_epochs,
  seed_region          = "Seed",
  target_region        = "Target",
  seed_lag             = 0,
  target_lag           = 0,
  covariates           = "x_within",
  test_ppi             = TRUE,
  orthogonalize_seed_x = FALSE,
  shared_error         = "auto",
  crosstrial_se        = TRUE,
  method               = "mmoms"
)
The walkthrough below develops Step 6 in four substeps directly paralleling the REPAIR two-step moment framework: specifying the latent structural equation (6.1), constructing the trial-specific error covariance matrices (6.2), estimating participant slopes via regularized M-MOMS (6.3), and pooling across participants (6.4).

title: Step 6: Trial-Level Connectivity and PPI
section: Goals, Inputs, and Outputs
text:
Goals, Inputs, and Outputs

Goals of Step 6

Disattenuate noisy neural predictors and PPI product terms: Construct per-trial predictor measurement-error covariance blocks \(\Psi_i\)—capturing both heteroskedastic interaction error \(x_i^2 s_i^2\) and off-diagonal seed–interaction error covariance \(x_i s_i^2\)—and subtract them from observed design moments.
Account for stationary and dynamic cross-parcel shared measurement error: Subtract expected per-trial seed–target error covariance \(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i \mid x_i, w_i)\) (shared_error = "auto") estimated by Step 4’s subspace-debiased Adaptive-POET + LTZ-gated dynamic covariance-regression engine across task drive, covariates, Step-2 rwls bursts, and frame-level variance_confounds.
Support clear direct and residualized-seed PPI parameterizations: Allow analysts to choose explicitly between unresidualized seed coupling (orthogonalize_seed_x = FALSE) and task-residualized seed coupling with exact error-covariance projection (orthogonalize_seed_x = TRUE).
Deliver calibrated single-subject (\(N = 1\)) and cohort uncertainty: Compute cross-trial (\(i \neq j\)) hybrid operator + gated onset-kernel sandwich SEs and Satterthwaite df within each participant (crosstrial_se = TRUE), and pool across cohorts (\(S \ge 2\)) via leverage-guarded HKSJ random-effects inference.



Inputs: What Step 6 Receives and Why



Input
Structure
Why Step 6 Uses It

Named subject_epochs list (preferred), stacked group_panel, .rds / Parquet, or pipe-delimited CSV/.csv.gz from medusa_write_table()

Parcel names and peri-event lags (e.g., seed_lag = 0, target_lag = 0 or lagged seed_lag = 0, target_lag = 4)
Select the paired seed readout \(\widehat{z}_{S,i}\) and target readout \(\widehat{z}_{T,i}\) along with their trial-specific measurement SEs.

When testing directed cross-lag grids (e.g., lags = c(0, 2, 4)), setting multilag_control = TRUE (or control_seed_lags = c(0, 2, 4)) enters companion seed lags and pre-target target lags jointly with full cross-lag measurement-error covariance subtraction so deconvolution smoothness across adjacent lags never creates off-diagonal false positives.

title: Step 6: Trial-Level Connectivity and PPI
section: Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points
text:
Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points

6.1 Specify the latent trial connectivity or PPI structural equation
Within a participant (after centering seed, target, and task covariates within each run), let \(\theta_{S,i}\) denote true latent seed amplitude at seed_lag, \(\theta_{T,i}\) denote latent target amplitude at target_lag, and \(x_i\) denote an error-free centered task modulator on trial \(i\):
\[
\theta_{T,i} = \beta_S \theta_{S,i} + \beta_x x_i + \beta_P (\theta_{S,i} x_i) + \varepsilon_i.
\]
Each coefficient answers a distinct biological question: \(\beta_S\) is baseline trial-to-trial seed–target coupling at the mean of \(x_i\) (\(x_i = 0\)), \(\beta_x\) absorbs direct task activation in the target parcel so shared main-effect responses are not mistaken for coupling, and \(\beta_P\) is the PPI slope—how much seed–target coupling changes per unit change in \(x_i\) (for \(x_i \in \{-1, +1\}\), \(2\beta_P\) is the slope difference between task conditions).
Choice point — Seed parameterization (orthogonalize_seed_x), operator resolution matching (match_resolution), and multi-lag directed partialing (control_target_seed_lag & multilag_control):

Task-orthogonalized vs. unresidualized seed (orthogonalize_seed_x): By default (orthogonalize_seed_x = TRUE), Step 6 residualizes each run’s seed readout against the resolution-matched task covariates (projecting seed error moments symmetrically through \(P_s = I - M_s M_s^\top\)) prior to forming PPI products—preventing direct linear task drive on the seed (\(\beta_{S,x} x_i\)) from injecting quadratic \(x_i^2\) variance into seed_c:x_c and attenuating intrinsic task-modulated coupling. Set orthogonalize_seed_x = FALSE when testing a structural equation defined directly on total (task-driven + intrinsic) seed amplitude.
Seed–target resolution & PPI product matching (match_resolution = TRUE): Across regions with distinct GCV smoothing parameters or HRF shapes (\(M_S \neq M_T\)), and even under equal smoothing where post-demixing elementwise multiplication satisfies \((M_S \eta_S) \odot x \neq M_T (\eta_S \odot x)\), uncorrected latent moments shift EIV slopes by \(H_{SS}^{-1} H_{ST}\). With match_resolution = TRUE (default), decon_connectivity_repair() reads exact run-level trial resolution matrices (run_trial_operators, or embedded 8-lag trial_res_vec bands on rbindlist()-stacked and CSV panels) to align predictor and error moments to Target’s transfer operator automatically.
Concurrent vs. multi-lag partialed directed coupling (control_target_seed_lag & multilag_control): When testing a single lagged pair (target_lag > seed_lag), setting control_target_seed_lag = TRUE includes target activity at seed_lag as an error-corrected control so \(\beta_S\) and \(\beta_P\) test subsequent target change. When sweeping a \(K \times K\) grid of (seed_lag, target_lag) pairs (for example, lags = c(0, 2, 4)), running 9 separate marginal single-lag regressions allows regularized deconvolution autocorrelation to project a true Seed(0 s) -> Target(4 s) effect onto (0 -> 2), (2 -> 4), and (4 -> 4). Setting multilag_control = TRUE (or passing control_seed_lags) fits a joint multi-lag EIV equation that partials out companion seed lags and preceding target lags simultaneously while subtracting their full cross-lag measurement-error covariance (lag_noise_vec / lag_error_cor)—isolating the true directed lag cell cleanly.




6.2 Construct trial-specific predictor and shared-error covariance matrices
In practice, Step 4 provides de-mixed additive-error readouts \(\widehat{z}_{S,i} = \theta_{S,i} + u_i\) and \(\widehat{z}_{T,i} = \theta_{T,i} + v_i\) rather than latent \((\theta_{S,i}, \theta_{T,i})\), with known conditional sampling variances \(s_{S,i}^2 = \texttt{se\_demixed}_{S,i}^2\) and \(s_{T,i}^2 = \texttt{se\_demixed}_{T,i}^2\). Forming the observed predictor row \(X_i = [\widehat{z}_{S,i},\, x_i,\, \widehat{z}_{S,i} x_i]^\top\) and observed outcome \(Y_i = \widehat{z}_{T,i}\) induces predictor error \(e_{X,i} = [u_i,\, 0,\, x_i u_i]^\top\).
Notice that even though \(u_i\) is a scalar on trial \(i\), both the seed column (\(\widehat{z}_{S,i}\)) and the ppi column (\(\widehat{z}_{S,i} x_i\)) contain the same noise draw \(u_i\), producing a structured \(3 \times 3\) predictor measurement-error covariance block on trial \(i\):
\[
\Psi_i = \operatorname{Cov}(e_{X,i} \mid x_i) = s_{S,i}^2 \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & x_i \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ x_i & 0 & x_i^2 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Two properties follow immediately from \(\Psi_i\): interaction error variance scales heteroskedastically with \(x_i^2 s_{S,i}^2\), and whenever \(x_i \neq 0\), the predictor and interaction errors covary with signed entry \(x_i s_{S,i}^2\).
At the same time, scanner drift, physiological pulsatility, head micro-movements, and vascular proximity can induce correlated observation error \(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i \mid x_i, w_i) = c_i\) between seed and target parcels—including trial-varying error covariance when physiological arousal, sub-scrubbing motion jolts, or respiration fluctuates with task demands—shifting the observed cross-moment \(X_i Y_i\) by \([c_i,\, 0,\, x_i c_i]^\top\). Under shared_error = "auto", Step 6 evaluates per-trial \((s_{S,i}^2, s_{T,i}^2, c_i)\) directly from Step 4’s Adaptive-POET + LTZ-gated dynamic covariance-regression model (shared_error_model in operator mode—including on-the-fly dynamic covariance evaluation against the PPI modulator even when Step 3 was run covariate-agnostically with covariates = NULL, plus exact Step-2 rwls frame_weights jolt propagation—or inner products of the per-trial Block-PAF vectors shared_noise_vec and lag_noise_vec on stacked/CSV panels, projected onto the positive semi-definite cone).
Choice point — Cross-parcel shared error (shared_error): Use shared_error = "auto" (paired with shared_error_method = "poet_covreg" and variance_confounds in Step 4) as the standard setting, and compare against shared_error = "zero" to see how much stationary and dynamic background noise correlation contributed to the raw coupling estimate.



6.3 Estimate participant slopes via regularized Modified Method of Moments (M-MOMS)
Given observed trial vectors \((X_i, Y_i)\) and error moments \((\Psi_i, c_i)\), medusa_fit_mmom() estimates each participant’s structural coefficients in three non-iterative moment steps (Fuller, 1987; Vig & Hallquist, 2026):

Error-corrected preliminary normal equations: Subtracts predictor error covariances from \(X^\top X\) and shared seed–target error covariances from \(X^\top Y\): \[
\left(X^\top X - c(\hat{\lambda}_1, \alpha_1)\sum_{i=1}^n \Psi_i\right) \widehat{\beta}^{(1)}
= X^\top Y - c(\hat{\lambda}_1, \alpha_1)\sum_{i=1}^n \begin{pmatrix} c_i \\ 0 \\ x_i c_i \end{pmatrix},
\] where Fuller’s generalized-eigenvalue factor \(c(\hat{\lambda}, \alpha)\) prevents subtracting more error variance than the sample design matrix supports.
Structural disturbance variance & composite trial weights: Uses \(\widehat{\beta}^{(1)}\) to estimate measurement-error-corrected structural disturbance variance \(\hat{\sigma}_\varepsilon^2\) and forms per-trial composite residual variances \(\hat{w}_i = \hat{\sigma}_\varepsilon^2 + s_{T,i}^2 - 2\widehat{\beta}^{(1)\top}\psi_{XY,i} + \widehat{\beta}^{(1)\top}\Psi_i\widehat{\beta}^{(1)}\).
Weighted M-MOMS update & conditioning guard: Re-estimates \(\widehat{\beta}\) and sandwich standard errors using inverse composite weights \(\hat{w}_i^{-1}\). Under method = "mmoms", an adaptive step-up search selects the smallest regularization constant \(\alpha \ge p + 1\) that keeps the corrected predictor block well-conditioned—preventing small-denominator outliers in low-reliability participants while matching unmodified M-MOM whenever signal reliability is moderate to high.

Choice point — Moment estimator (method): Use method = "mmoms" as the primary estimator, and fit method = "naive_unweighted" in the same coordinates (use_whitened = FALSE) alongside it so the magnitude of measurement-error disattenuation is directly visible.



6.4 Pool participant slopes and compare against naive regression
Across independent participants, decon_connectivity_repair() pools participant slopes \(\widehat{\beta}_s\) and standard errors using dispersion-scaled finite-sample random-effects \(t\)-intervals (Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman, HKSJ meta-regression, with leverage protection against extreme precision weights), anchoring group degrees of freedom to the number of participants \(S\).
To see how M-MOMS behaves when disattenuating genuine trial-level PPI (Genuine PPI scenario in simulate.R: 120 simulated cohorts of \(S = 16\) participants, 2 runs × 60 trials, true population interaction \(\beta_P = 0.35\), seed and target measurement error SDs \(= 0.70\), independent errors), compare the top three rows of the benchmark table and left panel of Figure 10.1:

Naive regression is attenuated by roughly one-third (0.230 vs. true 0.350), yielding 0.0% 95% CI coverage because tight group SEs center around the attenuated value.
M-MOMS removes the attenuation (0.343), cuts population RMSE more than threefold (from 0.123 to 0.039), and restores nominal 95.0% confidence-interval coverage.

title: Step 6: Trial-Level Connectivity and PPI
section: Practical Diagnostics, Dynamic POET Covariance Regression, and Scope
text:
Practical Diagnostics, Dynamic POET Covariance Regression, and Scope

Resolving dynamic task- & confound-modulated shared noise (poet_covreg) vs. unmeasured sensitivity
What happens when physiological or motion noise correlation between two regions changes magnitude with task condition or respiration—for instance, condition-locked breath-holding or head motion during high-\(x_i\) trials?
Two distinct regimes arise depending on what data are available:

Full MEDuSA pipeline with multi-parcel BOLD & variance_confounds (poet_covreg): When decon_epoch_regression(..., shared_error_method = "poet_covreg", variance_confounds = conf) has access to multi-parcel whitened residuals (\(P = 9\) parcels) and frame-level variance envelopes (FD, DVARS, RVT), Adaptive-POET + LTZ-gated covariance regression estimates trial-varying cross-parcel error moments \(c_i\) directly—and embeds them onto panel$shared_noise_vec so even a CSV-exported stacked table retains full parity with operator mode. In Table 10.1 (Dynamic Shared-Noise Null: 24 cohorts of \(S = 16\) participants, zero true coupling or PPI, pervasive physiological factor plus RVT-modulated bursts and two pure-null confound columns), ignoring shared error (Zero Shared Error) yields strong false main coupling (0.161, 75.0% false positives) and stationary-only shrinkage (Legacy Stationary (auto)) still inflates Type I error (0.041, 20.8% false positives). POET + CovReg eliminates the bias in both operator mode and CSV-restored stacked mode (seed_c mean -0.002 / -0.002, 4.2% Type I error, 95.8% coverage; seed_c:x_c 87.5% coverage). Likewise, in single-subject (\(N = 1\)) rapid-ITI scans (mean ITI = 2.2 s), enabling crosstrial_se = TRUE accounts for serial trial error correlation via Satterthwaite df (55.5 vs. Inf), improving CI coverage from 83.3% to 85.8% (see the 15-Study Validation Suite Pillar 15 for full multi-regime power and calibration curves).

Bare two-parcel tables or unmeasured pairwise-only confounds (post-hoc sensitivity curve): If a panel was stripped of shared-error columns—or if a purely local, unmeasured vascular artifact flips correlation exclusively between two adjacent regions (Shared-error null in Figure 10.1, right: bare 2-parcel table with \(\beta_P = 0\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i \mid x_i) = 0.65 x_i \sigma^2\), zero run-wide average correlation, and no multi-parcel or variance_confounds signature)—then \(\mathbb{E}[x_i u_i v_i] = r \sigma^2 \neq 0\) produces a positive naive artifact (0.214) that predictor disattenuation magnifies (0.322), returning to zero (-0.018) once the condition-specific cross-error moment is supplied. Plotting the implied M-MOMS slope across hypothesized condition-modulated cross-error correlations \(r(x)\) (Figure 10.2) makes transparent how extreme an unmeasured local artifact would need to be to explain an observed PPI.







Figure 10.2: Sensitivity curve in the shared-error null scenario: implied population PPI slope as a function of hypothesized condition-dependent cross-error correlation amplitude (crossing zero at the generating value 0.65).





Reporting checklist and scope boundaries

Report circuit, lag, and estimand choices: Document seed_region, target_region, seed_lag, target_lag, orthogonalize_seed_x, control_target_seed_lag, and multiplicity adjustment across region pairs (see Appendix A: Reporting MEDuSA in Empirical Papers for an adaptable Methods template).
Present naive and M-MOMS side by side: Include "naive_unweighted" alongside "mmoms" and summarize ppi$subjects (r_shared_error, alpha_final, lambda_final, participant/trial counts, and convergence; see the Visual QC Gallery for side-by-side participant connectivity distributions under intact vs. stripped shared_error metadata).
Scope boundaries: Just as in Vig & Hallquist (2026), Step 6 treats first-stage error variances (se_demixed^2) and selected regularization constants as fixed plug-in quantities, requires full-rank within-person predictor designs with adequate seed reliability, and corrects within-trial second moments rather than asymmetric cross-parcel resolution differences (\(K_S \neq K_T\)). For mathematical derivations and full-covariance extensions, see Propagating BOLD Noise into Trial Standard Errors and Latent Connectivity Beyond Per-Trial Disattenuation.

title: Visual QC and Troubleshooting Gallery
text:
Overview
When an end-to-end single-trial fMRI analysis yields unexpectedly weak slopes, implausibly shifted peri-event peaks, or inflated connectivity estimates, identifying which pipeline stage introduced the distortion is much faster when you know the visual signature each failure mode leaves behind. Because MEDuSA preserves explicit diagnostic summaries, operator resolution metrics, and propagated standard errors at every stage (see the end-to-end data-flow schematic), most upstream mis-specifications can be localized in a few lines of R before fitting group models across hundreds of parcels.
The snippet below collects the six fastest pre-flight checks across a completed or pilot participant workflow:
# 1. Step 0: Check motion censoring share, dummy frames, and event clock bounds (in seconds)
print(sub01$confounds$summary[, c("run", "n_volumes", "pct_censored", "n_non_steady_state")])
lapply(split(sub01$events$onset, sub01$events$run), range)

# 2. Step 1: Check out-of-sample HRF task relevance and AR(p) rho stationarity ceiling (0.90)
lapply(hrf_fit$selections, function(s) summary(s$selected_task_p))
lapply(hrf_fit$noise, function(n) quantile(n$rho[, 1], probs = c(0.5, 0.9, 0.99), na.rm = TRUE))

# 3. Step 2: Check deconvolution conditional self-gain and attenuation
diagnose_crossrun_recovery(decon, events = sub01$events)$summary

# 4. Step 3 & 4: Audit trial-level SE distribution and BOLD-coverage NA gating
summary(epochs$panel$se_demixed)
mean(is.na(epochs$panel$decon_demixed))

# 5. Step 5: Verify predictor centering (run/person mean ~ 0) and random-effect singularity
tapply(group_panel$rpe_within, group_panel$id, mean, na.rm = TRUE) |> summary()

# 6. Step 6: Inspect M-MOMS attenuation factor (alpha_final) and shared cross-parcel error
summary(ppi$subjects[, c("estimate", "r_shared_error", "alpha_final", "converged")])

title: Visual QC and Troubleshooting Gallery
section: Visual Diagnostic Pairs Across the Pipeline
text:
Visual Diagnostic Pairs Across the Pipeline

1. Steps 0 & 1: Event-Clock Shifts, Onset-Unit Errors, and AR(1) Ceiling Pile-Ups






Figure 11.1: Healthy versus mis-specified diagnostics in Steps 0 and 1. A: True feedback RPE slope (0.60 at lag 0 s, TR = 2.0 s) recovered cleanly when initial dummy volumes are masked via valid_rows (blue), versus physically dropping 3 dummy volumes without setting time_offset = 6 (solid red, shifting the recovered peak backward to -6 s) or supplying events$onset in TR indices rather than seconds (dashed amber, compressing all events into the first half of the scan and destroying the association). B: Parcel-level hrf_fit$noise$run1$rho across 36 parcels (true \(\rho \in [0.30, 0.62]\)) on detrended BOLD (blue) versus BOLD contaminated by an unmodeled mid-run shim step and low-frequency drift (red, pinning 100% of parcels against the 0.90 stationarity ceiling).



What to look for in Figure 11.1:

Event-clock shifts (Panel A, solid red): If an external script slices \(k\) initial dummy volumes out of the 4D NIfTI file (Y <- Y[-c(1:k), ]) while events.tsv remains referenced to the first scanner trigger (time_offset = 0), row 1 of the matrix is actually acquired at \(t = k \cdot \text{TR}\) rather than \(t = 0\). Every neural response then appears in the BOLD record \(k \cdot \text{TR}\) seconds earlier than the event table expects—producing an unmistakable “pre-stimulus” peak at \(-k \cdot \text{TR}\) (-6 s here for 3 dropped 2.0 s volumes) and near-zero effect at 0 s.
Onset-unit mismatches (Panel A, dashed amber): Passing 0-based or 1-based volume indices instead of seconds when \(\text{TR} \ne 1.0\text{ s}\) rescales the entire task timeline by \(1 / \text{TR}\). Step 1’s cross-run HRF selector finds almost no out-of-sample variance explained (selected_task_p shifts toward uniform noise), and Step 3 lag profiles flatten to zero.
Stationarity ceiling pile-ups (Panel B, red): Step 1 bounds REML \(\text{AR}(p)\) roots inside a causal, stationary region (rho <= 0.90 for \(\text{AR}(1)\)) so prewhitening stays invertible. A natural physiological distribution spans roughly 0.25–0.70 depending on \(\text{TR}\). When a large share of parcels stacks directly on 0.90, the noise model is absorbing deterministic low-frequency drift, coil/shim jumps, or unmasked motion bursts rather than stationary innovations.


# Diagnostic check & remedy for Steps 0-1
stopifnot(max(sub01$events$onset) <= max(sub01$confounds$summary$n_volumes) * sub01$tr)
mean(hrf_fit$noise$run1$rho[, 1] >= 0.89, na.rm = TRUE)  # healthy: typically < 0.05

# Remedy: keep intact 4D runs + valid_rows, and ensure drift + FD censoring are active
sub01   <- read_fmriprep_subject(..., strategy = "24p", fd_threshold = 0.5, include_non_steady_state = TRUE)
hrf_fit <- estimate_crossrun_hrf(sub01, kernel_grid = candidates, drift_order = 2L, pooling = "parcel")

For full walkthroughs of clock-preserving ingestion and prewhitening choices, see Step 0 and Step 1.



2. Step 2: Over-Smoothing Gain Collapse and Uncensored Spike Ringing






Figure 11.2: Healthy versus mis-specified continuous deconvolution in Step 2. A: Continuous restored activity trace \(\widehat{a}_r(t)\) across 67–117 s of Run 1 containing two true neural events (76 s and 108 s, green dotted lines) and a framewise motion artifact at 91 s (red dashed line). Healthy deconvolution with valid_rows censoring and automatic \(\lambda_v\) / RWLS recovers crisp phasic peaks at 76 s and 108 s while suppressing 91 s (blue). Fixing lambda = 8.0 flattens true neural peaks nearly to zero (amber), whereas leaving the 91 s spike uncensored with rwls = "none" produces strong positive and negative deconvolution ringing lobes across 82–96 s (red). B: diagnose_crossrun_recovery() immediately flags over-smoothing via collapsed mean_gain (0.043 vs. 0.317), whereas uncensored spike artifacts leave deterministic operator mean_gain almost unchanged (0.300) and therefore require inspecting censoring masks or RWLS weights.



What to look for in Figure 11.2:

Gain collapse from over-regularization (amber): Because continuous deconvolution trades variance reduction against temporal shrinkage via the resolution matrix \(D_r H_r\), setting lambda manually to a large value crushes the diagonal self-gain of diagnose_crossrun_recovery() below 0.05. Notice that deconvolve_crossrun_hrf() scales penalties cleanly when scaling = "noise_sd" and lambda = NULL; manual lambda overrides are rarely needed outside sensitivity analyses.
Why spike ringing requires both operator and residual/weight checks (red): Look closely at Panel B: the uncensored spike run (rwls = "none", no valid_rows mask) still reports a healthy-looking mean_gain = 0.300 in diagnose_crossrun_recovery(). That is because mean_gain audits the linear operator \(D_r H_r\), which depends on the HRF, run schedule, and \(\lambda_v\)—not on an isolated BOLD outlier in \(y_r\). An unmasked motion spike acts like a delta impulse that does not follow the slow hemodynamic shape \(h_r\); inverting \(H_r\) therefore surrounds the spike with alternating positive and negative side-lobes across neighboring timepoints. Masking high-FD frames via valid_rows (Step 0) and keeping rwls = "auto" (Step 2) prevents these artifacts from contaminating nearby trials.


# Check both operator gain AND adaptive RWLS outlier downweighting
rec <- diagnose_crossrun_recovery(decon, events = sub01$events)
print(rec$summary[, c("run", "mean_gain", "mean_abs_gain_error", "mean_abs_excess_leakage")])

# Inspect minimum RWLS observation weights per run (weights << 1 indicate downweighted residual spikes)
lapply(decon$rwls_weights, function(w) quantile(w, probs = c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.5), na.rm = TRUE))

For details on Sobolev versus ridge penalties, scaling = "noise_sd", and rwls = "auto", see Step 2.



3. Steps 3 & 4: Motion-Scrubbing Shadows in Trial SEs and Shrunken Outcome Misuse






Figure 11.3: Healthy versus mis-specified trial epoching and panel assembly in Steps 3 and 4. A: Propagated trial-level standard error (se_demixed) across 16 feedback trials in Run 1. In an uncensored run (blue), interior trials share uniform precision (se_demixed \(\approx 0.062\)) with an expected uptick only on Trial 16 (215.5 s, whose causal HRF tail is truncated by scanner shutoff at 220 s). When 3 frames on Trial 7’s HRF peak are motion-scrubbed (red), se_demixed spikes selectively at Trial 7 (0.076) so downstream precision weights downweight it automatically; when 10 frames covering Trial 11’s HRF are scrubbed, min_bold_coverage gates Trial 11 cleanly to NA (red dashed line). B: Entering decon_demixed + precision_weight_cohort in mixed_by() across 16 participants recovers the generating slope (0.454 vs. truth 0.50, blue), whereas mistakenly entering empirical-Bayes shrunken decon_eb as the outcome shrinks the estimated population slope nearly in half (0.231, red).



What to look for in Figure 11.3:

Protective se_demixed spikes vs. run-wide degradation (Panel A): Seeing isolated spikes in panel$se_demixed (like Trial 7) or run-boundary upticks (like Trial 16) is not a software bug—it is the propagated sandwich covariance \(\Omega_{r,\tau}\) faithfully recording where censored frames or run-end truncation reduced effective BOLD observations inside that event’s hemodynamic window. When precision_weight_cohort is passed to mixed_by(), Trial 7 receives lower inverse-variance weight automatically, and Trial 11 (NA) is omitted without shifting event_index. Intervention is only warranted when a run has so many censored frames that most trials sit at elevated se_demixed or NA.
Outcome vs. predictor column roles in Step 4 panels (Panel B): Step 4 exports both unshrunken decon_demixed (\(\widehat{z}_{ri} = \theta_{ri} + e_{ri}\)) and empirical-Bayes shrunken decon_eb (\(\tilde{z}_{ri} \approx \bar{z} + \kappa_{ri}(\widehat{z}_{ri} - \bar{z})\), where \(\kappa_{ri} = \widehat{\tau}^2 / (\widehat{\tau}^2 + s_{ri}^2) < 1\)). Entering decon_eb on the left-hand side of mixed_by() multiplies the true fixed-effect slope by \(\bar{\kappa} < 1\) (0.231 vs. 0.454 here), biasing population inference toward zero.


# Audit per-run NA gating rate and high-SE tail in Step 3/4 panels
panel_dt <- data.table::as.data.table(epochs$panel)
panel_dt[, .(
  pct_gated_na = 100 * mean(is.na(decon_demixed)),
  median_se    = median(se_demixed, na.rm = TRUE),
  p95_se       = quantile(se_demixed, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)
), by = run]

# Always pair decon_demixed + precision_weight_cohort when neural activity is the outcome
group_models <- mixed_by(group_panel, outcomes = "decon_demixed",
                         rhs_model_formulae = ~ rpe_within + (1 + rpe_within || id) + (1 | id:run),
                         split_on = c("parcel", "evt_time"), weights = "precision_weight_cohort")

For full guidance on min_bold_coverage, (T, O) de-mixing, and column-role assignment, see Step 3 and Step 4.



4. Steps 5 & 6: Multilevel Centering/Random-Slope Pitfalls and Connectivity Shared Noise






Figure 11.4: Healthy versus mis-specified group inference (Step 5) and trial-level connectivity (Step 6). A: Across 36 participants (16 target trials/person) where true within-person trial coupling is +0.45 but between-person trait coupling is -0.35 with participant slope SD 0.42, decomposing x_within + x_mean with (1 + x_within || id) recovers +0.434 (df = 35, blue). Entering uncentered x_raw conflates within- and between-person variance and flips the estimated slope to -0.258 (red), while omitting the random slope (1 | id) understates uncertainty with pooled-trial degrees of freedom (df = 573, amber). B: Participant connectivity slopes (ppi$subjects, term == "seed_c") across 16 participants where true seed-to-target neural coupling is 0.35 and shared cross-parcel measurement error is \(r_{ST} = 0.55\). M-MOMS with shared_error = "auto" recovers 0.295 (blue); stripping unit_error_cor / shared_noise_loading (shared_error = "zero") disattenuates shared noise up to 0.751 (red); naive OLS without measurement-error repair attenuates down to 0.178 (amber).



What to look for in Figure 11.4:

Within/between conflation and inflated degrees of freedom in Step 5 (Panel A): Any predictor that varies both across trials within a person (e.g., trial-by-trial RT, value, arousal) and in mean level across people (fast vs. slow responders, high vs. low baseline value) carries two distinct biological associations. Entering raw x_raw forces lmer() to estimate a precision-weighted blend of \(\beta_{\text{within}}\) and \(\beta_{\text{between}}\)—which can attenuate or even reverse the sign of the trial effect (-0.258 vs. +0.45). Equally important, inspect the df column of coef_df_reml: a within-person fixed effect tested across \(S = 36\) participants should have Satterthwaite df near \(S - 1\) (35), never in the hundreds (573), which signals that the random slope (1 + x_within || id) was omitted or collapsed to zero.
Asymmetric bias modes in Step 6 connectivity (Panel B): When deconvolved seed activity moves to the right-hand side as a noisy predictor (Target ~ Seed * Task), two opposing biases act simultaneously: seed estimation variance \(s_{S,i}^2\) attenuates naive OLS toward zero (0.178), while correlated scanner/physiological noise shared across parcels (\(r_{ST} > 0\)) inflates coupling. If you export panel to a plain .csv file without shared_noise_loading or the participant unit_error_cor matrix (forcing shared_error = "zero"), M-MOMS subtracts seed error variance in the denominator without subtracting shared error covariance in the numerator—magnifying shared noise (0.751). Passing the intact subject_epochs list (or preserving shared_noise_loading in tabular exports) allows shared_error = "auto" to correct both terms simultaneously (0.295).


# Step 5 audit: check Satterthwaite df on within-person terms (should scale with N_subjects, not N_trials)
subset(group_models$coef_df_reml, term == "rpe_within")[, c("parcel", "evt_time", "estimate", "std.error", "df")]

# Step 6 audit: confirm r_shared_error is non-zero when expected and check convergence
ppi <- decon_connectivity_repair(
  subject_epochs, seed_region = "Seed", target_region = "Target",
  covariates = "x_within", shared_error = "auto", method = "mmoms"
)
summary(ppi$subjects[, c("r_shared_error", "alpha_final", "converged")])

For complete coverage of group trajectory modeling and M-MOMS connectivity repair, see Step 5 and Step 6.


Simulation Details & Reproduction

All four healthy-versus-pathological figure pairs and Table 11.1 are generated from live medusa calls (estimate_crossrun_hrf(), deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(), diagnose_crossrun_recovery(), decon_epoch_regression(), mixed_by(), and decon_connectivity_repair()) with fixed seed 20261116:

Pair 1 (Steps 0 & 1): 3 runs \(\times\) 140 volumes at TR = 2.0 s, 16 jittered feedback events/run with true lag-0 RPE slope 0.60; compares valid_rows dummy masking (1:3) against physical truncation (Y[-c(1:3), ] with time_offset = 0) and onset-unit mis-specification (on_sec / tr_slow). Step 1 rho check simulates 36 parcels (true rho uniform on [0.30, 0.62]) with and without an unmodeled mid-run shim step + 0.008 Hz drift.
Pair 2 (Step 2): 3 runs \(\times\) 180 volumes at TR = 1.0 s; compares valid_rows censoring + automatic GCV \(\lambda_v\) + rwls = "auto" against lambda = 8.0 and an uncensored 91 s spike with rwls = "none".
Pair 3 (Steps 3 & 4): 3 runs \(\times\) 220 volumes (16 trials/run, Trial 16 at 215.5 s), comparing uncensored se_demixed against partial peak scrubbing on Trial 7 (3 frames) and full HRF scrubbing on Trial 11 (10 frames); plus a 16-participant cohort comparing decon_demixed + precision_weight_cohort against shrunken decon_eb as outcome in mixed_by() (true slope 0.50).
Pair 4 (Steps 5 & 6): Step 5 simulates \(S = 36\) participants (16 target trials/person, \(\beta_{\text{within}} = +0.45\), \(\beta_{\text{between}} = -0.35\), random slope SD 0.42). Step 6 simulates \(S = 16\) participants (80 trials/person, true seed-target slope 0.35, shared cross-parcel error correlation \(r_{ST} = 0.55\), trial SE 0.75).
