title: Spatial Graph Pooling: Voxelwise and Parcel-Wise NIfTI Workflows
text:
Overview
Volumetric fMRI analysis faces a classic spatial dilemma whenever trial-by-trial dynamics are estimated across the cortex:
MEDuSA resolves this trade-off by pooling estimation evidence and variance parameters over a sparse, anatomically and functionally adaptive graph—without ever smoothing raw BOLD or deconvolved neural time series. Starting from a single NIfTI/atlas bundle (read_nifti_ts() or read_fmriprep_subject()), the spatial pooling architecture supports both full-resolution voxelwise mapping and precision-weighted parcel-panel modeling seamlessly:
Notice the synergy in Pathway B: even when your final group hypothesis in Step 5 or Step 6 is parcel-wise, running Step 1 with pooling = "graph" (parcel_boundary = "soft") and Step 2 with lambda_mode = "auto" before aggregating into parcels in Step 4 lets interior gray-matter and pial-rim voxels retain their distinct whiteners and HRF strata while Step 4’s exact multi-stratum operator (\(\sum_v u_v D_v F_v\)) combines them cleanly.
crumbs: 12  Spatial Graph Pooling: Voxelwise and Parcel-Wise NIfTI Workflows

title: Spatial Graph Pooling: Voxelwise and Parcel-Wise NIfTI Workflows
text:
Pure single-voxel estimation preserves fine spatial specificity, but single 2 mm voxels have low per-trial signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Unpooled voxelwise fits suffer from noisy HRF latency selection in Step 1, unstable \(\text{AR}(p)\) autocorrelation estimates, oversmoothed global cross-validation (GCV) penalties in Step 2, and severe zero-collapse (\(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2 = 0\)) when estimating biological trial-to-trial variance in Step 3.
Rigid group-atlas parcel pooling boosts SNR dramatically when a participant’s functional organization aligns with nominal parcel borders. Yet individual functional boundaries routinely shift by 4–10 mm relative to group templates (such as Schaefer-200), sub-parcel focal hotspots can occupy \(< 15\%\) of a large parcel, and exterior pial-vein voxels carry much stronger physiological autocorrelation than interior gray matter inside the same parcel.
Traditional isotropic Gaussian BOLD smoothing avoids atlas rigidity only by blurring raw time series across sulcal CSF spaces, opposing gyral banks, and functional borders—destroying spatial resolution and inducing unmodeled spatial noise covariance.








NoteTwo Complementary Spatial Pathways from One NIfTI Bundle




Pathway A — Voxelwise Graph-Pooled Mapping (write_nifti_ts): read_nifti_ts(..., mask, atlas) \(\longrightarrow\) estimate_crossrun_hrf(..., pooling = "graph") \(\longrightarrow\) deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(..., lambda_mode = "auto") \(\longrightarrow\) decon_epoch_regression(..., tau2_shrinkage = "graph_eb") \(\longrightarrow\) write_nifti_ts(..., reference = decon) \(\longrightarrow\) ggbrain
Pathway B — Parcel-Wise Multi-Stratum Panel (backproject_medusa): read_nifti_ts(..., mask, atlas) \(\longrightarrow\) estimate_crossrun_hrf(..., pooling = "graph") (preserving intra-parcel HRF & rim-noise heterogeneity) \(\longrightarrow\) deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(..., lambda_mode = "auto") \(\longrightarrow\) decon_epoch_regression(..., parcel_groups = ts$parcel_ids, restore_scale = TRUE, whiten_panel = TRUE, return_panel = TRUE) \(\longrightarrow\) mixed_by(..., weights = "precision_weight_cohort") \(\longrightarrow\) backproject_medusa(..., brain_mask = decon) \(\longrightarrow\) ggbrain

Choosing Between Voxelwise Graph-EB and Parcel-Wise Panels



Analysis Dimension
Pathway A: Voxelwise Graph-EB
Pathway B: Parcel-Wise Step 4 Panel




Best suited for
Sub-parcel focal nuclei/hotspots, shifted individual functional borders, fine retinotopic/topographic gradients, exploratory whole-brain mapping
Hypothesis-driven network/ROI inference, multi-lag trajectory testing (medusa_multilag_infer()), and M-MOMS trial connectivity/PPI (decon_connectivity_repair())


Step 1 HRF & noise
pooling = "graph", parcel_boundary = "soft", spatial_fwhm = 6
pooling = "graph" (parcel_boundary = "soft") or pooling = "parcel" when parcels are small and homogeneous


Step 2 deconvolution
scaling = "noise_sd", lambda_mode = "auto" (monotone SNR-stratified smoothing)
scaling = "noise_sd", lambda_mode = "auto" (propagates per-voxel \(\lambda_v\) into Step 4)


Step 3 / 4 epoch readout
aggregate_by_parcel = FALSE, restore_scale = TRUE, tau2_shrinkage = "graph_eb"
parcel_groups = ts$parcel_ids, restore_scale = TRUE, whiten_panel = TRUE, return_panel = TRUE


Spatial smoothing of \(\widehat{a}(t)\) or \(\hat{\beta}\)?
No. Only cross-run HRF scores, REML noise \((\hat{\rho}, \log\hat{\sigma})\), smoothed task-\(R^2\) tiers, and variance parameters \((\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2, \hat{\sigma}_{\text{res}}^2)\) pool across concordant neighbors
Aggregates continuous deconvolved series within each parcel using SNR-optimal parcel_weights and propagates spatial covariance via task-free noise_innovations


Volumetric NIfTI export
write_nifti_ts(stat_vec, file, reference = decon) (uses carried voxel_map + geometry directly)
backproject_medusa(coef_df, brain_mask = decon, ...) (maps integer atlas_value parcels directly onto 3D/4D NIfTIs)

title: Spatial Graph Pooling: Voxelwise and Parcel-Wise NIfTI Workflows
section: End-to-End Code Recipes with ggbrain
text:
End-to-End Code Recipes with ggbrain

Shared Step 0: Ingest 4D NIfTIs + Ribbon Mask + Atlas & Inspect Graph Topology
Whether your inputs come from fMRIPrep (read_fmriprep_subject(..., atlas = atlas_nii)) or preprocessed 4D NIfTI runs (read_nifti_ts()), MEDuSA validates grid/affine alignment up front and attaches voxel_map (i, j, k, x, y, z, linear_index, atlas_value), parcel_ids, and NIfTI geometry to the returned "medusa_nifti_ts" object.

library(medusa)
library(ggbrain)

# 1. Stream in-mask cortical ribbon time series + Schaefer parcel labels into memory
ts <- read_nifti_ts(
  niftis    = c("sub-01_run-01_bold.nii.gz",
                "sub-01_run-02_bold.nii.gz",
                "sub-01_run-03_bold.nii.gz"),
  mask      = "sub-01_space-MNI152NLin2009cAsym_desc-ribbon_mask.nii.gz",
  atlas     = "Schaefer2018_200Parcels_7Networks_2009c_2mm.nii.gz",
  tr        = 1.0,
  run_names = c("run1", "run2", "run3")
)

# Optional: build and inspect the cortical-sheet neighborhood graph explicitly
# (estimate_crossrun_hrf(..., pooling = "graph") builds this automatically when omitted)
g_geo <- build_spatial_graph(
  ts,
  spatial_fwhm    = 6,         # 6 mm cortical-sheet Gaussian kernel along 26-connected lattice
  parcel_boundary = "soft",    # soft cross-parcel relaxation when profiles agree
  metric          = "geodesic" # stops at out-of-mask CSF sulci and fissures
)



Pathway A: Voxelwise Graph-Pooled Analysis & ggbrain Visualization

# Step 1: Out-of-sample cortical-sheet HRF & REML AR(1) noise estimation
hrf_fit <- estimate_crossrun_hrf(
  bold            = ts,
  events          = events,
  kernel_grid     = hrf_library(tr = ts$tr, preset = "medusa"),
  pooling         = "graph",
  spatial_graph   = g_geo,
  parcel_boundary = "soft",
  amplitude_model = "auto",
  selection_mode  = "soft_average",
  noise_pcs       = "auto"
)

# Step 2: Event-informed continuous deconvolution with SNR-stratified smoothing
decon <- deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(
  bold          = ts,
  hrf_fit       = hrf_fit,
  scaling       = "noise_sd",
  lambda_mode   = "auto",        # task-SNR tiers with monotone non-increasing smoothing
  nuisance_mode = "preproject",  # pre-projects < 1/128 Hz DCT drift, confounds, & noise_pcs
  noise_pcs     = "auto"
)

# Optional: export the realized per-voxel log10(lambda) SNR-tier map in 1 line
write_nifti_ts(
  log10(decon$settings$lambda_by_voxel),
  "sub-01_log10_lambda.nii.gz",
  reference = decon,
  fill      = NA_real_
)

# Step 3 (Voxelwise): Epoch de-mixing + edge-preserving neighborhood variance pooling
ep_vox <- decon_epoch_regression(
  deconvolution    = decon,
  covariates       = covariates,       # e.g., list(run1 = data.frame(rpe = ...), ...)
  events           = events,
  target_condition = "feedback",
  lags             = -1:3,
  restore_scale    = TRUE,
  tau2_shrinkage   = "graph_eb"        # pre-truncation neighborhood shrinkage + hotspot guard
)

# Export lag = 0 s voxelwise GLS t-map directly using decon's carried NIfTI geometry
lag0_vox <- subset(ep_vox$coefficients, lag == 0 & term == "rpe")
t_vec    <- stats::setNames(lag0_vox$t_gls, lag0_vox$voxel)
write_nifti_ts(t_vec, "sub-01_feedback_rpe_t_lag0.nii.gz", reference = decon, fill = NA_real_)

# Render axial brain map with Schaefer parcel outlines in ggbrain
t1_nii    <- system.file("extdata", "mni_template_2009c_2mm.nii.gz", package = "ggbrain")
atlas_nii <- system.file("extdata", "Schaefer_200_7networks_2009c_2mm.nii.gz", package = "ggbrain")

gg_vox <- ggbrain(bg_color = "white") +
  images(c(underlay = t1_nii, atlas = atlas_nii, tmap = "sub-01_feedback_rpe_t_lag0.nii.gz")) +
  slices(c("z = 6", "z = 8", "z = 10")) +
  geom_brain("underlay[underlay > 8]",
             fill_scale = ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient(low = "#30363D", high = "#E6ECF0"),
             show_legend = FALSE) +
  geom_brain("tmap[abs(tmap) > 2.0]",
             fill_scale = scale_fill_bisided(name = "GLS t", symmetric = TRUE)) +
  geom_outline("atlas[atlas > 0]", mapping = ggplot2::aes(group = value),
               outline = "#1F2933", size = 1, alpha = 0.35, show_legend = FALSE)
plot(gg_vox)



Pathway B: Parcel-Wise Multi-Stratum Panel, Cohort mixed_by(), & ggbrain Map

# Step 4 (inside decon_epoch_regression): Exact multi-stratum parcel pooling
# Reuses the exact same graph-pooled `decon` object from Step 2
ep_parcel <- decon_epoch_regression(
  deconvolution    = decon,
  covariates       = covariates,
  events           = events,
  target_condition = "feedback",
  lags             = -1:3,
  parcel_groups    = ts$parcel_ids,    # triggers Step 4 continuous parcel aggregation
  restore_scale    = TRUE,
  whiten_panel     = TRUE,
  return_panel     = TRUE
)

# Attach participant ID and stack across subjects for Step 5 mixed_by()
panel_sub <- data.table::as.data.table(ep_parcel$panel)
panel_sub[, id := "sub-01"]
# ... repeat across cohort into `group_panel <- data.table::rbindlist(subject_panels)` ...

group_fit <- mixed_by(
  data               = group_panel,
  outcomes           = "decon_demixed",
  rhs_model_formulae = ~ rpe + (1 + rpe || id),
  split_on           = c("parcel", "evt_time"),
  weights            = "precision_weight_cohort",
  padjust_by         = "term",
  padjust_method     = "BY"
)

# Backproject Schaefer parcels directly onto 3D NIfTI via decon's carried map
# (`parcel` character IDs and `evt_time` are auto-detected and matched to `atlas_value`)
coef_lag0 <- subset(group_fit$coef_df_reml, term == "rpe" & evt_time == 0)

nii_paths <- backproject_medusa(
  coef_df    = coef_lag0,
  brain_mask = decon,                  # uses carried voxel_map$atlas_value & geometry directly
  plot_cols  = c("estimate", "statistic"),
  output_dir = "group_maps",
  fill       = NA_real_
)

# Plot group parcel statistic map in ggbrain
gg_par <- ggbrain(bg_color = "white") +
  images(c(underlay = t1_nii, atlas = atlas_nii, gstat = "group_maps/statistic_rpe.nii.gz")) +
  slices("z = 8", title = "Cohort feedback RPE t-map (lag = 0 s)") +
  geom_brain("underlay[underlay > 8]",
             fill_scale = ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient(low = "#30363D", high = "#E6ECF0"),
             show_legend = FALSE) +
  geom_brain("gstat[!is.na(gstat)]",
             fill_scale = scale_fill_bisided(name = "Group t", symmetric = TRUE)) +
  geom_outline("atlas[atlas > 0]", mapping = ggplot2::aes(group = value),
               outline = "#1F2933", size = 1, alpha = 0.4, show_legend = FALSE)
plot(gg_par)

section: Volumetric Benchmark on the MNI152 Cortical Ribbon
text:
Volumetric Benchmark on the MNI152 Cortical Ribbon
To evaluate every component of the spatial and parcel pooling pipeline against known ground truth on genuine human cortical folding, simulate_spatial_pooling.R constructs a 3-slice cortical gray-matter ribbon slab (\(z = 6, 8, 10\text{ mm}\), V = 6,655 voxels across 61 Schaefer-200 parcels) from mni_template_2009c_2mm.nii.gz and Schaefer_200_7networks_2009c_2mm.nii.gz. Three 4D NIfTI runs (TR = 1.0 s, 170 TRs/run, 22 jittered cue + feedback trials per run = 66 total target trials with a unit-variance signed rpe covariate) are written to disk and ingested via read_nifti_ts().
Four realistic anatomical and physiological testbeds are embedded simultaneously on the cortical sheet:

Cross-fissure barrier + parcel-aligned active cortex (Parcels 10 & 89 vs. 109 & 194): Left Calcarine (Parcel 10, fast 2.8 s HRF peak, \(\beta_{\text{RPE}} = +0.55\)) and Left Superior Medial PFC (Parcel 89, slow 6.8 s HRF peak, \(\beta_{\text{RPE}} = +0.50\)) are homogeneously active across their entire parcel boundaries, while their homologous right-hemisphere neighbors across the 2–4 mm interhemispheric CSF gap (Parcels 109 & 194, canonical 5.1 s HRF peak) are purely null for feedback RPE (\(\beta_{\text{RPE}} = 0, \tau_{\text{bio}} = 0\)).
Shifted individual functional/vascular border (Parcels 78 & 79, Left Posterior Temporal Cortex): While the group Schaefer boundary between Parcel 79 and Parcel 78 sits near \(y = -55\text{ mm}\) on \(z = 8\text{ mm}\), this participant’s true neurovascular and computational transition sits anteriorly at \(y = -43\text{ mm}\)—splitting Parcel 78 cleanly into a posterior slow-HRF negative-RPE zone (\(y \le -43\text{ mm}\), 6.8 s HRF peak, \(\beta_{\text{RPE}} = -0.62\)) and an anterior fast-HRF positive-RPE zone (\(y > -43\text{ mm}\), 2.8 s HRF peak, \(\beta_{\text{RPE}} = +0.62\)).
Sub-parcel focal hotspot (Parcel 155, Right Insula): A compact 30-voxel spherical nucleus (\(r \le 4.6\text{ mm}\) around \((42, 6, 8)\), occupying \(13.3\%\) of Parcel 155’s 225 voxels) exhibits strong positive RPE coding (\(\beta_{\text{RPE}} = +0.92, \tau_{\text{bio}} = 0.78\)) surrounded by 195 quiet insular voxels.
Whole-ribbon pial-vein vs. gray-matter noise heterogeneity: Exterior cortical rim voxels bordering CSF (23.0% of the mask) generate high temporal autocorrelation (\(\rho = 0.76, \sigma = 0.38\)) compared to interior gray matter (\(\rho = 0.28, \sigma = 0.21\)), driven by spatially correlated \(\text{AR}(1)\) innovations along the geodesic sheet.



1. Cortical-Sheet (Geodesic) Neighborhoods vs. 3D Euclidean Shortcuts (build_spatial_graph())
On folded cortex, two gyral banks separated by a dark CSF sulcus or longitudinal fissure are often only 2–5 mm apart in 3D Euclidean space while lying centimeters apart along the cortical sheet. When build_spatial_graph() receives a volumetric "medusa_nifti_ts" object (or 3D mask/voxel_map carrying integer lattice indices i, j, k), metric = "auto" measures shortest-path step distances strictly through connected in-mask gray-matter voxels (metric = "geodesic", computed on the 26-neighbor lattice via Dijkstra’s algorithm in physical millimeter world coordinates: \(2\text{ mm}\) face, \(2\sqrt{2}\text{ mm}\) edge-diagonal, \(2\sqrt{3}\text{ mm}\) corner-diagonal).






Figure 12.1: Geodesic lattice topology vs. 3D Euclidean cross-fissure shortcuts on the MNI152 cortical ribbon (z = 8 mm).



In our slab, an unconstrained 6 mm Euclidean graph (metric = "euclidean") creates 8,051 directed shortcut edges that jump across out-of-mask CSF gaps (547 in-plane pairs on \(z = 8\text{ mm}\) alone; orange segments in Figure 12.1, right). Along the posterior midline, those shortcuts bleed Left Calcarine’s fast HRF across the interhemispheric CSF cleft onto Right Calcarine’s medial rim (Parcel 109 rim HRF MAE = 0.828 s vs. 0.617 s under geodesic pooling).



2. Step 1 Edge-Preserving HRF Pooling & Soft Parcel Relaxation
Geodesic distance alone prevents cross-CSF shortcuts where the mask resolves the sulcus, yet two challenges remain: (a) at 2 mm resolution, narrow sulci are sometimes bridged by partial-volumed voxels, and (b) functional transitions occur inside continuous gyri where group parcel boundaries are misregistered. estimate_crossrun_hrf(..., pooling = "graph") addresses both by weighting nearby cortical neighbors by both anatomical sheet proximity and out-of-sample functional similarity (an edge-preserving bilateral graph filter):

Strict target-run exclusion: For held-out target run \(r\), training score profiles, noise \((\hat{\rho}^{(-r)}, \log\hat{\sigma}^{(-r)})\), and spatial noise correlations are computed exclusively from runs \(s \neq r\).
Concordance weighting & anti-correlation stopping: Neighbor \(v\)’s influence on focal voxel \(u\) combines cortical-sheet Gaussian proximity with the noise-disattenuated cross-run correlation between their candidate HRF score profiles (\(\tilde{c}_{uv}\)). Negative concordance triggers a sharp brake \(\exp(-3.5\gamma c_-^2)\), halting pooling across opposite-tuned or distinct vascular borders even on a continuous gyral ribbon.
Soft cross-parcel relaxation (parcel_boundary = "soft", parcel_cross_weight = 0.35): Cross-parcel edges start downweighted at 0.35 when task signal is ambiguous, but smoothly relax toward \(1.0\) when neighboring voxels across a nominal atlas line share strong positive out-of-sample candidate concordance.
Spatial noise calibration & stratum grouping: Combined cross-run evidence is scaled to account for shared local scanner noise between neighbors so correlated background noise never triggers false HRF switches in null cortex, and soft-averaged kernels are grouped into at most max_hrf_strata = 48L representative waveforms so Step 2 operator evaluation stays fast.







Figure 12.2: Step 1 HRF peak-latency recovery across single-voxel, group-parcel, and bilateral geodesic graph pooling.

As shown in Figure 12.2 and Table 12.1, single-voxel selection (pooling = "voxel") is unbiased on average but noisy (Active MAE = 1.085 s). Group-parcel pooling (pooling = "parcel") denoises aligned parcels (10 and 89) well, but averages the fast (2.8 s) and slow (6.8 s) domains inside Parcel 78 into a flat intermediate plateau (Shifted Parcel 78 MAE = 2.062 s). Bilateral geodesic graph pooling with parcel_boundary = "soft" achieves the lowest error globally (0.334 s) and inside shifted Parcel 78 (0.430 s), tracking the participant’s true \(y = -43\text{ mm}\) transition cleanly.



3. Bilateral REML Noise Smoothing at Pial-Vein Borders
In Step 1, temporal autocorrelation (\(\rho\)) and marginal innovation scale (\(\log\hat{\sigma}\)) vary sharply at tissue boundaries: pial surface veins and CSF-adjacent voxels exhibit strong physiological pulsation (\(\rho = 0.76\)), whereas interior gray matter is much whiter (\(\rho = 0.28\)). Pooling noise uniformly across whole Schaefer parcels contaminates interior gray matter with pial-rim autocorrelation (Figure 12.3, orange violins).
Under pooling = "graph", Step 1 applies an edge-preserving (bilateral) noise filter that multiplies cortical-sheet proximity weights by similarity in pilot autocorrelation and log noise scale \((\Delta\hat{\rho}, \Delta\log\hat{\sigma})\) before grouping voxels into up to max_noise_strata = 10L noise strata. High-\(\rho\) rim voxels borrow strength along the pial rim while deep gray-matter voxels pool with interior gray matter, cutting single-voxel \(\hat{\rho}\) RMSE nearly in half in both compartments without blurring the tissue boundary (Table 12.1).






Figure 12.3: Bilateral REML noise smoothing preserves the sharp boundary between pial-vein/CSF rim autocorrelation and interior gray matter.






4. Step 2 SNR-Stratified Deconvolution (lambda_mode = "auto")
In volumetric fMRI, most gray-matter voxels exhibit weak or zero task modulation for any specific contrast while focal task-engaged regions carry high out-of-sample task \(R^2\). A single global deconvolution penalty (lambda_mode = "global") is forced into an awkward compromise: low enough to avoid crushing active peaks, yet leaving high-frequency inverse-filter noise across thousands of silent background voxels.
deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(..., lambda_mode = "auto") addresses this by stratifying voxels into task-SNR tiers and enforcing that smoothing never increases as task SNR rises:

Cross-run significance gate: Out-of-sample Step 1 run \(p\)-values are combined via Fisher’s method and adjusted across voxels via Benjamini–Hochberg FDR. On pure-null maps (no voxels passing \(q \le 0.10\)), "auto" collapses safely to 1 global stratum.
Edge-preserving task-\(R^2\) tiers: When task signal is present, Step 1 task \(R^2\) is stabilized locally over the cortical graph, separating a quiet background tier (\(q > 0.20\), \(R^2_{\text{stab}} < 0.025\)) from ascending active task-SNR quantiles (max_lambda_strata = 4L).
Monotone smoothing across tiers: Each tier tunes \(\lambda\) on its relevant cross-validation objective (pure prewhitened GCV + background level stability in the quiet tier; modulation-transfer-guarded GCV in active tiers), and a monotone ordering constraint (weighted pool-adjacent-violators, PAVA) enforces \(\lambda_{\text{quiet}} \ge \lambda_{\text{low-SNR}} \ge \dots \ge \lambda_{\text{high-SNR}}\). Crucially, each voxel’s exact \(\lambda_v\) is carried forward into Steps 3 and 4.







Figure 12.4: Step 2 SNR-stratified GCV tuning assigns strong noise suppression to quiet cortex while preserving sharp phasic impulses in focal active cortex.

Stratified tuning suppresses continuous background standard deviation in null voxels from 2.786 (global \(\lambda\)) down to 0.930 while maintaining crisp neural spike recovery in the 30-voxel Right Insula hotspot (\(r =\) 0.247 with generating continuous impulses; Figure 12.4).



5. Step 3 Voxelwise Bilateral Graph-EB (tau2_shrinkage = "graph_eb")
In Step 3 (decon_epoch_regression()), GLS precision weights and ZCA trial whitening depend on partitioning total trial-to-trial variance into propagated observation-noise variance \(s_{\text{obs},u}^2\) (known analytically from the Step 1–2 operator) and latent biological trial-to-trial variance \(\tau_{\text{bio},u}^2\). At the single-voxel level with 50–80 trials, raw method-of-moments estimation \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{raw},u}^2 = \hat{\sigma}_{\text{tot},u}^2 - s_{\text{obs},u}^2\) has wide sampling variance, creating two simultaneous distortions when truncated at zero (\(\max(0, \hat{\tau}_{\text{raw},u}^2)\)):

Active-cortex zero-collapse: 34.2% of genuinely active voxels randomly draw \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{raw},u}^2 \le 0\) and collapse to \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2 = 0\), reducing trial weights to pure inverse-measurement-error weights.
Null-cortex truncation bias: Nearly half of true \(\tau_{\text{bio}}^2 = 0\) voxels draw positive noise fluctuations, inflating average null \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2\) above zero (0.156).
Meanwhile, global Empirical Bayes (tau2_shrinkage = "eb") pools all 6,655 voxels toward one whole-slab prior dominated by the 85% null background—leaving 35.1% active zero-collapse unaddressed while pulling the 30-voxel Right Insula hotspot downward relative to local bilateral pooling (hotspot mean \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2 =\) 0.602 vs. 0.800 under Graph-EB).

tau2_shrinkage = "graph_eb" (the automatic setting under tau2_shrinkage = "auto" whenever deconvolution carries a spatial graph or voxel_map coordinates in voxelwise mode) addresses all three issues:

Pre-truncation scale-free pooling: Shrinks the untruncated dimensionless ratio \(\hat{\theta}_u = \hat{\tau}_{\text{raw},u}^2 / s_{\text{obs},u}^2\) across concordant cortical neighbors before applying \(\max(0, \cdot)\)—allowing positive and negative estimation errors in null cortex to cancel symmetrically around zero while reducing active zero-collapse to 21.7%.
Discounting shared scanner noise between neighbors: Because adjacent voxels share correlated scanner innovations (noise_innovations), their squared trial errors also covary (\(\operatorname{Corr}(Z_u^2, Z_v^2) = \rho_{uv}^2\) under Gaussian errors, by Isserlis’ identity); discounting for \(\rho_{uv}^2\) prevents shared noise from being mistaken for independent spatial replication.
Edge-preserving border stopping & focal hotspot protection: Downweights neighbors whose pilot variance ratios or trial-residual patterns disagree across a functional border, and caps how far any individual voxel can be pulled toward its neighborhood prior at \(2.5\sigma_u\) (Efron–Morris limited-translation shrinkage) so isolated focal hotspots retain their true biological variance (0.800 in the Right Insula core; Figure 12.5). Residual error scales ([scale_unw, scale_pw, scale_gls]) are similarly stabilized across concordant neighbors (Empirical-Bayes variance moderation; Smyth, 2004) to boost \(t\)-statistic degrees of freedom without ever smoothing trial slopes \(\hat{\beta}_u\).







Figure 12.5: Step 3 voxelwise biological trial-variance recovery across raw MoM, global EB, and bilateral geodesic Graph-EB.

The results crystallize the practical modeling guidance:

When functional anatomy aligns with the parcellation (Parcels 10 & 89): Step 4 parcel aggregation pools continuous deconvolved time series across 154–341 voxels using cross-run precision weights while propagating spatial innovation correlation accurately—cutting slope RMSE more than \(3\times\) relative to single voxels and achieving 100% detection power, with clean cohort-level inference in Step 5 (mixed_by() + BY control; bold black parcel outlines in Figure 12.6, Panel 4).
When individual functional boundaries shift across a parcel (Parcel 78): Averaging the posterior negative-RPE sub-domain (\(\beta = -0.62\)) and anterior positive-RPE sub-domain (\(\beta = +0.62\)) inside Parcel 78 cancels the parcel slope to nearly zero. Voxelwise Graph-EB resolves both sub-domains cleanly on the cortical ribbon without blurring across the \(y = -43\text{ mm}\) border.
When an effect is restricted to a sub-parcel focal nucleus (Right Insula Parcel 155 core): Averaging 30 active hotspot voxels with 195 silent surround voxels dilutes the parcel slope by nearly \(85\%\). Voxelwise Graph-EB—protected by SNR-stratified Step 2 \(\lambda\) and Efron–Morris limited translation—preserves the focal hotspot amplitude and detects it reliably while keeping false positives controlled across the 55 null parcels.



Practical Defaults for Atlas-Free, Atlas-Carrying, and Dense Parcellations

Default pooling = "voxel" on atlas-free vs. atlas-carrying NIfTIs: On atlas-free NIfTI inputs (read_nifti_ts(..., atlas = NULL)), estimate_crossrun_hrf(ts, ...) keeps pooling = "voxel" as a single-voxel fit unless you opt into pooling = "graph", whereas Step 3 (decon_epoch_regression(..., tau2_shrinkage = "auto")) still builds the 26-connected cortical neighborhood graph automatically from decon$voxel_map to stabilize voxelwise trial variances ("graph_eb"). On atlas-carrying NIfTI inputs, default pooling = "voxel" retains individual HRFs for task-supported voxels (spatial_strength = 0), pools AR(\(p\)) noise within parcels, and uses the parcel HRF as a "fallback_parcel" reference on low-SNR voxels; setting pooling = "graph" upgrades both HRF evidence and REML noise to edge-preserving cortical-sheet pooling across all voxels.
Parcel-level Graph-EB across dense parcellations (Schaefer-400 / 1000): When aggregate_by_parcel = TRUE (parcel_groups = ...) and no parcel-level spatial_graph is supplied, tau2_shrinkage = "auto" resolves to "none" because standard coarse parcels already have high multi-voxel SNR. For fine-grained parcellations with many small parcels, set tau2_shrinkage = "graph_eb" explicitly so decon_epoch_regression() constructs a precision-weighted 3D parcel-centroid Euclidean graph from decon$voxel_map (or supply cortical-surface geodesic parcel distances via build_spatial_graph(parcel_dist_mat)).

title: Spatial Graph Pooling: Voxelwise and Parcel-Wise NIfTI Workflows
section: Mathematical Details
text:
Mathematical Details


Show mathematical formulation of bilateral geodesic graph pooling, SNR-stratified PAVA, and pre-truncation Graph-EB


1. Sparse Geodesic CSR Graph and Bilateral Step 1 Weights
Let \(G = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})\) denote the sparse compressed-sparse-row (CSR) neighborhood graph built by build_spatial_graph() with Gaussian bandwidth \(\sigma_d = \text{FWHM} / \sqrt{8 \ln 2}\) and cutoff radius \(r_{\max} = 2\sigma_d\) (capped at \(k_{\max} = 32\) nearest in-mask neighbors via 26-connected lattice Dijkstra distances \(d_{\text{geo}}(u, v)\)).
For held-out target run \(r\), let \(S_u^{(-r)} \in \mathbb{R}^K\) denote voxel \(u\)’s out-of-sample adjusted partial-\(R^2\) profile across the \(K\)-kernel physiological HRF manifold, and let \((\hat{\rho}_u^{(-r)}, \log\hat{\sigma}_u^{(-r)})\) denote its target-excluded pilot \(\text{AR}(1)\) parameters. Neighbor \(v \in \mathcal{N}(u)\) receives bilateral HRF pooling weight: \[
w_{uv}^{(-r)} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{d_{\text{geo}}(u,v)^2}{2\sigma_d^2}\right) \cdot \pi_{uv} \cdot \exp\!\left(-3.5\,\gamma\,\max(0, -\tilde{c}_{uv})^2\right)
\] where \(\tilde{c}_{uv} \in [-1, 1]\) is the Spearman-disattenuated cross-run candidate-profile correlation between \(u\) and \(v\), and the parcel boundary factor \(\pi_{uv}\) equals \(1\) when \(g_u = g_v\), \(0\) under parcel_boundary = "hard", and smoothly interpolates from parcel_cross_weight (\(w_{\times} = 0.35\)) toward \(1\) as positive concordance \(c_+ = \max(0, \tilde{c}_{uv})\) increases under parcel_boundary = "soft": \[
\pi_{uv}^{\text{soft}} = w_{\times} + (1 - w_{\times})\, c_+^2 \quad (g_u \neq g_v).
\] To calibrate out-of-sample signal gating against spatially correlated scanner innovations \(Z^{(-r)}\), csr_quad_cor_cpp() evaluates the exact quadratic spatial correlation inflation factor on the normalized graph weights \(\tilde{w}_{uv} = w_{uv}^{(-r)} / \sum_{v'} w_{uv'}^{(-r)}\) in \(O(m k_{\max}^2 V)\) time: \[
v_{\text{quad}, u}^{(-r)} = \sum_{a \in \mathcal{N}(u) \cup \{u\}} \sum_{b \in \mathcal{N}(u) \cup \{u\}} \tilde{w}_{ua}\,\tilde{w}_{ub}\,\widehat{\operatorname{Corr}}\!\left(z_a^{(-r)}, z_b^{(-r)}\right)^2,
\] scaling Stouffer–Cauchy combined run evidence by \((v_{\text{quad}, u}^{(-r)})^{-1/2}\).


2. Step 2 SNR-Stratified Regularization with Weighted PAVA
Let \(\tilde{R}_u^2\) be the graph-stabilized out-of-sample Step 1 task \(R^2\) and \(q_u\) the Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted Fisher combination \(p\)-value across runs. When \(\min_u q_u \le 0.10\), voxels are partitioned into a quiet background tier (\(q_u > 0.20\) and \(\tilde{R}_u^2 < 0.025\)) and up to \(M - 1\) ascending active SNR quantiles with unconstrained tier penalties \((\hat{\lambda}_1, \dots, \hat{\lambda}_M)\). Monotone non-increasing smoothness penalties \(\lambda_1^\star \ge \lambda_2^\star \ge \dots \ge \lambda_M^\star\) are obtained via weighted pool-adjacent-violators: \[
\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\star = \arg\min_{\lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_M} \sum_{m=1}^M n_m \left(\log \lambda_m - \log \hat{\lambda}_m\right)^2.
\]


3. Step 3 Pre-Truncation Bilateral Graph-EB with Isserlis Discount & Efron–Morris Guard
At lag \(\tau\), let \(\hat{\sigma}_{\text{tot}, u}^2\) be voxel \(u\)’s residual trial variance across \(N\) target trials (with effective residual degrees of freedom \(\nu_u\)) and \(s_{\text{obs}, u}^2\) its operator-propagated measurement-error variance. Define the untruncated dimensionless biological-to-measurement variance ratio: \[
\hat{\theta}_u = \frac{\hat{\tau}_{\text{raw}, u}^2}{s_{\text{obs}, u}^2} = \frac{\hat{\sigma}_{\text{tot}, u}^2 - s_{\text{obs}, u}^2}{s_{\text{obs}, u}^2}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta}_u) \approx v_u = \frac{2}{\nu_u}\bigl(1 + \max(0, \tilde{\theta}_u)\bigr)^2.
\] For bilateral edge weights \(\alpha_{uv}\) (combining geodesic Gaussian kernel, Cauchy pilot-jump factor \([1 + (\tilde{\theta}_u - \tilde{\theta}_v)^2 / s_0^2]^{-1}\), and orthogonalized trial-residual sign concordance), Gaussian innovations with spatial correlation \(\rho_{ab}\) obey Isserlis’ identity \(\operatorname{Corr}(Z_a^2, Z_b^2) = \rho_{ab}^2\). Accounting for self-weight \(\alpha_{uu}\) and neighbor error correlation yields the local prior mean \(\mu_{\text{loc}, u}\), prior variance \(\tau_{\text{prior}, u}^2\), shrinkage factor \(B_u = v_u / (v_u + \tau_{\text{prior}, u}^2)\), and Efron–Morris limited-translation posterior estimate (\(M_{\text{EM}} = 2.5\)): \[
\theta_u^{\text{raw-EB}} = (1 - B_u)\,\hat{\theta}_u + B_u\,\mu_{\text{loc}, u}, \qquad
\theta_u^{\text{EM}} = \hat{\theta}_u + \operatorname{clip}\!\left(\theta_u^{\text{raw-EB}} - \hat{\theta}_u,\; -M_{\text{EM}}\sqrt{v_u},\; +M_{\text{EM}}\sqrt{v_u}\right),
\] followed only at the end by non-negativity truncation \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}, u}^2 = s_{\text{obs}, u}^2 \max(0, \theta_u^{\text{EM}})\).
Compiled C++ and internal R kernels (src/spatial_graph_kernels.cpp, R/spatial_graph.R, R/crossrun_hrf.R): csr_hrf_graph_pool_cpp(), csr_bilateral_noise_smooth_cpp() (called by hrf_estimate_noise()), csr_quad_cor_cpp(), smooth_scalar_csr_cpp(), hrf_pava_nonincreasing(), graph_eb_tau2_csr_cpp(), and moderate_scale_csr_cpp().

title: Autocorrelation Prewhitening Under Fast-TR Event Designs
text:
Overview: Why Not Use Nonparametric Lag Tapering?
A natural question from investigators familiar with classical univariate fMRI packages—especially FSL’s FILM prewhitening (Woolrich et al., 2001)—is why estimate_crossrun_hrf() fits a two-pass parametric restricted-maximum-likelihood (REML) \(\text{AR}(p)\) cascade rather than tapering sample autocorrelations of ordinary least-squares (OLS) residuals with a Tukey cosine window.
At slow repetition times (\(\text{TR} = 2.5\text{--}3.0\text{ s}\)) under low-rank condition-averaged block or event GLMs, nonparametric residual lag tapering is simple and effective. In modern fast-TR (\(\text{TR} \le 1.0\text{ s}\)) single-trial analyses, however, two structural pressures arise simultaneously:
crumbs: 13  Autocorrelation Prewhitening Under Fast-TR Event Designs

title: Autocorrelation Prewhitening Under Fast-TR Event Designs
text:
Unmodeled neurovascular shape variation contaminates residual autocorrelation: If noise is estimated in a single pass under an assumed canonical HRF, any region with a faster or slower hemodynamic peak leaves systematic task-locked waves in the residuals—driving estimated \(\text{AR}(1)\) persistence \(\widehat{\rho}\) artificially toward its stationarity ceiling (0.90).
High-rank trial designs distort raw-residual autocorrelations: Projecting dozens of free per-trial predictors out of a 300–400-volume run induces substantial negative finite-sample projection bias in raw OLS sample autocorrelations (\(\operatorname{Cov}(r) = M_X \Sigma M_X^\top \neq \Sigma\)), which cosine lag tapering shrinks toward zero rather than debiasing.







NoteCore Methodological Question & Connection to the Pipeline



How can we separate regional HRF shape mismatch from genuine physiological autocorrelation—and keep both correlation shape \(\Sigma_{\text{cor}}\) and marginal observation scale \(\sigma_{\text{obs}}\) calibrated when propagating trial covariance \(\Omega_{r,\tau}\)?
This chapter provides the statistical rationale and empirical benchmarks behind Step 1 (estimate_crossrun_hrf()) and Step 2 (deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(..., scaling = "noise_sd")).

title: Autocorrelation Prewhitening Under Fast-TR Event Designs
section: 1. Revisiting Woolrich et al. (2001) in the Fast-TR Single-Trial Regime
text:
1. Revisiting Woolrich et al. (2001) in the Fast-TR Single-Trial Regime
Woolrich, Ripley, Brady, and Smith (2001) established three enduring principles for fMRI temporal noise modeling: (a) mean-model misspecification spills directly into apparent serial correlation, (b) noisy voxelwise autocorrelation estimates benefit substantially from local spatial regularization within tissue classes, and (c) prewhitening requires coherent variance and correlation structure. In FILM, sample residual autocorrelations \(\widehat{r}(\ell)\) are stabilized by multiplying lags \(0 \le \ell < M\) by a smooth Tukey cosine window:
\[
\widehat{r}_T(\ell) =
\begin{cases}
\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl\{1 + \cos(\pi \ell / M)\bigr\}\widehat{r}(\ell), & 0 \le \ell < M, \\
0, & \ell \ge M.
\end{cases}
\]
When translating that estimator from condition-level GLMs at \(\text{TR} = 3\text{ s}\) to trial-resolved deconvolution at \(\text{TR} = 0.65\text{--}1.0\text{ s}\), two physical and algebraic properties change:

Physical time span of a fixed lag window shrinks with TR: A window of \(M = 15\) lags spans \(45\text{ s}\) at \(\text{TR} = 3.0\text{ s}\), comfortably covering hemodynamic and Mayer-wave persistence, whereas the same 15 lags span less than \(10\text{ s}\) at \(\text{TR} = 0.65\text{ s}\). Widening \(M\) in volume units accumulates estimation variance across dozens of lag parameters.
Subspace projection bias scales with design rank: Let \(X_r\) collect the run’s free trial predictors and low-frequency drift basis, and let \(M_X = I - X_r(X_r^\top X_r)^{-1}X_r^\top\) denote the residual-forming projection matrix. Even under known true covariance \(\Sigma\), raw OLS residuals \(e_{\text{OLS}} = M_X y_r\) have covariance \(M_X \Sigma M_X^\top\) rather than \(\Sigma\). When \(X_r\) occupies 25–40 degrees of freedom per run, raw sample autocorrelations dip systematically negative at intermediate lags (visible in green in Figure 13.1, even on a pure null parcel with zero neural signal). Multiplying \(\widehat{r}(\ell)\) by a cosine taper dampens long lags without removing that negative subspace dip.

title: Autocorrelation Prewhitening Under Fast-TR Event Designs
section: 2. How MEDuSA Translates and Extends These Principles
text:
2. How MEDuSA Translates and Extends These Principles
Rather than tapering raw OLS residuals under a fixed canonical HRF, medusa separates neurovascular timing from serial correlation in two stages while accounting analytically for the residual subspace \(M_X\):



Noise-modeling principle
How medusa implements it
Why it matters downstream




Decouple HRF shape mismatch from residual persistence
Two-pass target-excluding REML refit in estimate_crossrun_hrf(): Pass 1 estimates preliminary whitening under a canonical HRF plus temporal derivatives; once each parcel’s HRF is learned out of sample from non-target runs \(s \ne r\), Pass 2 refits run \(r\)’s \(\text{AR}(p)\) noise model conditioned on the learned HRF while keeping HRF selection strictly frozen
Eliminates task-locked shape residuals in fast- or slow-HRF regions without circularity on the target run.


Account for high-rank trial projection loss
Profile REML \(\text{AR}(1)\) likelihood evaluated directly on the projected subspace \(M_X\), paired with projection-debiased residual \(\text{AR}(q)\) Yule–Walker refinement (up to cascaded \(\text{AR}(3)\))
Avoids the negative mid-lag autocorrelation dip induced by high-rank event designs while keeping the parameter count compact across TRs.


Share noise information spatially without cancelling signed signals
Pools REML log-likelihood profiles across voxels within anatomical parcels (pooling = "parcel") or local autocorrelation-concordant cortical neighborhoods (pooling = "graph") rather than averaging raw BOLD traces
Voxels with positive, negative, or null task responses contribute constructively to noise estimation while pial-rim pulsatility stays isolated from deep gray matter.


Keep correlation shape and marginal amplitude coherent
deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(..., scaling = "noise_sd") estimates outlier-trimmed, leverage-adjusted GLS innovation scale under the Pass-2 HRF and \(\text{AR}(p)\) model, converting innovation SD analytically into stationary marginal noise_sd (\(\sigma_{\text{obs}}\))
Prevents compensating errors between \(\sigma_{\text{obs}}^2\) and \(\Sigma_{\text{cor}}\) inside propagated trial covariance \(\Omega_{r,\tau} = \sigma_{\text{obs}}^2 B_{r,\tau}\Sigma_{\text{cor}}B_{r,\tau}^\top\).

section: 3. Benchmark 1: Recovering True Autocorrelation Under Vascular Heterogeneity
text:
3. Benchmark 1: Recovering True Autocorrelation Under Vascular Heterogeneity
To isolate these two mechanisms, consider the three-run fast-TR benchmark from Step 1 (\(R = 3\) runs, \(\text{TR} = 0.65\text{ s}\), \(T_r = 360\) volumes, 24 jittered events per run, and 8 voxels each in a Fast HRF parcel, a Slow HRF parcel, and a pure Null parcel, generated under cascaded \(\text{AR}(3)\) noise with \(\rho = 0.65, \psi_1 = 0.20, \psi_2 = -0.30\)). We compare four noise estimators on identical data:

Single-pass canonical HRF: Parametric REML \(\text{AR}(p)\) noise fit locked to a fixed canonical HRF with no post-selection refit.
Two-pass REML refit (medusa): estimate_crossrun_hrf(), refitting run \(r\)’s \(\text{AR}(p)\) cascade under the cross-run selected HRF.
Oracle generating HRF: Parametric REML \(\text{AR}(p)\) conditioned on the exact generating HRF of each parcel.
Raw-residual Tukey lag tapers (\(M \in \{10, 15, 28\}\)): Pooled cosine-tapered sample residual autocorrelations under either the canonical or cross-run selected HRF.

MEDuSA’s two-pass REML refit (blue dotted) tracks the generating covariance (black solid) across all three vascular regimes, whereas locking noise estimation to a single-pass canonical HRF (amber dashed) inflates apparent persistence whenever the true HRF is faster or slower, and raw-residual Tukey tapering (green dot-dash) dips negative from trial-design projection bias even in the Null parcel.



Two conclusions emerge directly from Table 13.1 and Figure 13.1:

Refitting noise under the cross-fitted HRF removes vascular spillover: Under a single-pass canonical HRF, unmodeled early or late BOLD lobes inflate apparent autocorrelation (RMSE = 0.260 in Fast, 0.314 in Slow). Refitting \(\text{AR}(p)\) parameters under the out-of-sample selected HRF reduces ACF RMSE more than thirtyfold to 0.006 and 0.008—matching the oracle-HRF benchmark (0.006 and 0.008) with zero target-run circularity.

section: 5. Implications for Applied MEDuSA Analyses
text:
5. Implications for Applied MEDuSA Analyses



Modeling choice
Recommended setting
Takeaway from this chapter




Spatial pooling of noise (pooling)
"parcel" for homogeneous ROIs; "graph" on volumetric cortical ribbons
When anatomical parcels straddle CSF/pial borders and deep gray matter, pooling = "graph" (Spatial Graph Pooling) weights local smoothing by autocorrelation concordance so vascular-rim pulsatility does not contaminate interior cortex (Olszowy et al., 2019; Parlak et al., 2023).


Autoregressive order (ar_order)
"auto" (cascaded up to \(\text{AR}(3)\))
Captures multiband serial correlation cleanly across \(\text{TR} \in [0.65, 2.0]\text{ s}\); for ultra-fast acquisitions (\(\text{TR} < 0.5\text{ s}\)), include physiological nuisance regressors (RETROICOR / aCompCor) alongside motion_bandstop_bpm.


Step 2 amplitude scaling (scaling)
"noise_sd" (paired with restore_scale = TRUE in Step 3)
Anchors continuous deconvolution penalties and Step 3/4 propagated covariances to the Pass-2 GLS marginal observation noise SD rather than task-inflated total run variance.


Cross-parcel noise vs. temporal whitening
Retain subject_epochs for Step 6 (shared_error = "auto")
Prewhitening within each parcel calibrates within-region \(\Omega_{gg}\), whereas cross-parcel shared noise \(\Omega_{ST}\) is captured separately via Step 2’s task-free noise_innovations (see Propagating BOLD Noise into Trial SEs).





Implementation Pointers & Reproduction

Inside medusa, the two-pass REML noise refit and covariance-consistent marginal noise scale are implemented in R/crossrun_hrf.R (estimate_crossrun_hrf(), fit_crossrun_decon(), hrf_estimate_noise(), hrf_estimate_gls_noise_sd()), with standalone second-difference fallback scaling in R/deconvolve_reglin.R (estimate_decon_noise_sd()).

title: Propagating BOLD Noise into Trial Standard Errors
text:
Overview: What Exactly Does se_demixed Measure?
When analysts inspect a Step 3 or Step 4 output panel (epochs$panel), every trial-by-parcel-by-lag row carries both a de-mixed neural estimate (decon_demixed) and an analytical standard error (se_demixed). Before using these quantities in multilevel outcome models (Step 5) or measurement-error-corrected connectivity models (Step 6), a foundational question arises:
How do we get an individual standard error for a single trial when that trial was never repeated—and how does se_demixed differ from a mixed-model slope SE or an Empirical-Bayes posterior SD?
In MEDuSA, se_demixed is the conditional measurement-error standard deviation of the linear estimator that maps a noisy BOLD run vector \(y_r\) onto trial \(i\)’s de-mixed readout \(\widehat{z}_{ri} = \theta_{ri} + e_{ri}\). Because continuous deconvolution (\(D_r\)), collateral event subtraction, target-trial demixing, and within-run centering compose into one explicit linear operator \(B_{r,\tau}\), any stationary observation noise covariance \(\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_r) = \sigma_{\text{obs}}^2 \Sigma_{\text{cor}}\) propagates algebraically from acquisition frames to trials:
\[
\underbrace{\sigma_{\text{obs}}^2 \Sigma_{\text{cor}}}_{\text{Run BOLD noise (Steps 1–2)}}
\ \longrightarrow\
\underbrace{\widehat{\Omega}_{r,\tau} = \operatorname{Cov}(e_{r,\tau} \mid B_{r,\tau})}_{\text{Centered trial error covariance (Steps 3–4)}}
\ \longrightarrow\
\underbrace{s_{ri} = \sqrt{[\widehat{\Omega}_{r,\tau}]_{ii}}}_{\text{`se_demixed`}}
\ \longrightarrow\
\underbrace{\Psi_i(s_{S,i}^2),\; c_i}_{\text{M-MOMS error moments (Step 6)}}.
\]

title: Propagating BOLD Noise into Trial Standard Errors
text:
NoteCore Methodological Question & Connection to the Pipeline



Why does Step 5 weight outcomes by \((\widehat{\tau}_{\text{eff}}^2 + s_{ri}^2)^{-1}\) (precision_weight_cohort), whereas Step 6 subtracts pure measurement variance \(s_{S,i}^2\) (se_demixed^2) inside \(\Psi_i\)—and why does run-centering introduce a \((1 - 1/m)^{-1}\) finite-sample factor?
This chapter traces the exact variance-propagation chain connecting Steps 1–2, Steps 3–4, and Step 6 (decon_connectivity_repair() / medusa_fit_mmom()).
crumbs: 14  Propagating BOLD Noise into Trial Standard Errors

title: Propagating BOLD Noise into Trial Standard Errors
section: 1. Anchor Run-Level Observation Noise Scale Prior to Trial Regression
text:
1. Anchor Run-Level Observation Noise Scale Prior to Trial Regression
For run \(r\) and a single voxel (or parcel stratum), recall the linear neurovascular forward model on retained acquisition frames:
\[
y_r = H_r a_r + Z_r \gamma_r + \varepsilon_r,
\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_r) = \sigma_{\text{obs}}^2 \Sigma_{\text{cor}},
\]
where \(H_r\) is causal Toeplitz convolution with the cross-fitted HRF, \(Z_r\) collects low-frequency drift and nuisance covariates, \(\Sigma_{\text{cor}}\) is the unit-diagonal temporal correlation matrix from Step 1’s two-pass REML \(\text{AR}(p)\) cascade (restricted to unmasked acquisition timestamps \(\Sigma_{\text{AR}}[I_r, I_r]\) whenever motion scrubbing creates gaps), and \(\sigma_{\text{obs}}\) is the marginal observation-noise standard deviation (not the white-noise innovation SD).
Estimating \(\sigma_{\text{obs}}\) accurately requires shielding the scale estimator from true task-evoked BOLD deflections and isolated motion glitches:

Primary cross-run estimator (deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(..., scaling = "noise_sd")): Conditions on Step 1’s cross-fitted HRF and Pass-2 \(\text{AR}(p)\) correlation matrix, projects out the event and nuisance subspace in whitened coordinates, computes outlier-trimmed (Winsorized), leverage-standardized GLS innovation scale, and converts innovation scale analytically into stationary marginal observation SD \(\widehat{\sigma}_{\text{obs}}\).
Standalone single-run and omitted-event safeguard (deconvolve_reglin()): When cross-run event designs are unavailable or degrees of freedom are low, MEDuSA estimates marginal noise SD from second differences \(d_t = y_t - 2y_{t-1} + y_{t-2}\), which annihilate smooth hemodynamic trends while combining sample SD with zero-centered median absolute deviation (\(\operatorname{MAD}_0\)), normalized analytically by lag-1 and lag-2 autocorrelations \((\widehat{r}_1, \widehat{r}_2)\):

\[
\widehat{\sigma}_{\text{obs}}
= \frac{0.5\,\operatorname{SD}(d) + 0.5\,\operatorname{MAD}_0(d)}
       {\sqrt{6 - 8\widehat{r}_1 + 2\widehat{r}_2}}.
\]
Crucially, both estimators determine \(\widehat{\sigma}_{\text{obs}}\) before any behavioral covariate or seed-parcel connectivity hypothesis is tested, avoiding circular variance tuning.
crumbs: 14  Propagating BOLD Noise into Trial Standard Errors

title: Propagating BOLD Noise into Trial Standard Errors
section: 2. Propagate Covariance Through Deconvolution, Demixing, and Run-Centering
text:
2. Propagate Covariance Through Deconvolution, Demixing, and Run-Centering
Conditioning on the learned HRF, smoothness penalty \(\lambda_v\), adaptive frame weights, nuisance projection, and \(\text{AR}(p)\) parameters, Step 2 deconvolution is an explicit linear map \(\widehat{a}_r = D_r \tilde{y}_{r,o}\). In Step 3 (decon_epoch_regression()), local kernel readout \(S_\tau\), non-target event subtraction, ridge-stabilized target-trial demixing \(W_\tau\), and diagonal gain restoration \(\tilde{G}_\tau\) compose with \(D_r\) into the run’s trial-readout operator \(B_{r,\tau}\). Applying the linear covariance law \(\operatorname{Cov}(Ay) = A\operatorname{Cov}(y)A^\top\) gives the uncentered \(m \times m\) trial error covariance across the \(m\) valid target trials of run \(r\):
\[
\Omega_{r,\tau,\text{raw}}
= \sigma_{\text{eff}}^2 \, \widetilde{B}_{r,\tau} \Sigma_{\text{cor}} \widetilde{B}_{r,\tau}^\top,
\]
where \(\widetilde{B}_{r,\tau}\) absorbs input run-centering and whitened nuisance projections. In our independent algebraic audit (worked/mmom-check.R), MEDuSA’s factored cascade propagation matches brute-force dense \(\text{AR}(3)\) Toeplitz matrix multiplication to 1.11e-16.

Why run-centering introduces \((1 - 1/m)^{-1}\)
Because BOLD runs lack an absolute baseline unit across scanner acquisitions, within-run trial regressions center trial vectors within each run using \(Q_m = I_m - \frac{1}{m}\mathbf{1}_m\mathbf{1}_m^\top\). Centering \(m\) noisy trial estimates subtracts the sample mean error \(\bar{e}_r = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^m e_{rj}\) from every trial. Even if uncentered errors had variance \(\sigma^2\), the expected squared centered error is \(\mathbb{E}[(e_{ri} - \bar{e}_r)^2] = \sigma^2(1 - 1/m)\), so sample inner products over centered trials lose one degree of freedom per run (just like Bessel’s \(n/(n-1)\) sample-variance correction). Dividing by \(1 - 1/m\) calibrates the centered covariance matrix so \(\sum_{i=1}^m [\widehat{\Omega}_{r,\tau}]_{ii}\) is an unbiased estimator of expected centered error sum of squares \(\mathbb{E}[\|Q_m e_r\|_2^2]\) in Step 6 normal equations:
\[
Q_m = I_m - \frac{\mathbf{1}_m\mathbf{1}_m^\top}{m},
\qquad
\widehat{\Omega}_{r,\tau} = \frac{Q_m \Omega_{r,\tau,\text{raw}} Q_m}{1 - 1/m},
\qquad
\boxed{\texttt{se\_demixed}_{ri} = \sqrt{\max\!\bigl(0,\, [\widehat{\Omega}_{r,\tau}]_{ii}\bigr)}}.
\]
Why do individual trials within the same run have different values of se_demixed? Three geometric factors enter \([\widehat{\Omega}_{r,\tau}]_{ii}\):

Temporal crowding: Closely spaced trials require stronger off-diagonal demixing weights in \(W_\tau\), amplifying propagated variance relative to well-isolated trials.
Motion-scrubbing shadows: Censored frames inside a trial’s causal HRF window reduce effective BOLD observations supporting that event, selectively elevating its diagonal entry (see Pair 3 in the Visual QC Gallery).
Run boundaries: Trials near scanner shutoff lose late HRF tail samples, increasing uncertainty smoothly before extreme truncation triggers min_bold_coverage NA gating.



Preserving scale equivalence and spatial parcel correlations
When Step 2 standardizes series by \(\widehat{\sigma}_{\text{obs}}\) (scaling = "noise_sd"), setting restore_scale = TRUE in Step 3 multiplies both decon_demixed and se_demixed back by \(\widehat{\sigma}_{\text{obs}}\) so every run of a parcel shares physical BOLD units. More generally, rescaling any neural variable by a constant \(c\) rescales its SE by \(|c|\) and its error variance by \(c^2\).
When voxels are aggregated into anatomical parcels in Step 4 (parcel_groups), summing voxel variances naively would underestimate parcel noise because neighboring voxels share physiological and thermal fluctuations. MEDuSA instead propagates Step 2’s task-free whitened noise_innovations through each voxel’s operator stratum to compute exact spatial noise covariance within each parcel, while storing low-rank cross-parcel innovation vectors (shared_noise_loading and unit_error_cor) for Step 6.

title: Propagating BOLD Noise into Trial Standard Errors
section: 3. Matching Exported Variance Quantities to Downstream Models
text:
3. Matching Exported Variance Quantities to Downstream Models
A frequent source of confusion in two-stage neuroimaging workflows is mixing up pure measurement-error variance, biological trial-to-trial variance, and composite total variance. Table 14.1 maps each exported Step 4 panel field to its exact downstream role:



Table 14.1: Mapping exported Step 3–4 variance and weight columns to their structural role in Steps 5 and 6.





Exported field
Mathematical definition
Correct downstream role




se_demixed^2 (\(s_{ri}^2\))
\([\widehat{\Omega}_{r,\tau}]_{ii}\), pure conditional BOLD-noise variance on trial \(i\)

se_whitened^2
Transformed error variance of ZCA-decorrelated decon_demixed_whitened
Diagnostic variance of within-run whitened Step 5 series (use_whitened = TRUE)







Constructing \(\Psi_i\) and calling medusa_fit_mmom() directly for Behavior ~ Neural
When testing parcel-to-parcel connectivity or PPI (Target ~ Seed * Task), decon_connectivity_repair() builds the \(3 \times 3\) trial error block \(\Psi_i\) automatically:
\[
\Psi_i = s_{S,i}^2
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & x_i \\
0 & 0 & 0 \\
x_i & 0 & x_i^2
\end{bmatrix},
\]
capturing both heteroskedastic interaction noise \(x_i^2 s_{S,i}^2\) and the off-diagonal covariance \(x_i s_{S,i}^2\) induced because Seed and Seed:x share the same noisy neural realization \(u_i\).
What if your scientific question instead places deconvolved neural activity on the right-hand side to predict a trial-level behavioral outcome—such as log reaction time, continuous confidence ratings, or drift-diffusion boundary shifts (Behavior ~ Neural + Task)? Because behavioral outcomes do not carry fMRI scanner noise (err_y = 0, err_xy = 0), you can call medusa_fit_mmom() directly per participant using se_demixed^2:


Show supporting code
library(medusa)
set.seed(20261110)
n <- 300L
theta_neural <- rnorm(n)
task_cov <- rnorm(n)
se_trial <- runif(n, 0.30, 0.70)
trial_df <- data.frame(
  decon_demixed = theta_neural + rnorm(n, sd = se_trial),
  se_demixed    = se_trial,
  task          = task_cov,
  rt_z          = 0.60 * theta_neural + 0.25 * task_cov + rnorm(n, sd = 0.80)
)



X <- cbind(neural = trial_df$decon_demixed, task = trial_df$task)
Psi <- array(0, dim = c(ncol(X), ncol(X), nrow(X)))
Psi[1, 1, ] <- trial_df$se_demixed^2   # neural predictor error variance; task is error-free (0)

fit <- medusa_fit_mmom(
  outcome        = trial_df$rt_z,
  predictors     = X,
  err_x          = Psi,                # q x q x N predictor error covariance array
  err_y          = rep(0, nrow(X)),    # error-free behavioral outcome
  regularization = "step_up"           # M-MOMS conditioning protection
)

title: Propagating BOLD Noise into Trial Standard Errors
section: 4. Scope Conditions and What se_demixed Does Not Capture
text:
4. Scope Conditions and What se_demixed Does Not Capture

Distribution-free second moments vs. plug-in conditioning: Conditional on the linear operator \(B_{r,\tau}\) and noise covariance \(\Sigma_r\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(B_{r,\tau}\varepsilon_r) = B_{r,\tau}\Sigma_r B_{r,\tau}^\top\) holds for any zero-mean noise process with finite variance (Winsorized/MAD scale factors calibrate efficiency under Gaussian innovations). Like REPAIR (Vig & Hallquist, 2026), downstream Step 5–6 estimators treat first-stage se_demixed^2 as known plug-in variances and anchor group uncertainty to between-participant dispersion.
Observation noise vs. unequal source resolution: se_demixed^2 measures random scatter \(B_{r,\tau}\Sigma_r B_{r,\tau}^\top\) around \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat{z} \mid \theta] = K\theta\), not deterministic resolution mismatch \((K - I)\theta\) when strong smoothing or severe HRF mis-specification leaves \(K_S \neq K_T\). How unequal resolution and cross-trial error correlations behave—and how extended measurement models address them—is examined in Latent Connectivity Beyond Per-Trial Disattenuation.



Implementation Pointers & Numerical Verification

title: Simultaneous Bands and Familywise Calibration Across Lags
text:
Overview: Two Distinct Multiplicity Families—and Two Finite-Sample Stressors
When an investigator plots a peri-event neural regression curve across 6–12 lags in Step 5 (medusa_multilag_infer()), reviewers routinely raise two sharp inferential questions:
crumbs: 15  Simultaneous Bands and Familywise Calibration Across Lags

title: Simultaneous Bands and Familywise Calibration Across Lags
text:
Finite-sample and missing-edge calibration: In cohorts of \(S = 15\text{--}30\) participants where trial residuals correlate serially within runs and several participants lose late epoch lags to motion scrubbing or run-end truncation, do simultaneous Max-|T| confidence bands, 1D threshold-free cluster enhancement (1D TFCE), and planned window contrasts actually achieve nominal 5% false-positive rates and 95% simultaneous coverage?
Trajectory-wide vs. study-wide multiplicity: If p_maxT and p_tfce already control familywise error across all lags of a trajectory, what additional adjustment is needed when testing dozens or hundreds of cortical parcels?







NoteCore Methodological Question & Connection to the Pipeline



How does medusa_multilag_infer() calibrate simultaneous bands across correlated lags with missing participant edges—and where does within-trajectory familywise control end and multi-parcel multiplicity begin?
This chapter provides the mathematical mechanism and 180-cohort Monte Carlo stress benchmarks underlying Step 5 Substeps 5.3–5.4 (medusa_multilag_infer()).
crumbs: 15  Simultaneous Bands and Familywise Calibration Across Lags

title: Simultaneous Bands and Familywise Calibration Across Lags
section: 1. Why Naive Trajectory Bands Undercover—and How MEDuSA Repairs Them
text:
1. Why Naive Trajectory Bands Undercover—and How MEDuSA Repairs Them
Suppose we estimate population regression slopes \(\widehat{\beta} = (\widehat{\beta}_1, \dots, \widehat{\beta}_L)^\top\) across \(L\) peri-event lags for a single (parcel, term) pair across \(S\) participants. Even when true neural slopes are zero everywhere (\(\beta = 0\)), adjacent lags share strong positive correlation from hemodynamic overlap and smooth underlying activity. Three statistical subtleties govern finite-sample calibration:

Uncertainty in the \(L \times L\) cross-lag covariance matrix: If we knew the exact population covariance \(V_\beta\) of \(\widehat{\beta}\), simulating Gaussian draws \(z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, R_\beta)\) would yield exact simultaneous critical values \(c_{0.95}\) for \(\max_\ell |T_\ell|\). With \(S = 20\) participants, however, \(\widehat{V}_\beta\) is itself estimated with \(S - 1\) degrees of freedom; plugging \(\widehat{V}_\beta\) into Gaussian draws ignores denominator variance uncertainty and produces anti-conservative bands. medusa_multilag_infer() instead generates studentized Wishart null draws that account jointly for cross-lag correlation and finite-participant covariance uncertainty.
Available-case cross-lag pooling when edge lags drop out: In real task runs, final trials or motion-censored blocks occasionally leave a participant with zero valid observations at an outer lag (e.g., +4 s) while interior lags (-1..3 s) remain intact. Dropping the entire participant listwise wastes interior precision, whereas ignoring unequal sample sizes distorts cross-lag off-diagonals. medusa_multilag_infer() pools pairwise overlapping participant sets across lags with positive-semidefinite projection so interior lags retain all \(S\) participants while edge lags reflect exact effective \(n_\ell\).
Evaluating planned window contrasts prior to P-spline smoothing (contrast_source = "unsmoothed"): Penalized splines borrow strength across neighboring lags to visualize smooth trajectories, which slightly shrinks sharp transitions between early and late windows. Computing linear contrast vectors \(w^\top \widehat{\beta}\) and \(\sqrt{w^\top \widehat{V}_\beta w}\) directly on the unsmoothed lag vector preserves unbiased window differences and exact \(t\)-interval coverage.
crumbs: 15  Simultaneous Bands and Familywise Calibration Across Lags

title: Simultaneous Bands and Familywise Calibration Across Lags
section: 2. Stress-Test Design: Complete vs. Serially Dependent Gapped Cohorts
text:
2. Stress-Test Design: Complete vs. Serially Dependent Gapped Cohorts
To evaluate these mechanisms where their assumptions are actively stressed, each Monte Carlo replication simulates \(S = 20\) participants, \(R = 2\) runs per participant (\(20\) trials/run, jittered \(3\text{--}9\text{ s}\) ISIs), \(L = 6\) peri-event lags (-1 to 4 s), 1 active parcel (Signal, true lag profile (0, 0.06, 0.22, 0.26, 0.19, 0.08)), and 2 null parcels (Null A and Null B, true profile 0 at every lag):

Realistic heteroskedasticity and spatial/lag correlation: Run 2 carries \(1.6\times\) the residual SD of Run 1 (precision_weight downweights Run 2 accordingly); residuals share cross-parcel noise (\(r = 0.55\)) and Toeplitz cross-lag correlation (\(0.65^{|\ell - \ell'|}\)); and every parcel includes true between-participant random slope heterogeneity (\(\text{SD} = 0.13\)).
Two benchmark regimes (180 independent cohorts each):

Complete / independent trials: Full lag support (-1..4 s) in all 20 participants with independent trial innovations within each run.
Gaps / serially dependent trials: Introduces strong within-run \(\text{AR}(1)\) serial autocorrelation in both behavioral predictors (\(\rho_x = 0.65\)) and trial neural errors (\(\rho_e = 0.62\)), censors interior trial bursts (4 of 20 trials per run), and censors the final edge lag (+4 s) completely in 3 of the 20 participants (17 participants at lag +4 s, 20 participants at lags -1..3 s).

Evaluated estimands: Each replicate runs medusa_multilag_infer() (trajectory_mode = "none", contrast_source = "unsmoothed", n_perm = 799 studentized Wishart draws) and evaluates both single-trajectory error/coverage (Null A and Signal) and study-family error across all three parcels (Signal, Null A, Null B), alongside a planned late_minus_early contrast ([3, 4] s minus [0, 1] s, true difference \(+0.005\)).

(Note scope isolation: this benchmark begins at the participant panel to isolate cross-lag covariance estimation, available-case edge pooling, and multiplicity control under known lag structure; full BOLD-to-panel pipeline benchmarks are synthesized in What Validation Proves.)

Three practical lessons stand out across Table 15.1, Figure 15.1, and Figure 16.2:

Within-trajectory tests remain calibrated under serial dependence and missing participant edges: Studentized Wishart draws hold single-trajectory false positives near 5% in complete cohorts (3.9% for Max-|T|, 5.0% for 1D TFCE, 2.8% for Omnibus) and remain well controlled when trials correlate serially and 15% of participants lose the final edge lag (7.2%, 6.1%, and 2.8%; every 95% Monte Carlo interval spans 5%).
Simultaneous bands and unsmoothed window contrasts hit 95% nominal coverage: Across all 6 lags jointly, conf.low.sim–conf.high.sim encloses the entire true population trajectory in 96.1%–95.0% of complete cohorts and 92.8%–96.7% of gapped/serial cohorts. Likewise, the unsmoothed [3, 4] - [0, 1] s contrast covers the true window difference in 95.6% and 97.8% of cohorts with near-zero bias (+0.005 and +0.002).
Why within-trajectory FWER does not replace cross-parcel multiplicity control: p_maxT and p_tfce control FWER across lags within one (parcel, term) curve. When screening \(P\) parcels simultaneously, unadjusted 5% trajectory tests still accumulate false positives across null regions (\(1 - 0.95^{P_0}\)); applying Holm (p.adjust(omnibus_p, "holm")) or Benjamini–Yekutieli ("BY") across the planned parcel family keeps study-wide discoveries calibrated (1.7% and 1.7% across the 3-parcel benchmark, where Signal is active and 2 of 3 parcels are null).

title: Latent Connectivity Beyond Per-Trial Disattenuation
text:
Overview: Where Does Per-Trial M-MOMS Succeed, and Where Are Its Boundaries?
In Step 6 (decon_connectivity_repair()), MEDuSA adapts the REPAIR measurement-error framework (Vig & Hallquist, 2026; Fuller, 1987) to trial-level functional connectivity and psychophysiological interaction (PPI): it subtracts per-trial seed measurement variance (se_demixed^2) from \(X^\top X\), subtracts task-free cross-parcel error covariance (shared_error = "auto") from \(X^\top Y\), guards against ill-conditioned denominators via step-up regularization (method = "mmoms"), and pools participant slopes using finite-sample Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman (HKSJ) \(t\)-intervals.
A mathematically minded colleague or reviewer may push one layer deeper: Per-trial M-MOMS treats each trial’s measurement error as additive around an unblurred latent truth (\(\mathbb{E}[\widehat{z} \mid \theta] = \theta\)). What happens in extreme fMRI regimes where (1) seed and target parcels undergo unequal temporal smoothing (\(K_S \neq K_T\)), (2) observation errors correlate across consecutive trials (\(\Omega_{SS}, \Omega_{ST}\) non-diagonal), or (3) sample sizes drop to \(S = 12\) participants?

title: Latent Connectivity Beyond Per-Trial Disattenuation
text:
NoteCore Methodological Question & Connection to the Pipeline



What are the exact mathematical conditions required for unbiased, nominal-coverage latent connectivity and PPI inference—and how do those conditions explain both Step 6’s design choices (shared_error = "auto", use_whitened = FALSE, HKSJ pooling) and its scope limits?
This chapter develops the full cross-trial measurement-error theory extending Step 6 (decon_connectivity_repair()) and tests three frontier measurement models across 400-replicate paired stress simulations.
crumbs: 16  Latent Connectivity Beyond Per-Trial Disattenuation

title: Latent Connectivity Beyond Per-Trial Disattenuation
section: 1. The Full Trial-Vector Measurement Interface
text:
1. The Full Trial-Vector Measurement Interface
For participant \(s \in \{1, \dots, S\}\) and trial \(i \in \{1, \dots, m_s\}\), recall the latent within-person connectivity and PPI structural equation from Step 6 with centered task modulator \(x_{si}\):
\[
\theta_{T,si} = \alpha_s + \beta_S \theta_{S,si} + \beta_x x_{si} + \beta_P (x_{si}\theta_{S,si}) + \eta_{si},
\]
where \(\beta_S\) is baseline seed–target coupling at \(x_{si} = 0\), \(\beta_x\) absorbs direct task activation in the target region (Cole et al., 2019), and \(\beta_P\) is task-modulated PPI coupling.
Stacking all \(m_s\) trials of participant \(s\) into column vectors reveals the complete linear measurement relationship produced by deconvolution and epoch readout:
\[
\begin{bmatrix} \widehat{z}_{S,s} \\ \widehat{z}_{T,s} \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} K_{S,s} & 0 \\ 0 & K_{T,s} \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} \theta_{S,s} \\ \theta_{T,s} \end{bmatrix}
+
\begin{bmatrix} u_s \\ v_s \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}\!\begin{pmatrix} u_s \\ v_s \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\Omega_{SS,s} & \Omega_{ST,s} \\
\Omega_{ST,s}^\top & \Omega_{TT,s}
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Writing the interface in block matrix form makes three structural properties transparent at a glance:

Mean resolution (\(K_{S,s}, K_{T,s}\)) vs. noise covariance (\(\Omega\)): Subtracting error variances \(\Omega_{SS,s}\) and \(\Omega_{ST,s}\) removes bias caused by random observation noise \((u_s, v_s)\), which yields exact consistency whenever Step 3 demixing restores \(K_{S,s} \approx I\) and \(K_{T,s} \approx I\). If strong regularization or unmodeled HRF mismatch leaves \(K_{S,s} \neq K_{T,s}\) (for instance, a heavily smoothed low-SNR seed predicting a sharp high-SNR target), variance subtraction alone cannot undo the mismatch in deterministic resolution.
Non-commutativity of smoothing/whitening and PPI products: Notice that multiplying a linearly transformed seed vector \(K \theta_S\) elementwise by the task vector \(x\) is not equal to transforming the latent interaction \(\operatorname{diag}(x)\theta_S\): \[
K\,\operatorname{diag}(x)\theta_S \neq \operatorname{diag}(x)\,K\theta_S.
\] The exact same non-commutativity applies to separate parcel ZCA whitening matrices (\(T_S \neq T_T\)), which is why decon_connectivity_repair() defaults to use_whitened = FALSE so Seed, Target, and Seed:x remain in matched run-centered trial coordinates.
Trial-level vs. participant-level inference units: Even after unbiased moment subtraction within each participant, off-diagonal serial entries in \(\Omega_{SS,s}\) and \(\Omega_{TT,s}\) make trial-level score contributions correlated within a scan. Treating pooled rows as independent understates uncertainty, whereas clustering or pooling at the participant level respects the true independent sampling unit.
crumbs: 16  Latent Connectivity Beyond Per-Trial Disattenuation

title: Latent Connectivity Beyond Per-Trial Disattenuation
section: 2. Three Exact Routes When Moving Beyond Diagonal Per-Trial M-MOMS
text:
2. Three Exact Routes When Moving Beyond Diagonal Per-Trial M-MOMS
When rapid event schedules or low regional SNR push \(K_S\) and \(K_T\) away from the identity matrix, three principled measurement models characterize what can and cannot be recovered:

Route A: Unpenalized likelihood-only readouts in a full-rank trial basis
Suppose each parcel \(g\)’s run BOLD vector follows a finite \(m\)-trial forward design \(y_g = G_g \theta_g + Z_g \gamma_g + \varepsilon_g\) under its cross-fitted HRF, and the trial spacing keeps \(G_g\) full column rank. Fitting unpenalized generalized least squares in whitened coordinates yields linear trial readouts \(\widehat{z}_g = B_g y_g\) satisfying exact identity resolution:
\[
B_g G_g = I_m
\quad \Longrightarrow \quad
\mathbb{E}(\widehat{z}_g \mid \theta_g) = \theta_g,
\qquad \Omega_{gg} = B_g \Sigma_g B_g^\top,
\qquad \Omega_{ST} = B_S \Sigma_{\varepsilon_S, \varepsilon_T} B_T^\top.
\]
This route is the exact fMRI analog of REPAIR’s likelihood-only OLS stage-1 score reconstruction (Vig & Hallquist, 2026; Abdulrahman & Henson, 2016). In our numerical verification (likelihood_only_bridge.R: 16 events over 180 volumes, distinct regional HRFs, shared serial \(\text{AR}\) noise), \(B_g G_g = I\) holds to 8.88e-16, and a 10,000-draw Monte Carlo audit matches analytical trial SDs within 1.5%. Its practical boundary is collinearity: at sub-2-second jitter or when unmodeled sustained intervals occur between events, unpenalized \(G_g\) becomes ill-conditioned—motivating Step 2–3’s mildly regularized demixing (\(K_g \approx I\)).


Route B: Subspace de-penalization on identifiable contrasts
In continuous TR-grid deconvolution (\(T_r = 180\) latent timepoints), a Bayesian/penalized posterior precision takes the form \(C_{\text{post}}^{-1} = J + P_{\text{prior}}\). Can we subtract \(P_{\text{prior}}\) globally on the TR grid? No: in likelihood_only_bridge.R, the 180-column Toeplitz convolution operator has numerical rank 178 because the HRF acts as a low-pass filter. Unshrinking is mathematically well-posed only after projecting onto lower-dimensional trial or window subspaces where Fisher information \(J\) is nonsingular—precisely what Step 3’s target demixing operator \(W_\tau\) performs at target event times.


Route C: Retaining \(K_S\) and \(K_T\) explicitly in a joint latent Gaussian model
When regional SNR is so low that any inverse \((K_S)^{-1}\) explodes variance, \(K_S\) and \(K_T\) can instead be kept forward inside a joint Gaussian marginal likelihood over \((\widehat{z}_{S,s}, \widehat{z}_{T,s}) \mid x_s\). In joint_gaussian_demo.R under deliberately mismatched resolution (\(K_S \neq K_T\)) and known \(\Omega\), joint maximum likelihood recovers connectivity 0.507 (truth 0.550) and PPI 0.336 (truth 0.350), trading parametric Gaussian latent priors and numerical optimization for exact resolution invariance.


Gaussian conditional-expectation calibration note

If one substitutes Empirical-Bayes shrunken seed predictions \(m_S = \mathbb{E}(\theta_S \mid \widehat{z}_S, x)\) into a target regression (eb_predictor intuition), non-identity target resolution \(K_T\) and shared cross-parcel error \(\Omega_{TS}\) require transformed regressors \(K_T m_S\) and \(K_T\operatorname{diag}(x)m_S\) (not \(\operatorname{diag}(x)K_T m_S\)) together with an explicit shared-noise control term \(\Omega_{TS}(K_S V_S K_S^\top + \Omega_{SS})^{-1}(\widehat{z}_S - K_S \mu_S)\).

title: Latent Connectivity Beyond Per-Trial Disattenuation
section: 3. Full Cross-Trial Corrected-Score Estimating Equations
text:
3. Full Cross-Trial Corrected-Score Estimating Equations
When source resolution is approximately unbiased (\(K_S \approx K_T \approx I\)) while trial errors correlate serially across adjacent events (\(\Omega_{SS,s}, \Omega_{ST,s}\) non-diagonal), we can generalize per-trial M-MOM to a full cross-trial corrected score (Nakamura, 1990; Buonaccorsi, 1996). Letting \(\widehat{X}_s = X_s + U_s\) collect participant \(s\)’s centered [Seed, x, Seed:x] matrix and setting \(\Psi_s = \mathbb{E}(U_s^\top U_s \mid x_s)\) and \(c_s = \mathbb{E}(U_s^\top v_s \mid x_s)\) from the full \(m_s \times m_s\) matrices \((\Omega_{SS,s}, \Omega_{ST,s})\), each participant contributes a zero-mean estimating equation:
\[
q_s(\beta) = \widehat{X}_s^\top \widehat{z}_{T,s} - c_s - \bigl(\widehat{X}_s^\top \widehat{X}_s - \Psi_s\bigr)\beta,
\qquad \sum_{s=1}^S q_s(\widehat{\beta}) = 0,
\]
with participant-cluster sandwich covariance:
\[
\widehat{V}_{\text{cluster}} = H^{-1}\left[\frac{S}{S - 1}\sum_{s=1}^S q_s(\widehat{\beta}) q_s(\widehat{\beta})^\top\right]H^{-\top},
\qquad H = \sum_{s=1}^S \bigl(\widehat{X}_s^\top \widehat{X}_s - \Psi_s\bigr).
\]

4. Stress-Test Benchmarks: Shared Noise, Serial Errors, Unequal \(K\), and Small \(S\)
To see exactly what each modeling ingredient buys—and what fails when an ingredient is omitted—we evaluate 400 paired Monte Carlo cohorts per scenario (\(S = 60\) participants, or \(S = 12\) in Few participants; 24 trials/participant; true \(\beta_S = 0.55\), \(\beta_x = 0.25\), \(\beta_P = 0.35\), or \(\beta_S = \beta_P = 0\) under Null; serial trial error correlation \(0.55\); shared cross-parcel error correlation \(0.45\), under both Gaussian and heavy-tailed \(t_5\) errors):






Figure 16.1: Mean coefficient bias across three stress regimes (Shared / serial Gaussian, Shared / serial t5, and Different resolution where \(K_S \neq K_T\)). Horizontal intervals show \(\pm 1.96\) Monte Carlo SEs. Subtracting full cross-trial and cross-parcel error moments eliminates bias under both Gaussian and heavy-tailed \(t_5\) serial/shared noise, whereas unequal deterministic resolution (\(K_S \neq K_T\)) requires inverting or modeling \(K\) (Undo K + full).









Figure 16.2: Empirical coverage of nominal 95% confidence intervals across the same three stress regimes (exact Clopper–Pearson 95% intervals around empirical coverage; dashed vertical line marks 95%). Notice that under serial trial errors, row-level SEs (Full + row SE) undercover on main connectivity even when point estimates are unbiased, whereas participant-cluster SEs (Full + cluster SE) achieve 95% coverage.

title: Latent Connectivity Beyond Per-Trial Disattenuation
section: 5. Implications for Applied Step 6 Connectivity Analyses
text:
5. Implications for Applied Step 6 Connectivity Analyses
Every result in Figure 16.1, Figure 16.2, and Table 16.1 explains a specific design rule in decon_connectivity_repair():

Why shared_error = "auto" (poet_covreg) is essential (never strip cross-parcel noise metadata): In Figure 16.1 (Shared / serial Gaussian and t5), subtracting seed variance without subtracting shared seed–target error covariance (No shared error and Diagonal moments) severely over-estimates main connectivity, and under Null serial + shared falsely rejects the null in 95.0% of cohorts—compared with 5.0% once \(\Omega_{ST}\) is subtracted. Under shared_error_method = "poet_covreg" (default in decon_epoch_regression()), MEDuSA estimates both stationary Adaptive-POET + multi-lag Toeplitz error correlations and LTZ-gated dynamic covariance-regression envelopes (across task drive, covariates, Step-2 rwls, and variance_confounds), embedding Block-PAF vectors (shared_noise_vec, lag_noise_vec, trial_cor_vec) onto panel so subject_epochs, .rds/Parquet panels, and pipe-delimited CSV exports via medusa_write_table() all retain full cross-parcel error parity.
Why decon_connectivity_repair() combines crosstrial_se = TRUE within subjects with HKSJ \(t\)-intervals across subjects: In Figure 16.2, treating correlated trials as independent rows (Full + row SE) drops connectivity coverage to 86.0%, while participant-cluster SEs restore 94.8% at \(S = 60\)—yet asymptotic normal cluster \(z\)-intervals still drop to 91.8% at \(S = 12\) (MacKinnon, Nielsen & Webb, 2022). In decon_connectivity_repair(), crosstrial_se = TRUE (default) evaluates a hybrid operator + gated onset-kernel cross-trial (\(i \neq j\)) sandwich covariance with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom within each participant (giving calibrated single-subject \(N = 1\) inference under rapid ITIs), and when \(S \ge 2\), HKSJ random-effects pooling anchors cohort degrees of freedom to \(S - 1\) even in modest neuroimaging samples.
Why seed and target smoothing policies should match (\(K_S \approx K_T\)): Under Different resolution, variance disattenuation alone overshoots connectivity (0.767 vs. truth 0.550), whereas inverting well-conditioned resolution operators (Undo K + full) restores 0.551. In empirical studies, keep Step 2–3 regularization and demixing settings matched across seed and target parcels (demix_target_trials = TRUE, use_whitened = FALSE) and inspect diagnose_crossrun_recovery() self-gain in both regions before interpreting asymmetric seed–target slopes.

title: What Validation Proves—and Building Study-Specific Checks
text:
Overview: Why No Single Simulation Answers Every Empirical Question
Across the stepwise tutorials (Part II), spatial workflows (Part III), and methodological deep dives (Part IV), every core component of medusa is paired with numerical checks and Monte Carlo simulations. A thoughtful investigator or peer reviewer should still ask a sharper meta-question:
Which properties of MEDuSA are guaranteed by linear algebra, which depend on empirical regularity conditions tested in Monte Carlo benchmarks, and how can I verify that my own study’s event schedule, motion censoring, and sample size support calibrated inference before testing substantive hypotheses?

Where do general package benchmarks end and study-specific design geometry begin—and how do you turn an empirical events table and valid_rows mask from Step 0 into a custom end-to-end calibration check?
This capstone chapter synthesizes the evidence across all four Part IV deep dives and the 14-Study Validation Suite, then provides a compact R template for study-specific synthetic calibration.
